en: *Zhengyuan Lueji*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇas (Bǎolún, Jìyuán, Gāomín, Liǎozhēn) of Wéiyáng;
edited by Dázhēn of Guīqīng, Tiantái.
The Dharma heirs of National Teacher Tianyin Xiu of Qingshan, the thirty-fourth generation under Mount Nanyue (five persons):
Chan Master Jingao Benyu of Jia Shan in Jingkou, whose late style name was Huifu. He was the son of the Chen family of Kunshan. At ten [years of age]...

9. He left the white robes [to become a monk] at Yao Peak in Gusu. While reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, upon reaching the line "one should give rise to the mind where there is nothing on which it dwells," he had an awakening.
When he first went to visit Boshan, Boshan said, "Before entering the golden cage, whose wild bird is this?
The Master replied, "A crane soars through the azure heavens from the Nine Curves; a horse that lacks a thousand-li stride does not chase the wind. Boshan said, "To move..."
The hatchet is not from Ying, yet it cannot avoid leaving scars. The Master said, "As for those in various quarters who raise their fly-whisks and lift their eyebrows, what kind of matter is that?
The monk replied, "A single cloud spans the seas and mountains; the woodcutters all think of returning home.
The Master said, "It is no wonder the tiger beneath the cliff suddenly startles people in the dark. Later, he went to visit Master Miyun Wu. It was already late that day, so he immediately asked:

When the Master was staying overnight with someone, he asked, "How about here? Wuzhun said, "One cannot rest here. The Master said, "Is there no expedient means? Wuzhun picked up his staff; the Master seized it and gave him a shove, saying, "I have seen through you!

He then departed. Later, he went to visit Master Xiu of Qingshan. Xiu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "Wulin. Xiu said, "How do you know about this place of mine? The Master said: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly after the Master's response.

The full dialogue continues with Xiu asking, "What is the meaning of 'How do you know'? to which the Master replied, "Because I am not like you," and Xiu said, "You have arrived at the point where I am. The Master then bowed.*
"A foul reputation is hard to conceal. Xiu said, "It defiles your ears. The Master then gave a shout. Xiu asked, "What is it like after the shout? The Master said, "Still, you do not know.
Xiu said, "The old monk does not know; what do you know? The Master was about to strike him with his palm when Xiu said:
"It is still like playing with something empty," the Master said. He then prostrated. One day, Xiu said, "These days, students are unwilling to apply their minds with sincerity;
that is why the Dharma-gate has become desolate. The Master said, "Even so, for the most part, the fault lies with the teachers.
Had Huanglong Nan not been severely broken by Master Ciming, how could he have known that the Way transcends ordinary circumstances?"
Xiu said, "How could this be something obtained through oral transmission or ear-to-ear instruction? The Master stuck out his tongue.
On another day, Xiu entered the room and said, "I doubt that you understand the circumstances regarding the encounter between Attendant Kuò and Huá-yán.
The Master said, "It is not only you, Master, who doubts me; all the people in the entire world doubt me. Xiu said, "All the people in the entire world doubt you."
"That may be so; do not let this old monk doubt you. The Master said, "If that is the case, then I am at fault.
Xiu said, "It is just like when Xinghua and Mindé engaged in the guest-host dialogue of the four shouts.

Xinghua said, 'Just now, had it been anyone else, thirty blows would have been given, and not even a single blow would have been spared. Why? Because he understood how to employ a shout as something other than a mere shout. What does that mean?"
This was his realization that a single shout is not merely used as a shout. The Master said, "Let me go; I shall convey another message.
Xiu said, "Do not utter a word. The Master then composed a verse: "When guest and host meet, there is the family of letting go and seizing;
Beneath the shout, one sees a live snake amidst the clouds. From the tip of the staff, the unobstructed emerges; How could this be understood as a mere transmission of sand?"
Xiu then dismissed him. The Master had been teaching the Dharma at Shiqiao in Zhongshan; Xiu subsequently went to Ba’en Temple to express his gratitude for the Dharma.
Xiu took the *ruyi* (wish-fulfilling gem) and handed it to him, saying, "This is something this old monk has used for forty years without exhausting its utility.

Take it with you to polish and refine yourself; do not let it be forgotten. The Master held the *ruyi* and entered the hall, saying, "This is the Elder of the Hall acting as the Preceptor for the Senior Seat."
Regarding this inexhaustible koan, I dare ask: is there anyone who can realize its function through its common characteristics?
After a long silence, he struck the wooden board once and then departed. Ascending the hall, he said: "If one discusses this matter, the mind cannot be sought and wisdom cannot be learned.
Cut off the hundred layers and thousand folds; cast away all inferior capacities at once. Only when you emerge in solitary peril can you be made to soar."
Precipitous! Gathering it all together, it is neither mind nor form, neither like nor different. When you wish to employ it, you employ it; when you wish to relinquish it, you relinquish it;
when you wish to act, you act; when you wish to conceal it, you conceal it. To entertain even a hair’s breadth of thought is to fall into the gateway of birth and death.
At this point, how can one be saved? He said again: "The sovereign body atop the mountain of the five aggregates."

"Clearly manifest, every single thing responds to the Heavenly Truth; the Sudden Teaching is directly before you, beyond thought. When the profound and the essential are fully present, one sees the original person.
[The Master] strikes the meditation staff once and shouts, then addresses the assembly: "Before the fifteenth day, all of you let forth the mountain streams.
After the fifteenth day, all of you cut off the firewood. On this very fifteenth day, I, the mountain monk—"
I have seen through you all at a single stroke: if you wish to go out, you cannot; if you wish to enter, you cannot.
Unable to go out and unable to enter, the eyebrows within the fire are starkly black. You must urgently investigate your own nostrils; the blue-eyed barbarian monk constantly faces the wall.
One day, while the Master was opening the mountain site, he held a withered vine in his hand and said to a monk: "This..."
"This is a daughter of the Cao family. The monk said, "But she is missing the young master of the Xie family. The Master said, "As long as there is a daughter, why worry about there being no master?

The monk said, "She must be complete before it is right. The Master passed a rattan cane to the monk; as the monk reached out to take it, the Master immediately threw it down and said, "This does not match.
A monk asked: "The moon has set at the third watch, and the lamp in the ancient hall is nearly spent. Is there [anyone here]?"
A person without face comes. How do you meet him? The Master said, "It makes people laugh to death! It makes people laugh to death! The monk asked, "What are you laughing at, Monk?
The Master gave a shout and said, "You do not even recognize the question. A monk asked, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?
The Master said, "Mount Sumeru stands upside down in mid-air. The monk asked, "What is the penetration of the Dharma?"
Regarding the matter of the body, the Master said: "A monkey swallows an elephant. A monk asked, "What is space? The Master said, "You are also within it.
The monk said, "I do not see space. The Master said, "You blind fellow! You deserve thirty blows of the staff. Addressing the assembly, he said:
"Pressing oil from stone; taking fire from water. This is not merely the labor of moving about; it is simply..."
It is fitting that you speak forth from the position of honor. This old man of Zhaozhou is far too clever; one must strictly avoid saying, "The monk’s robe from Qingzhou weighs seven pounds.
A monk asked: "Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, flowers bloom upon a withered tree—is this a phrase of the guest or a phrase of the host?"

The Master said: "The stone woman weeps for the azure heavens. A monk asked: "When heaven does not cover and earth does not support, where can one find a place to settle the body and establish one's life?
The Master struck him and left the abbot’s quarters. The next day, the monk asked again: "Yesterday I received a blow;

today, does the Master still feel the pain? The Master struck him once more and left. In the winter of the Bingxu year of the Shunzhi era, he calculated the date of his passing and spoke a verse of farewell.
The assembly interred his entire body to the right of the mountain gate. Zen Master Mian of Tiantong inscribed the epitaph for his stupa.
The Master authored the *Chongmen Chengfan* (Models of the Chan School) in four fascicles, along with his recorded sayings (*yulu*), both of which circulate in the world.
Chan Master Ruan’an Wen of Lian’an at Nanjian in Hangzhou was the son of the Yu family of Wujiang. His father, Mr. Yan-chang, later lamented having no heir;
consequently, he established a hundred-day *amogha* (unrestricted) assembly at Juefeng Temple, and [the Master] was born in response to his prayers.
Having lost his mother at a young age, he fell gravely ill; he was fond of drinking and lacked self-discipline.

At the age of sixteen, he was suddenly struck with alarm and said to himself, "How can I allow my body and mind to have no ground upon which to stand? He resolved to apply himself to study. One day, while passing by a mountain temple, he saw the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states:
"This body and mind, extending outward to empty space, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are the wondrously luminous reality."

There was something within my heart that remained doubtful, so I went specifically to visit Xiu of Qingshan. He instructed me to contemplate the koan: "The original face before one's parents were born.
One day, while Xiu was standing by a mountain stream with some guests, he held up the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. As I opened my mouth, Xiu suddenly struck me and asked, "What is this mind?
At that moment, I was unconsciously overcome by a sense of self-loss. At the age of twenty-four, I suffered through the hardships of marriage.
Harassed by these circumstances, he fled through the night until he reached Wulin, where he shaved his head under the great master Fayu of Nanjian.

He once knelt before a Buddha lamp at night, single-mindedly holding the phrase: "What is one's original face before one's parents were born? Finding no resonance with this, he resolved to travel abroad to seek instruction.
Hearing that Master Wuzu Fayan was at Beichan, he packed his belongings and hurried into the Wu region, where he received a severe beating as an instruction.
He subsequently went up to Qingshan, where he again met Master Shanzhi Jigong. While staying together in the mountains, at the fifth watch of the night, he heard the sound of a gale;
his doubts were instantly resolved. Before his eyes, all was pure and naked, with not a single dharma to obstruct the mind. Directly...
This was a state of universal joy throughout his entire being. He composed a verse, saying: "A thousand origins and ten thousand wonders, layered upon one another;
Within this, there is no partiality—nothing is permitted. A single melody from the stringless lute, Blown by the cold cliff’s wind at the fifth watch. He presented it to Xiu. Xiu said:
"I do not ask about the profound mystery. What is the phrase that is not separated [from reality]? As the Master was about to respond, he was struck with a staff.

"In this place, moreover, one cannot go. Seeing that the Master was stuck in doubt and stagnation, Xiu showed him a verse, saying: "A thousand waves and ten thousand ripples, layer upon layer of separation."
Once you have recognized it, it flows forth everywhere and penetrates all places; root and object are cast off, and the whole body functions as its own use.

When things are brought forth one by one, they finally become relaxed and at ease. The Master looked at the verse and understood it himself, yet he was still unable to act with spontaneous freedom when faced with the critical moment.
One day, he recited Baizhang’s verse on “closing off the throat and lips”: "When the throat and lips are closed off, the three mouths are wide open."
"One foot. At midnight, the pillar meets [the staff]. Blowing a holeless iron flute horizontally, he presents it for correction.
Xiu said, "Does the pillar have a mouth? The Master said, "It speaks incessantly. Xiu said, "You have spoken only half.
The Master said, "And how about you, Preceptor? Xiu said, "Whence comes this question? At that moment, struck by this single blow, [the Master] was immediately like a mass of glowing heat.
"It is like iron meeting fire. The next day he presented this to Xiu. Xiu said, "You must not burn off your eyebrows. The Master then gave a shout.
Xiu said, "But you have already burned them off. The Master turned around and said, "Watch this old fellow make a complete mess of things," and then he left.
He went up to the hall and walked straight across, looking toward the flagpole. This was still the act of a mediocre fellow; it was like a flash of lightning.
"Passing the needle through the eye [of the spindle]. Running a horse upon a bowstring—this must be a true monk before it can be achieved.
Those who cannot be lifted by a spoon are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; those whom a thousand thrusts cannot turn back are likewise as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds.
Setting aside for a moment the matter of cutting off the tongues of all people in the world, tell me: what is your own sentence of total liberation? He raised his whisk.
He said: "A net covering the heavens, a hundred thousandfold. Entering the hall, he said:
"The Chan of this place of mine leaves you all nowhere to rest your feet; it leaves you all nowhere to lean upon; it leaves you all nowhere to calculate or measure.
It is, right here and now, like a mass of glowing red-hot iron and flames. The moment you intend to rest your feet, your heels will be burned away."
The moment you intend to rely on or depend upon [it], your eyebrows have already been singed away.
The moment you intend to calculate or deliberate, you have already lost your own eyes and nostrils. If you do not act in this way at all, what breath or vitality remains?
To congregate and settle; one cannot congregate and settle with him. To hide and avoid; one cannot hide and avoid him.
It is only by your own fierce extraction that you may succeed. To say "fierce extraction" is already to have missed the mark for some time.
At this point, what will you all do? Looking left and right, he threw down his staff and returned to the Abbot’s quarters. —Xueqiao Xinfu.
Yangshang went on to ask, "You belong to that side; why are you here on this side? The Master said, "A single drop of ink forms two dragons.
Yangshang said, "I do not understand how you can produce clouds and mist. The Master said, "Today I grant the Great Master a pardon.
During tea, Yangshang said, "In my daily practice, I teach people only to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Master said, "How many people [do you have]?"
Xuanzhen said, "You have misunderstood the Great Master's meaning. Xiangyan said, "Even if you did not misunderstand it, you would still be far from it.
The Master said, "The Great Master should not deceive people. As they were walking in front of the mountain gate, they saw a dog barking. Xiangyan said, "This thing that lacks Buddha-nature.
The Master said, "But you have scratched the very place where the Great Master itches. Xiangyan laughed loudly; the Master also laughed loudly. The assembly [applauded].
During the ritual sequence, Xìn looked around left and right; the assembly stood waiting. Xìn said, "Everyone here is a man of integrity.

The Master said, "In the presence of the Great Master, who would dare to raise a hand? Cánzī Chánshī asked, "Śākyamuni’s 'closing the room' and Vimalakīrti’s 'silence' both belong to the realm of expedient teachings (*upāya*).
They do not fall within the present moment. I ask the Master to provide a single phrase. The Master said, "Before you have even asked."
"I have already answered this before. [The monk] asked, "Who can testify to this? The Master said, "Liao the Bearded at the crossroads.
He asked again, "It is common knowledge that our late teacher did not bring his affairs to completion. How will you bring them to completion for him? The Master said:

“Amidst the azure heavens, grievous suffering is further added. He said, “It is not that I, your brother, do not understand. The Master said, “When meeting people, take care not to misrepresent [the teaching].
He asked again, “For ten years we have studied together, never parting from our clappers. Now that you have departed for Lianhua Monastery, will you still see me?
The Master said, “In a place where there is no one, we gaze at each other with hands pressed to our foreheads. He said, “He has no face; what is there to look at? The Master—

[The Master] said, "The grass-robbers have been utterly defeated. [The student] asked, "Setting aside for a moment the brandishing of the mallet and the raising of the whisk, tell me the brand-new decree.
The Master said, "A single palm-strike; a handful of blood. [The student] said, "This must come from you, elder brother. The Master said, "That is my own fault.

He asked again, "To discuss the profound and explain the subtle is what the former sages condemned; to blink the eyes and raise the eyebrows is the decadence of Chan in this age. To depart from these two..."
Tou asked, "What is your brother’s way of being? The Master said, "I do not corrupt the sons and daughters of others.
Tou said, "That is truly a compassionate heart. The Master said, "It is easy to distinguish dragons from snakes, but difficult to deceive a patch-robed monk.
A monk asked, "Of the thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion, which one is the true eye? The Master said, "Lowering the fishing line at a rapids. A monk asked, [the question continues].
"How is it when one does not recognize that which is facing them? The Master said, "A blade or an axe cannot cut it open.

The questioner asked, "What are the three kinds of illnesses of the Dharmakāya? The Master said, "Scars from moxibustion. He asked, "What are the two kinds of light? The Master said, "If you look at them, you will go blind.
The questioner asked, "A person who has attained ultimate penetration is fundamentally free from birth and death; why then is their life-root (*jīvamūla*) not severed? The Master said, "A snail."

In the summer of the Yiwu year of the Shunzhi era (1655), after the summer retreat at Qingshan had concluded, the Master took all the utensils belonging to the abbot’s quarters and personally wrote individual inscriptions for each, distributing them to various quarters as his final legacy.
He then set out on a pilgrimage with his staff, traveling to Ba’en Temple in Wukang to pay respects at the pagoda.
There he met Chan Master Xiu, to whom he fully entrusted the great affairs of the Dharma and fixed the date of his passing for the ninth month.
On the twenty-seventh day of the second month, he traveled to Wujiang and stayed at Yingtian Temple. As scheduled, he passed away while seated in meditation.

His disciples escorted his reliquary shrine (kaṅ) to be enshrined in a stupa at Nanjian. Chan Master Hongjue Mǎn composed the inscription for the stupa. His *Recorded Sayings* were submitted to the throne and requested for inclusion in the Buddhist canon;
additionally, his *Continued Lamp: Collected Drafts* (*Xùdēng Cúngǎo*) circulates in the world.
Chan Master Yulin Tongxiu of Ba’en Temple in Huzhou was the son of the Yang family from Rongcheng.
During his childhood, an elder once ordered several junior practitioners to each close their eyes for a moment and then reflect inwardly upon the arising of thought.

When the other children had each declared that they had finished observing the arising of thought, the Master remained silent for a long while and then said, “When I looked back, no thought could be found. He then went to study under Master Tianyin Xiu.

At Qing Shan, he was appointed to serve in the *shisong* (attendant office). While sitting in the incense session with the assembly, one night before the period of silence had even begun, the Master went directly to the Abbot’s quarters.
Xiu Jian asked, "Why have you finished your incense session so early today? The Master replied, "It is simply because I did not go to sit in the incense session. Xiu Jian said:
Seeing this profound principle, Xiu did not leave his seat. The Master said, "Even now, there is no non-sitting.
Xiu suddenly picked up the *Shiwu Lu* (Record of Stone House) on the table and asked, "What is this? The Master said, "I beg the Venerable One to speak.
Xiu said, "If you do not speak, I shall make the Old Monk speak. The Master said, "I knew well that the Venerable One would not dare to speak. Xiu said, "The *Shiwu Lu*."
"I am truly afraid to speak," he said. The Master replied, "Let him go as he will. Xiu said, "The old monk is being falsely accused!
Unable to penetrate the Master's meaning, he stood weeping with tears falling like rain until late that night, his eyes not closing for a single moment, standing by the side of his meditation seat.
He completely forgot to enter the quarters. At the fifth watch, Xiu called out, "There is no need to hurry. I shall relate an ancient story for you.
Long ago, there was a Layman Pang; when he first met people, he was just like you—standing all alone and remote."
Opening his mouth, he immediately asked people, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
At that time, Mazu stepped forward one pace and said, "Wait until you can swallow up all the waters of the West River in a single draught;
then I will tell you. The Master said, "I have a verse on this. Xiu asked, "What is your verse? The Master presented the verse: "Not taking the myriad dharmas as a companion,"
"For whom? "No one. "Who, then, establishes the initial connection? "If you have a mind that seeks and pursues, you will become increasingly estranged;

if you are without the consciousness of seeking, there is no contradiction. Xiu said, "I do not ask about your companionship with the myriad dharmas; I require that you understand how to swallow the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and immediately brushed his sleeves and departed. Thereafter, whenever he was questioned or examined, he...
The Master did not yield to the circumstances. Xiu deeply approved of this. The Master had confined himself in retreat at the banks of the Yangtze River in Rongcheng;
Xiu subsequently moved to Baoyuan Temple in Wukang and sent a series of letters urging the Master, saying: "I, the old monk, am at Baoyuan Temple; my spirit is daily failing compared to before.

You should know that I will certainly not remain much longer in this world. Upon receiving this letter, come immediately; I have most essential words to entrust to you. When the Master received the letter, he broke [the retreat].
Guangyi approached Xiu. Without performing a prostration, he stepped forward with his hands joined and said, "In the land of a madman, even a father cannot tolerate such excess.
Is this peak still the dwelling place of the old man? Xiu said, "Stand still for a moment, and I shall tell you."
The Master suddenly overturned the incense table and exited. Xiu called out loudly, "Bring me my staff! The Master responded from afar, "The sword has long since departed.
The following day, Xiu ascended the hall. Just as the Rector was about to strike the gavel, the Master shouted to stop him, saying, "Wait until I have finished my question, then strike the gavel.
He then asked: "In the Great Tang of old, there were no Zen masters; now, in this country..."
"Is there anything more within? Xiu took up his staff, made a gesture as if to strike, and said, "Look at this staff! The Master then shouted. Xiu also shouted. The Master shouted once more.
Turning away, he said, "It is not that this wild child has much spirit; it is simply because he has already passed through the highest barrier.
He then departed. Xiu let out a shout, and the Master also shouted. From afar, he heard the rector striking the gavel again for the formal announcement. Thereupon, the Master—
He cried out in a loud voice, "Alas for the breath of death! At the Hall of Bao'en, he ascended the seat, held up his staff, and said:
"A wondrous and extraordinary cause and condition must be brought forth by an extraordinary person. A sentence that startles the multitude must be proclaimed at a place that startles the multitude.

Today, having met an extraordinary person and being present at an extraordinary occasion, this is truly a place that startles the multitude. Let us proclaim the sentence that startles the multitude. But tell me, what is it that startles the multitude?"
"How do you bring up this phrase? He suddenly called out to the assembly, "The Stone Buddha of Wuzhong...

Addressing the assembly, he cited the karmic conditions concerning how Daowu always carried a wooden sword, saying: "A Han-lu hound barking at the void and chasing clods of earth bites into a man who is half-awake and half-drunk;
in the end, he cannot avoid rolling in the grass with everyone else. If Daowu, when that monk was just about to take up his sword—"
He then kicked it over with one foot. Had he known his error, not only would he have caused the other to suddenly change its skin and fur, but he himself would have been upright from head to tail.
How could one fail to provide fodder suited to one's own capacity? A wooden sword has ultimately become a mere toy. [The Master] addressed the assembly:
To break through the final, secure barrier—Yun’an was right to scold. To penetrate the fundamental principles of the successive patriarchs—Miaoxi still rebuked him.
You all who aspire to this Dharma-gate must be extremely careful: "The stream ahead is swift and the fish move with difficulty;
the wind atop the ridge behind is high and the birds find it hard to perch. Addressing the assembly, he cited the karmic conditions of the birth crisis of Aṅgulimāla.
He said, "Now tell me: what principle is contained in these two words of the World-Honored One that they are so efficacious as to save a family from the perils of childbirth?
He gave a sudden shout and said, "Do not dream! For you all, I shall offer this analogy:
it is like a person coming to buy ginger, yet the World-Honored One gives them a large handful of ginseng."
At that time, as he was about to depart, he ended up using it as fresh ginger.

He brought trouble upon others by having them chew on it aimlessly—swallowing it when they could not spit it out, and spitting it out when they could not swallow it. If anyone here can emerge without chewing on it aimlessly, I shall give you thirty blows of my staff.
Why? Because the World-Honored One lost his capital back then; today, I am making him pay it back.
Shangli addressed the assembly. He cited Chan Master Zun of Dacheng in Tangzhou, who said while ascending the hall:
"Those who come up do not question; those who go down do not doubt. Not knowing whether it is so or not—if it is so, how truly marvelous! The Master [Shangli] said:
"At that time, the immeasurable great assembly all attained the Way at once. The Master asked the attendant: "How many Bodhidharmas are there in the rice bucket?"
The Master stared blankly, at a loss for words. He asked the kitchen steward, "Do the Buddhas of the three periods of time truly preach the Dharma within the flames?
The steward was likewise at a loss. The Master pointed to a monk standing nearby and said, "Only this monk can answer the question.
He then returned to the abbot’s quarters. The Master asked a monk, "What is it like when the tree withers and its leaves fall? The monk stepped forward and said:
"Not separated by so much as a single hair. The Master said, "If the faculty does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison. The monk shouted. The Master then struck him.
A layman asked, "I clearly know that daily life is never separate from this; why then can it not be spoken? The Master said:
"The single word 'knowing' is the gateway to all calamities. A monk asked, "In the past, the High Ancestor said: 'The mud ox at the bottom of the sea chews the moon as it runs;
the stone tiger before the cliff cradles its cub and sleeps; the iron snake drills into the diamond eye;
K'un-lun rides the elephant while the egret leads. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "A fine son never uses his father's money. He addressed the assembly:
This mountain monk has composed a fine discourse on the Buddha-dharma; it is hung upon the Yu Hua Bridge. Let each of you in the assembly look at it for yourselves.
After a long silence, he said: "Bo Le once visited three times; who could have added a thousand pieces of gold? You offered it to me, but I did not accept;

I keep the flawless gem leaning against a withered vine. Addressing the assembly: "In this old window and dilapidated house, with a paper curtain and a blue lamp—within this, there is one who attains [it]."
Do you have even a slight inkling of its meaning? Last night the wind was biting; it has already brewed three parts of snow. A monk asked, "What is the fundamental matter?
The Master said, "I manage the household smoke, whether it rises thick or thin. A monk asked, "Regarding the beating of drums and the ringing of bells..."

"What is the purpose of this? The Master replied, "To exchange people's eyes. The Master had first presided over Baoen Monastery; he was the youngest in years, yet his reputation for the Way spread in all directions.
In the spring of the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era, an imperial decree invited him to the capital, where he was commanded to reside at Wanshan Hall.

The Emperor personally visited the palace, and as the Master ascended the seat, he raised the koan of Xiyu’s "Lion in the Village of Duan. After descending from the seat, the Emperor was greatly pleased.
The Great Awakened Chan Master was granted purple robes and a golden seal. In that year, the Master requested leave to return to his mountain retreat.

In the autumn of the following year, the Emperor attained realization while on horseback and issued successive imperial edicts earnestly inviting him to the capital. There, he investigated the profound mysteries daily; the Emperor then issued another edict to the Master.
He conferred the Bodhisattva Mahāśīla upon fifteen hundred monks and was additionally enfeoffed as the National Preceptor Pujie Nengren.
In the autumn of the *Yimao* year of the Kangxi era, he manifested illness; after reciting a verse, he passed away. He was sixty-two years of age and had spent forty-three summer retreats.
His disciples enshrined his whole body in the East Valley of Tianmu, where his stupa was named Qiong Yun. [The inscription was composed by] Wang, Grand University Scholar of the Baohedian.
Xi composed an inscription for him. His *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings) was submitted for inclusion in the Buddhist canon.
Chan Master Ciji of Lueluo Mountain on Mount Nanyue was the son of the Li family from Tongzhou in the region of Han.

In his childhood, his father encountered a physiognomist who said, "Your son’s skeletal structure is too ethereal; his lifespan may not be long. Consequently, he was renounced as a child and entered the monastic life. Initially, he attended upon...
The Dharma Master Ruomai of Dongyin attended lectures with great realization, after which he took his leave to travel to various regions. He went to visit Master Wuzu from Jinsu Temple;
upon seeing him, Wuzu immediately asked, "What is it like when the guests have dispersed and the hall is empty? Wuzu said, "What kind of time is this? The Master gave a shout. Wuzu struck him.
The Master shouted again. Wuzu struck him again. The Master bowed and said, "From this day forward, I shall serve you, Master."
He went up to Qing Shan to visit Master Xiushan. He asked, "In the past I heard of your reputation; today I meet you face-to-face.

Regarding this one phrase of meeting face-to-face, I beg the Master to grant me its transmission. Xiushan said, "Try to say it yourself. The Master then bowed. Xiushan said, "Even that does not suffice."
The Master turned around and went out. One day, Xiu asked, "Regarding Baizhang, what exactly did he obtain under Mazu’s shout?
The Master said, "If there were anything obtained, that would have been a failure to do justice to Mazu. Xiu said, "But he said that [Mazu] was deaf for three days—what does that mean?
The Master said, "I, too, must not harbor the understanding of a wild fox spirit. Thereupon, Xiu ceased questioning. One.
Rixiu asked, "The ancients spoke of 'having a phrase' and 'not having a phrase. How do you understand this? The Master said, "The rocks grow rootless grass;
the mountains harbor unmoving clouds. Rixiu said, "It is like a vine leaning against a tree, is it not? The Master said, "I have always applied myself most earnestly to this very point."
Xiu said, "The tree has fallen and the vines are withered. What then? The Master lowered his head and departed.
The Magistrate Huang Du'an invited the Master to reside at Dongming, the ancestral seat. The Master said, "I have heard that when you, Layman, attained realization at Kaixian, you toppled Mount Lu."
"Yes," the layman said. "Do you see Mount Lu? The Master said, "Wait until I have helped you up. The layman said, "Just now you called me 'Dongming' (East Light).
The Master said, "An adept, an adept! The layman then withdrew. After a short while, the layman asked, "Where has the Great Master been staying all this time?
The Master said, "Layman, tell me: where am I staying right now? The layman said, "Out."
The Master said, "This gate cannot be exited. The Master asked, "Layman, can you exit this gate? The Layman hesitated.
The Master said, "In fact, it is you, Layman, who cannot exit this gate. While staying at Luluo, the Master ascended the hall and said:

"In my place, I do not discuss the profound (xuan), nor do I discuss the subtle (miao). I do not discuss Chan, nor do I discuss the Way. I simply want you all to resolve the matter of birth and death."
Break through the mind. If the mind of birth and death is not broken, it is a public summons to eat iron bars before the Old Lord Yama.
Therefore it is said: "Investigation must be real investigation; awakening must be real awakening. The Great King Yama does not fear much talk.
Do not trouble yourselves by standing for long. Be careful. While residing at Nanyuan, he addressed the assembly: "In various quarters there is mysterious and wondrous Chan, and..."
There is the Chan of Nature and Principle; there is the subtle and refined Chan; there is the Chan of daily progress;
there is the Chan of "resting and ceasing"; there is the Chan of Great Dharma and Small Dharma. These are the various kinds of Chan used for engaging with people and for them to chew upon.
In my own place, I have none of these many types of Chan; I have only that single blunt iron hoe left behind by our distant ancestor, the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang.

The head requires people’s use every day. When one becomes thoroughly proficient in this use, if one reaches the point where effort is forgotten by the self and the hand is forgotten by the mind, such that before one's eyes there is no field to be opened, and beneath one's feet there is no ground to stand upon.
Suddenly, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are overturned by the hoe and shattered into a hundred fragments, revealing the two eyes of the person right here and now.
"Great assembly, at this very moment, in whose hands does the handle lie? [The Master] suddenly hurls down his staff and says, "Held forth in the open light for all to see!
A monk asked, "When one who has died the Great Death returns to life, what is it like? The Master said, "Call him here and I will give him to the mountain monk."
[The Master] washed his feet. A monk asked, "What is the place where a student turns their body? The Master said, "Quickly prostrate three times.
The monk asked, "What is the intimate phrase for a student? The Master said, "Take note of it clearly.

A monk asked, "An ancient said, 'When meeting someone beyond three thousand miles, one does not inquire. Whom does he meet? The Master said, "It is no other person. In the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era, the Master...
He ascended Mount Nanyue, captivated by the splendor of Mount Zhurong. He settled beneath Zhibo Peak and dwelt there in a thatched hut; though it was effectively a tiger’s den, he paid it no mind.
When the Prince of Guilin heard of this and marveled at him, he came in person to seek his counsel and dispatched palace attendants to wait upon him, their presence never ceasing along the road.

The Prince wished to invite him into the palace, but he firmly declined and would not comply. Consequently, the Prince followed his tracks in secret and departed. The Prince could not [contain his curiosity].

Delighted, he burned the hermitage. He made an offering before the pomegranate tree in front of the hut, saying, "Monk from the South, do you truly possess the Way? The tree immediately bore fruit in winter;
before long, it blossomed and produced more fruit. The King’s respect and faith increased all the more, and he went to visit the place where the Master had planted his staff.
He humbled himself by traveling three hundred *li* on foot to visit him. [The Master] further built a hermitage for him to provide for his needs.
A monk asked, "What is the phrase that transcends the Buddhas and surpasses the Patriarchs? The Master held up his staff and said, "Realize it right here. The monk then gave a shout.
The Master struck him. As the monk prepared to offer a word in response, the Master chased him out with a continuous succession of blows.
A monk asked, "What is the place where a student establishes his body and sustains his life? The Master said, "Wait until this mountain monk has a place to establish his body and sustain his life;
then I shall tell you. A monk asked, "Holding a sharp sword in one's hand, why does the monkey not die? The Master said, "It is entirely due to its own power."
In the spring of the Jiashen year, bandits ravaged the mountains of the Three Chu regions. With no food to sustain them day by day, they gathered *wei* roots to relieve their hunger;
however, they mistakenly ate wild celery. Both who ate it together sought medical treatment. The Master said, "Why must you do so? and then sat upright and passed away.

His disciples enshrined his entire remains and erected a stupa at Luluo. Chan Master Ruohan Wen composed an inscription for the stupa. His *Recorded Sayings* were submitted to the throne and requested for inclusion in the Tripitaka.
Additionally, the *Lamp Record of the Chan School of Mount Nanyue* and the *Continued Collection of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye* have been circulated in the world.
Chan Master Zhongtong Yinzhong of Yangshan Songji was the son of the Yan family of Wucheng. At the age of seventeen, he left home to become a monk at Mount Daochang.

He went to attend upon Master Xiu of Qingshan, who assigned him the koan of the "Dog" (Wu). After investigating it with great effort for a long time, one day upon hearing the sound of a brush painting eyebrows, he attained a realization.
He hurried to see Master Xiu, who raised his fist and said, "Speak! Speak! The Master replied, "The board is sounding."

"Please, Master, come to the hall. Xiu agreed. In the ninth year of the Chongzhen era, he went forth to reside at Mingqing in Namama, then moved to Chongyi, and later succeeded to the seat at Qingshan.
He ascended the hall and said: "The gate faces a thousand peaks of azure; the stream follows a secluded path."

Seeking further for the profound and mysterious essence is like stirring ashes to search for bubbles on the surface of water. Thereupon, the Master descended from his seat. By nature, the Master was fond of quiet retirement;
as social interactions became too frequent, he soon took his leave and lived in seclusion at Mount Yang. A monk asked, "What is the place where you, Master, attained awakening?
The Master replied, "One cannot deceive others. The monk asked again, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge? The Master replied, "The magpie at the corner of the hall."
The Pigeon Cries. A monk asked about the incident where Xuefeng ascended the seat and rolled out a wooden ball, and Xuansha seized it and placed it back in its original spot.
The Master said, "Yangshan would have no objection to rolling it again," and then he entered the abbot’s quarters.

A monk asked, "The twenty-five sages were originally without superiority or inferiority; why did he single out the faculty of hearing as the perfect penetration? The Master said, "The green becomes the feathers of the dead."
He spoke these verses of parting: "The ancients knew their error at fifty; I have reached fifty and know when to stop.
Do not say that affairs arise only as the sun rises; you must believe in this clear and direct pointing. Having cast down his brush, he passed away.
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Xueqiao Xin (four individuals):
Chan Master Jicui Wenyi Run of Hangzhou. A native of Meidong in Zhejiang, his clan name was Yang. At the age of twenty-three, he left the household life and received full ordination.
He traveled extensively to visit various venerable masters, including those of Zhenji, Huangbo, Boshan, and Jinsu, and [received their] instruction from all of them.
A karmic affinity was established. [Case] 35. While attending Zen Master Xueqiao Xin at the Budong Xuan (Immovable Studio), he attained a karmic resonance upon hearing a single word.

He subsequently spent several years traveling with and serving under Kuangnan Kaixian. Later, when Xin began teaching the Dharma at Dongta in Huzhou, he appointed the Master as the First Seat and sent him to the quarters of the Head Seat.
Upon entering, Xin asked, "Head Seat, why do you not utter a single phrase? The Master gave him a slap.
When the Master arrived at Kuangnan, he received formal certification (in'ka). He then presented the verse "The Lamp of Mind Continues its Flame," which says:
"Within the unshakable hall, the conversation has long since faded; At Kaixian, three times I seized the high banner. East of Fucheng, the west wind blows fiercely;
With a single palm, I repay my debt in the Head Seat’s quarters. In the spring of the Dinghai year, Xinxian moved to Yunmen. The Master stayed at Jiyuan in Lukcheng to recuperate from his illness.

In the eighth month, his news passed away. On the day the report of his death arrived, the Master was overcome with great grief and lay prostrate upon his pillow; he then drafted a letter of succession to the Dharma and offered it before the altar.
He entered nirvana on the nineteenth day of the ninth month of the Dinghai year of the Shunzhi era. His stupa was erected behind the hermitage.
Chan Master Cheshan Cheyaya Hongxie of Yunmen in Yuezhou was the son of the You family of Chu and Huang.
He left the household life at Xilin on Mount Lu and studied under Yunmen Xin at Kaixian. One day, Xin said to the assembly: "I have a single phrase."
"Pure and exhausted, there is no principle; yellow leaves hang empty upon the treetops. The golden wind reaches the *bìluó* vines.

When someone offered these words with intimacy, he was made the second-generation successor of Yunmen. When the assembly offered their own words but failed to accord with him, the Master said, "It is not I who am at fault;

you nearly took this as a mere intellectual puzzle. Xinxing asked, "If it is not taken as an intellectual puzzle, what then? The Master stepped back and said, "I have committed a transgression! Xinxing [laughed].

He said, "The old monk shall divide it with you. After Xinxin entered nirvana, he was invited to succeed him on the seat. At the third anniversary of Xinxin’s passing, the Master held up the incense and said:
"Three years have yielded the true news; I bring forth the waters of Ye Creek flowing upstream. This is no matter of being carried away by the Lingnan mountains;
Swift as wind and rain, let people gather it as they will. Passing through Ziyun, he ascended the hall. He said: "When crossing the river, there are river waves."
[The Master] rose. A bamboo pole was leaning against a bamboo grove; a monk entered the temple to stay the night. Thieves ransacked a house that was not poor.

Today, this mountain monk has been unjustly caught by thieves. Is there anyone here who can catch and defeat them? One monk stepped forward. The Master struck him, saying, "The thief’s identity is already revealed.
He then said, "An ancient said: 'When we meet, he does not raise his eyebrows; you go east, and I go west. Crimson clouds pierce through..."
The azure void; the white sun circles Mount Sumeru. When those ancients met one another, they possessed the eye that truly sees.
I, this mountain monk, have been a fellow student with Ziyun for ten years; today I am merely passing by, borrowing his path. How shall I bring forth a word for our meeting?
Within the shadows of purple clouds, the song flows smoothly; atop Mount Qinwang, it is harmonized in perfect unison.
The Master entered nirvana on the tenth day of the ninth month of the Dingyou year of the Shunzhi era. He was forty-eight years of age and had twenty years of monastic seniority.
Chan Master Hongnao Mingguoxingshan of Quzhou was a native of the Chen family from Anlu in Chu. He went to Mount Jingshan to study under Yunmen Wenyan.
He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Wenyan said, "There is no such thing; sit down and drink some tea.
The Master replied, "Today I have personally met a venerable elder with clear eyes. Wenyan nodded his head in approval, and the Master immediately composed a eulogy for his portrait. Source.
The lineage was entrusted [to him]. The Master taught at Fatai, Tianxi, Quzhou Tianning, Wushi Mingguo, Shaoxing Dashi, Yunmen, and Yingfeng in Haisal.

While presiding over the assembly, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: "A thousand feet of line are cast down to fish for a fierce dragon; when a fierce tiger stands before the gate, how does one avoid it?
The Master said: "Watch over your life. The monk said: "If that is so, then this humble one shall lose his body."

[The monk] departs. The Master says, "Today I have committed a transgression. He then says, "To realize 'once you know the One, all things are finished'—this is still merely a matter on the side of the Dharmakāya.
You must know that there is a matter beyond the Dharmakāya. Rain falls and wets the ground; when the sky clears, the sun comes out.
To awaken in such a way is still a half-month's journey from Tianxi. (Kangxi Jiayin, Year 2)
On the fourth day of the first month, the Master passed away while seated at Tianning Temple. His disciples escorted his coffin to Mingguo Temple, where a stupa was erected for him.
He was seventy-six years old and fifty-three years since his ordination.
Master Chan Master Ming Honglu of Kaixian on Mount Lu ascends the hall to deliver a discourse upon the conclusion of the retreat.

The wind whistles, the rain whistles. You who travel as eminent streams of the Way, let not your minds be distressed. Pick up your bowl-bag and look at it from the beginning: your entire livelihood lies within that old ladle.

At Kaixian, for this one period, the knots have been untied; we may rejoice in this era of Great Peace. To bind them is for emptiness to gather together; to untie them is for the Great [Function] to manifest.
The ground is level and spread out; let him go east or west as he pleases. Who cares whether he comes from the Hu or the Han?
Shouldering the sun and moon, treading upon the waters and clouds, he walks on and enters the ancestral home of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; with every step he treads the fields of the patriarchs.

He is expansive and relaxed, following conditions as they arise, carefree and at ease. [He] brandishes his staff and says: "Stop! Stop! If you suddenly encounter one with hands like those used for biting pigs and dogs—"
He thrust out his sky-reaching staff and held it directly before him, not letting it pass.
"What then? After a long silence, he said, "Understand this for thirty years. A monk asked, "In the study of Chan, the priority is to resolve birth and death.
What if one has not resolved them? The Master said, "Study [Chan]. The monk said, "Thank you for the instruction. The Master said, "This is a great injustice to people."

Under the lineage of Qingyuan, the Chan Master Zhishou (幻休) of the Zongjing (宗鏡) school had as his successor the Chan Master Fannian (方念),
known by his courtesy name Qingliang (清涼), of Beiping Dajue Temple. He was a native of Tang County and belonged to the Yang clan.
At the age of ten, he went to the Elder Guangde Daci at Jintai to receive the tonsure.

Reflecting that the matter of birth and death was of great importance, he received full ordination and thoroughly investigated the essential tenets of both the *Xing* (Nature) and *Xiang* (Phenomena) schools. Realizing these were not the ultimate point, he subsequently traveled to Shaolin to study under Master Huanxiu Run.
Run asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the North. Run said, "As for the teachings and methods of the North, compared to this..."
"How is this? the Master said, "A single source flows out, dividing into a thousand streams. Yunrui said, "If that is so, then why must one come to this?

The Master said, "A single source flows out, dividing into a thousand streams. Yunrui approved of this. He then appointed the Master as the Chief Steward (Karmadāna) and retired to seclusion at Mount Wutai.
During the day he took but one meal; at night he sat alone. After some time, he reflected upon the distinctions [of phenomena].

Wisdom must not fail to be clear. Thereupon, he traveled extensively through various regions. As for all those ascetic practices that cause people to wince in distress, the Master experienced them all personally.

Later, upon arriving at Shicheng, his intensity of exertion exceeded the limit, and suddenly both his eyes went blind. The Master said, "This illusory body does not truly exist; from where could illness come?
He then let go of both body and mind simultaneously and sat rigidly for seven days, after which both his eyes were restored to sight.
The Master should have been invited to reside at Dongta on Hezhuo, Yunju on Yu, and Mount Kūanglu. Ascending the seat, he struck the *maṇḍala* (the circle) gesture and asked, "Do you understand?
If you can understand it right here, you will be secure and at ease. If you seek it elsewhere, you will instead be hindered by this very thing.
The mountain monk formerly stayed at Gudao; there I observed him interrogating the mind through the seven locations, and I personally felt a sense of vast emptiness.
Aha! Had it not been for tearing open the face of Bodhidharma before the rock wall, one would have remained a mere imitation of the original, with no end in sight.
O assembly, as for the very face of Bodhidharma—each of you must see it directly once before it will do.
Otherwise, you will merely prattle about "yellows" and "blacks" in the eastern streets and western markets, failing to avoid exposing your flaws when meeting those from your own household.
"Unfurling [the banner]. Now tell me: who is the one from within the family? He took up his staff and said, "A face seen is not as good as a name heard.

He threw down the staff and descended from the seat. Later, wishing to spend his final years at Mount Tai (Wutai Shan), the monastics and laypeople of Yue province earnestly entreated the Master to return to the Baolin Monastery.
After he passed away, his Dharma heir, Master Zhanran Cheng, escorted his reliquary casket to be enshrined in a stupa at Mount Nan of Xiansheng Monastery.

At the foot of this mountain, there was Chan Master Huanglong Shouchang Wuming Huijing of Jianchang, a dharma successor of Chan Master Linshan Zhong. He was the son of the Pei family of Chongren in Fuzhou; he was born...
At that time, she faced a difficult labor. Her grandfather recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and she was delivered; consequently, he named her Gyeong (Sutra).

From birth, she was exceptionally gifted, and as she grew, her appearance became mature and ancient-looking. At nine years of age, she entered a local school, where she immediately asked, "What is this 'vast and sublime qi' (*hao ran zhi qi*)?

The teacher marveled at her. Later, she followed National Preceptor Chung of Im-san Mountain to leave the household life. She constantly harbored doubts regarding the four-line verse of the *Vajracchedikā*.
Zhiju happened to see a verse by Master Fu Dashi which said: "If one discusses the four-line gāthā, it should never depart from the body.

He suddenly felt a sense of liberation and, having taken leave of Lingshan, went into seclusion on Mount E. Once, while ascending the summit and looking out across the landscape, he composed this verse:
Treading upon the first peak above the clouds, the vastness before one’s eyes makes the empty sky seem small. At that time, though I wished to see you, there was no way to meet face-to-face;
today we have met, and everywhere is the same. For three years he dwelt in a thatched hut, unknown to anyone.
While reading the *Chuan Deng Lu*, he saw a monk ask Xingshan, "What is the Way? Shan replied, "A magnificent mountain. The Master contemplated this day and night until he forgot everything else.
While he was eating and sleeping one day, as he was moving a stone, it was so solid that it could not be lifted. As he pushed with all his might, he attained a sudden and great enlightenment.
He immediately composed a verse, saying: "If you wish to study the Way of Unsurpassed Bodhi, Hurry to clear away this great mountain.
Only when you know the Way do you realize the mountain is no good; Turn yourself around and leap out of the Patriarchs' Barrier. He then went to Linsan to present the verse to Zhonghe.

Shang immediately granted his approval, finally permitting him to shave his head and receive full ordination. From that time forth, he served at his master’s side with diligent devotion, studying and refining himself day and night.
For twenty-four years he remained within the mountains, never venturing outside. When he reached the age of fifty-one, he went to reside at Baofang Monastery.
Entering the hall, he struck his staff once and said: "The matters of the ancestral vehicle are difficult to express in words; such is the gateway to the Great Way."
It brooks no deliberation or conjecture. At ease, he lets loose a single pivot; it is like the great sword *āyudha* drawn from its scabbard—those who encounter it die before time has passed.
It is like a drum smeared with poison; those who hear its strike perish before their heels have even turned. As it is said: "The steep peaks of the Wondrous Summit leave wild beasts no place to hide;
the crystalline radiance of the Jewel Tree leaves no sanctuary for the numinous birds. Its function is to chase the golden-haired lion alone.
Returning to the wild caves, he pursued Tie'e directly into the deep mountains. He swept away the fox-tracks of the world and brushed aside the dregs of human defilement.
He rescued those fallen into pits and ravines and revealed those who were lost, obstructed, or trapped within their shells.

His merit was such that he caused the Dharma-realm, the world-realm, and the space-realm to be perceived as a single essence; and he enabled the paths of Buddhas, humans, and hell-beings to be seen as one.
Fahong said, "Although it is so, it is still not yet the matter of the ultimate upward direction. Tell me: what is the one phrase that transcends all categories and limits?
When the true command is not yet exercised, the head is struck off first; with a single nudge of the great capacity, the sages and worthies are moved to sorrow."
"Long standing, take care. [He] ascends the hall. "A true son of the dragons and elephants: sometimes he can lift it up but cannot let it down;
sometimes he can let it down but cannot lift it up. He does not play with the head of a dead snake, yet he seeks to stroke the tail of a live tiger.
Sometimes he strides upon the back of a golden-haired lion, and naturally a pure breeze rises from beneath his feet. Do you understand? When the water does not dry up, the fish of themselves..."
In a secluded place where the mountains are green and serene, birds dwell in tranquility. A monk came to take his leave.
The Master asked, "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman on the platform—I have thoroughly exposed her for you. Ultimately, in what way was she exposed?
The monk said, "Today, you, Master, have been caught in a lapse. The Master said, "Throughout my entire life, I could not help it. Let me show you how it is. If...
"Indeed, it is a meeting. Bring it forward and show it to me. As the monk was about to offer a word, the Master struck him with a staff and said:

"This fellow who plunders the void! To have a beginning but no end is the livelihood of a patch-robed monk; to have an end but no beginning is the constant rule of a patch-robed monk; to have both beginning and end is the household gear of a patch-robed monk;
to have neither beginning nor end is the very core of a patch-robed monk. If you can penetrate this single phrase, [you will transcend] birth and death."
Mastery. If one penetrates two phrases, one comes and goes with freedom. If one penetrates three phrases, one may serve as a teacher for humans and devas.
If one penetrates all four phrases, one may serve as a teacher for Buddhas and patriarchs. "Great assembly, how will you penetrate them? After a long silence, he said:
"Five tigers soar through the void, clustering around the jade hare; two phoenixes ascend to the heavens, chasing the golden crow. A monk asked the Master:
"Why do you not travel on foot? The Master said: "The wooden horse refuses the whip and stretches its legs across; the iron ox does not pull the rope and simply lowers its head.
The white crane pecks at the fish with its neck held straight; the turtledove calls for rain with its beak hooked. Do you understand? The monk had no reply.
The Master said: "Setting out on a pilgrimage. Ascending the hall, he said: "When the sinews are pulled out, the skin does not move; when the bones are replaced, no blood is seen.

When the tendons and bones are all made empty, one wanders about without falling. Great Master Bodhidharma understood extinction but not birth; the Elder Śākyamuni understood birth but not extinction.
If you wish to know that birth and extinction do not interfere with one another, it must be the dried dung-stick from those years."
[The Master] let out a shout. A monk asked, "What is it like before we have met? The Master said, "Today I will not answer questions.
The monk pressed further, "And what about after we have met? The Master said, "I told you I would not answer questions.

As the monk was about to pose another question, the Master struck him, saying, "This is a total waste of people! The Master resided at three monasteries—Baofeng, E'feng, and Shouchang—and separately established a hermitage.

The monastery comprised more than twenty buildings. Even at the age of seventy, he still mingled with the laboring monks, never ceasing his work of plowing and digging. His chamber was desolate, containing nothing but his tools for manual labor.
King Yi held the Master’s virtue and wisdom in high esteem and praised him deeply, often sighing, "The time since the Sage has passed so long;
it is fortunate that this old man remains. On the seventh day of the twelfth month of the Ding-si year of the Wanli era, the Master returned from the fields and addressed the assembly.
He said, "From this day forth, this old monk shall no longer lay stones. The assembly was all struck with astonishment.

On the eve of the year’s end, he ascended the hall and said, "This year, there is only this moment remaining. Let me ask you all: do you know it or not? That matter has not yet been personally struck;
you must truly apply yourselves with the effort of one facing death. He further said, 'This is the final instruction of this old monk.'"
Everyone should cherish this deeply. On the thirteenth day of the new year, he manifested a slight illness. He subsequently ceased eating and said, "This old monk is not ill;

it is time for me to depart. The assembly sat around him in attendance, feeling distressed. The Master admonished them with a verse, saying: "Human life involves receiving, yet there is no recompense.
Do not be panicked by old age, sickness, and death. How laughable! The Dharma-patience of non-arising— By what karmic consciousness shall it be extinguished?"

At one time, the clouds cleared and auspicious light radiated forth; the Buddhas and Patriarchs briefly rested in this *dōjō*. On the fourteenth day, he wrote his parting words for the monastics and the laity.
On the sixteenth day, he composed a verse for the lighting of the funeral pyre, saying: "From beginningless kalpas it has been only this very thing; today, once again, it is still this very thing.
Furthermore, by means of this very thing, one brings that other thing to completion; this very thing and that other thing abide together in peace and joy. He then commanded his attendant...

[He] acted on his behalf by lighting the fire and reciting verses. The following morning, he took water to wash his face, rinse his mouth, and wipe his body, saying, "There is no need for further bathing.
He then sought out a brush and wrote in large characters: "Today, the clear instruction has been given. Having cast down the brush, he sat upright and passed away. His body was cremated.
A five-colored light issued forth, and his cranial bone and teeth remained uncorrupted. A stupa was immediately erected in the abbot’s quarters of his original temple.
He was a Dharma successor of Chan Master Da’ue Nian, the fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan.
Chan Master Zhanyuan Yuancheng of Xian-sheng Yunmen in Yuezhou was the son of the Xia family of Huiji. His mother dreamed that a monk entered her room before she became pregnant.

On the twenty-eighth day of the intercalary fourth month, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture without illness, having spoken a verse. His stupa was erected atop Daque Tan to the east of the monastery.
Chan Master Baizong of Shanguan in Jingxi was a native of the Gong clan from Pingyang in Shanxi; he was ten years old [when he entered the order].
At age six, he left home at Sanyuan Hermitage and received the full precepts from Vinaya Master Yinguang of Putuo.
At twenty-nine, he visited Tiantong Wu and questioned him regarding the ultimate matter. Not long after, he went to consult Bao’en Xiu, who asked: "The entire earth is a single fiery pit;
what samādhi must one attain so as not to be burned? The Master replied: "Gold cannot be traded for gold. Xiu approved of this. Later...
He presented his *kāṣāya* robe to his teacher. When Xiu retired from his position as the Dharma Mother of the Great Hero (Śākyamuni), he charged his teacher to succeed him on the seat.

Subsequently, he moved to Haihui Temple and ascended the hall. His perfect capacity and great function were fully manifested everywhere; the true teaching beyond the categories was revealed according to the circumstances.
Therefore it is said: In heaven they form the celestial images; on earth they take shape as forms. In the sun and moon they provide illumination;

in the four seasons they manifest cold and heat. They fill the valleys when in the valleys and fill the pits when in the pits. When sentient, they move and act; when insentient, they stand in majestic array and shine brilliantly.
All beings among gods and humans alike receive this power of grace. Now tell me: how do they transcend the multitudes and rise above them?
*Jui* (Gathering). How would you say it? "Over the vast water fields, white egrets fly; in the deep summer trees, yellow orioles sing.
The Master was born on the thirtieth day of the tenth month in the Renzi year of the Wanli era. He entered nirvana on the nineteenth day of the ninth month in the Jiayin year of the Kangxi era.
His worldly age was sixty-three, and his monastic seniority was forty-seven. His stupa was built beside Haihui Temple. There is [a record].
Several volumes of his recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world.
Chan Master Foutui Yong of Gaotai on Mount Nanyue was the son of the Han family of Qiantang.
He received the tonsure under Yan Yun of Jishan and followed Chan Master Quan’an Jin up Mount Jinche to study with Da jue Xiu, who instructed him to investigate that which exists prior to birth.
One day, while on communal work duty (*pǔqǐng*), he saw a monk walking along carrying an empty basket and attained a realization.

Subsequently, while serving Master Xiu in the abbot’s quarters, Xiu asked the monk, "It is easy to transform mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into oneself; it is difficult to transform oneself back into mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
How do you understand this? The Master was standing nearby; having penetrated to the very source of the Dharma, his spiritual capacity and function from that point onward became transcendent.
Xiu took his robe and whisk and handed them to him. He emerged into the world at Fahai in Wuxing; subsequently, he resided at Gaotai. Entering the hall, he said:
"Those Zen guests with copper heads and iron jaws have a life-taking talisman slung across their elbows; yet they still cannot swallow this brazier."
Ice and frost refine the liver and gallbladder; suddenly, one turns the body from the Southern Dipper to the North.
Sitting amidst the fires of the Red County and the Divine Land—this is the Small Sermon. Three rooms of a dilapidated hut pierce the Heavenly Eye; a seven-foot black staff wipes clean the Great Void.
To clarify the three mysteries of Linji, one dances the *zhazi* in a thicket of thorns. Last night, the Unranked True Person rode backward...
A three-legged donkey goes straight up to the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom peak, wishing to deliver a message to all people.
He plants his staff and descends from the seat. Small Assembly Sermon: An oil jar hangs from the beak of an old crow; The moon falls upon the cold pines, causing a startle.
One slip of the tongue and the mouth falls off; meeting people, one shouts two or three times. But tell me, what is it that is being shouted?
[The Master] suddenly lets out a shout and descends from his seat. Small Assembly Sermon: A drunken face like a peach blossoms with a smiling mouth;
Withered willows hanging low unfurl spring eyebrows. How laughable is Lingyun’s wildness, Startling a myriad red petals from the branches. [He] looks at the assembly and says:

Is there anyone who has such a thorough realization? When this mountain monk speaks these words in this manner, all eighty-four thousand hairs of my body are cast entirely into the embrace of you, honorable ones.
If it is not yet so, simply prepare a heart of resolve, and I shall certainly not deceive you.

Chan Master Guruyāna (Guer-yen) of Ba’en Temple on Guyan Peak in Huzhou was surnamed Wen. His ancestors were from Huaren County in Shanxi;
his distant forebear was the Grand Marshal Xiangqing, who later migrated to Wucheng in Zhejiang, where the family became renowned for their hidden virtues.

From birth, the Master possessed extraordinary qualities and was deeply devoted to the Buddha Vehicle. He went to Master Shou of Yangshan to receive the tonsure and subsequently attended upon Master Yuan of Ba’en.
[The Master] was present. He heard Xiu instructing the assembly, saying: "Simply realize it before your parents were yet born; then it will naturally be vast, great, and perfect.
At these words, the Master attained a realization. One day, Xiu asked: "How is it that you maintain mastery during the bustling activity of midday?
The Master replied: "The real does not conceal the false. Xiu asked: "How is it that you maintain mastery during the sleep and dreams of the night?"
The Master said, "Crookedness does not conceal the straight. Xiu asked, "When one is fast asleep—without dreams, without thoughts, without seeing, and without hearing—where is the true host?
The Master answered with some dozen or so words, but Xiu did not accept them in any case. One day, the Master replied, "A household has no two masters.
Xiu said, "It is like a single donkey tied to a hitching post. At this, the Master was immediately set free from his doubts.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The azure green reaches to the heavens, the shade of the pines spreads wide. The peach branches are red, the plum branches are white.

He rubbed his middle finger with his hand. Suppose a monk were to come forth and say, "Venerable Sir, you deserve thirty blows"—one could not blame him either.
He was born on the tenth day of the first month in the Jiwei year of the Wanli era, and passed away on the twenty-sixth day of the sixth month in the Dingchou year of the Kangxi era.
As he toured the various quarters, he said, "The old monk shall not return. That evening, he briefly manifested a subtle sign.
He fell ill. He immediately sought out a brush and wrote a verse. An attendant monk, thinking the Master had over-eaten, tried to dissuade him with excuses.
The Master said, "Since you did not bring it [the brush] here, you must not say later that I have no verse. Thereupon, he ceased speaking. A day passed without him rising.

When the assembly requested him to preach the Dharma, the Master turned his body and passed away facing the wall. His worldly age was seventy-nine; his years as a monk were... (monk’s ordination years).
Fifty-nine. His entire-body stupa is located to the left of the main temple. His *yulu* (recorded sayings) circulates in the world.
Chan Master Xingyue of Qiyun at Ba’en Temple in Wukang, Huzhou, was born into the Shen family of Wucheng. His family had long been a prominent clan.
In his youth, he was enrolled as a scholar in the local school. Initially, while still a layman, he visited the Elder Dajue at Ba’en Temple during the Shunzhi era.

In the year of Yiyou (1065), he went to Da’jue to shave his head and don the robes of a monk. In the autumn of Dinghai (1067), while serving Da’jue in Huai-north, after providing for his own begging and cooking, Da’jue took the strength of his labor to carve him with an awl.

One day, he asked Da’jue: "When the state of emptiness is utterly desolate and the state of brocade is brilliantly radiant—when the brilliance of the brocade is the utter desolation of emptiness—what then?
Da’jue said, "Wait until you reach this realm, and I will tell you. The Master prostrated himself.
Xie Jue said, "This fellow has harbored deluded thoughts for a long time; today they are finally severed. The Master attained realization.

In the spring of the Gengzi year, he accompanied Jue back to the mountains in response to an imperial summons. He entered the Tongbai Palace on Mount Tiantai, where he wore grass garments, lived on wood and water, and practiced the dhūta austerities.

Three years passed, through both cold and heat. In the spring of the *guimao* year, Master Jue commanded me to succeed him at the seat of Baoen. In the evening assembly, he said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya.
To raise a model and draw a likeness is like having a thousand million emanations; it is like pressing one's eyes and seeing flowers where none exist.

He constantly reveals himself to people of this age, yet his appearance is quite disheveled. People themselves simply do not recognize him. Let us examine this briefly. He called out to the assembly: "Is there anyone who can offer praise?"
There is not even a fraction [of it]. [The Master] suddenly held up his whisk and said: "Offer this body and mind to every dust mote and land; this is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Evening Sermon: The season of autumn does not spare us. The west wind blows rain as the pond falls into evening gloom.
In the ancient hall, the shadows of pines open in winding patterns; the sound of the bell pierces through to the path ahead of the mountains. Look back quickly—what is it? Evening.
"Consider this. Great Master Linji said: 'A single phrase contains the three mysteries; each mystery contains the three essentials.

Service. One seeks only within a single phrase to reveal the ground of the mind and bring the Great Matter to completion.

A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? He replied, "A dried piece of dung. A monk asked Dongshan, "What is..."
"This is the Buddha. [The Master] took three *sheng* of hemp seed. A monk asked Fengxue, "What is the Buddha? [He replied,] "The bamboo-stalk whip beneath the Zhangling Mountains.
A monk asked Shoushan, "What is the Buddha? [He replied,] "The daughter-in-law riding the donkey, while her mother-in-law leads it.

[He] struck the whisk once more and said, "Do you understand yet? He then descended from his seat.

On the twenty-seventh day of the tenth month in the winter of the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, he passed away at the abbot’s quarters of Baoen Temple. His secular age was fifty-three, and his years as a monk were twenty-two.
He was interred in a western valley of the temple.
Chan Master Zixi Sen of Yuanzhao Temple in Hangzhou was the son of the Li family of Boluo, Huizhou. His mother dreamed that white light entered her bosom when he was born.
His features were elegant and refined, like a crane standing out from among a flock of chickens. He read widely through the classics and histories, grasping their meaning at first sight.
At the age of seventeen, he left home to follow Master Dugong Zongbao, where he shaved his head and received the full precepts. Subsequently, he traveled to Yunmen to seek further instruction.
Xin asked, "A purple swallow circles the flowered mansion; the plum fruit is at its peak of fragrance and ripeness. What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?

The Master said, "I have never heard of such a thing. Xin said, "It seems you have asked the wrong question. Later, he visited Dajue Xiu at Daxiong and was instructed to compose a verse on his "original face.
The Master immediately said: "The Teao Creek winds and turns, its waters babbling; ten thousand layers of passes and mountains, all beneath one..."

The surroundings were secluded. After a sudden rain followed by clearing skies and the dispersal of clouds, the wind and moon filled the heavens and reached the human world. Xiu nodded in agreement and subsequently appointed him to ordain monks.

His engagement with students was swift and incisive, and his reputation spread far and wide among the practitioners. He went forth to reside at Laozu and established the Dharma seat at Longxi. On the occasion of a small-scale *can* (sermon) for the Buddha’s birthday, he gave this address:
"According to ancient tradition, it is said that Śākyamuni Buddha was born today; I do not know whether this is true or not."

In the summer of the Jihai year of the Shunzhi era, Xiu responded to the imperial summons and returned to the mountains.

Clearly, clearly. What is asked about the face before birth? Who discusses the pear blossom smiling at the sun?

The Master asked the fire-tender, "Has the rootless tree been cut down yet? The tender had no reply. The next morning, the Master said, "Last night I was looking at the rootless tree;

Tang hesitated, as if deliberating. The Master struck him with his palm. He then ascended the seat, raised his whisk, and said: "A multitude of disciples come up; a multitude of disciples go down.
