The Master replied, "Today my ears are deaf. Yuanjue said, "Why do you not say, 'The subordinate official acts with haste'?
The next day, Yuanjue asked the Master again, "What is it to conceal the point within the matter? The Master pointed to the inkstone on the table.
Jue said, "The inkstone. All the people in the great earth cannot lift it. Jue asked, "What is 'concealing the point within principle'?
The Master said, "The void envelops the great thousandfold world-system. Jue asked, "What is 'concealing the point in both principle and phenomena'?
The Master said, "To call it the void is actually the inkstone; to call it the inkstone is actually the void. Jue asked, "What is 'not... [The text here is incomplete].

When Sheli entered the hall, the Master said, "I do not recognize this one. He struck him and drove him out. When the Elder Caotang passed away, Zhiyue grieved so deeply that he neglected his own appearance and ritual decorum;
the assembly likewise sealed the pots and closed the kitchen. Zhiyue gave a formal instruction, saying, "What would it be like if I were the Prince Nanda?
The Master stepped forward and said, "If there is joy, we share it together. Zhiyue then ordered the kitchen to be opened. This was in the autumn of the Yiwu year of the Shunzhi reign (1655).
The various donors of Jingxi earnestly entreated the Elder Dajue to take charge of Qingshan. Dajue then instructed Master Jueling to serve as the head of the assembly.
When he reached the age of seventy, Dajue finally ordered him to ascend the seat and open the hall, presenting him with a verse that said: "Reaching seventy years of age, you finally open the hall;
You have long been accustomed to entering the ranks of the assembly. Today, upon this throne of the Jewel-Flower King, [Your] black staff..."
"It is best to proclaim it where there is pain. A monk asked, "The great bell is on its stand; it responds as soon as it is struck. Before it is struck, where is the sound?
The Master said, "Rarely do we encounter those who truly understand. The monk pressed further, "Why is it that I do not hear it? The Master said, "How can you blame me, this mountain monk?
Another monk asked, "One overturns the great ocean and shakes the void; why then, on level ground, does one fail to lift their feet?"

[The Master] rose. The Master said: "It is easy to emerge from within the gate; it is difficult for the body to exit through the gate. A monk asked: "How does one advance further atop a hundred-foot pole?
The Master said: "Withdraw quickly! Withdraw quickly! [The monk] pressed further: "What is it like after withdrawing? The Master said: "A clumsy lacquer bucket.
In the spring of the Ding-si year of the Kangxi era, the assembly requested that he succeed to the seat at Tianmu. In the year Wu-wu, there was a great drought. In the following spring—
He took his alms bowl to Gusu and returned once more to Qishui, where he finally manifested parinirvāṇa. His worldly age was eighty-two.
His disciples escorted his reliquary casket and enshrined it in a stupa at the Shouzang (Life-Store) on Mount Qing. Ten volumes of his recorded sayings have been circulated in the world.
Chan Master Xingjue of Chongfu Jizhi Monastery in Liangzhu, Hangzhou, was the son of the Wang family of Cixi, Siming. He lost his father at a young age and endured hardship.

Upon reaching adulthood, he often reflected that the world is vast and expansive, and wondered from where it begins and ends. One day, while passing by a lecture hall, he happened upon a recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Immediately, he took up the urgent contemplation of birth and death and resolved to transcend the mundane world. At that time, he was twenty years old.
At twelve [years of age], having heard that Master Baoen was a great spiritual friend (*mahā-kalyāṇamitra*), he went forth to join the monastic order.

He was instructed to investigate the koan of "before one's parents were born. One day, upon entering the inner quarters, he requested further instruction on the koan of "no dreaming, no thinking, no seeing, and no hearing."
Before his words had even ceased, he was struck out with a staff by Jué. At that moment, the Master attained sudden enlightenment.
One day, Jué asked, "There is a phrase and there is no phrase, like a vine leaning against a tree. How do you understand this? The Master said, "Where there is water, it contains the moon;
where there is no mountain, it does not bear clouds. Jué said, "When the tree falls and the vine withers, what then? The Master said, "The clever rabbit moves its den to sleep in the tender grass."
"Grass! This deluded person still clings to a withered post. One day, Jue asked again, "Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman at Mount Tai has been thoroughly exposed by you.
Now tell me: was she exposed or not? The Master said, "She was exposed. Jue asked, "Where was she exposed?
The Master said, "Exhausting one's own mind, one laughs the other's mouth to pieces. Jue—
Yun said, "In that case, Zhaozhou is also included within this. The Master said, "If you know, then you have it. Jue laughed and said, "Do you feel your face growing heavy?
The Master then bowed his head low. Jue said, "This mountain monk has committed a transgression. The Master paid his respects.
Jue nodded in understanding. He then thatched a hut at Dàshèng Ān on the front stream, where he rested his head upon stones and tilled the clouds, living with refined ease and self-satisfaction.

After the Elder Dàjué had passed away, the Master accepted an invitation to reside at Chóngfú Temple. When a monk came for an audience, the Master asked him, "Are you reciting the *Pǔfó* [Universal Buddha] liturgy today?
The monk replied, "I am. The Master asked, "Who is it that recites the Buddha's name? The monk said, "I do not know. The Master said:
[The Master] rinsed his mouth and departed. A monk asked, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing—what is it?

The Master said, "This staff is seven feet long. The monk pressed further, "I do not understand. The Master said, "Help me across the waters of the broken bridge; accompany me back to the village of bright moonlight.
In the evening assembly, [the Master] raised the following: "In the past, Zen Master Dahui said: 'At Mount Jing’s estate, there is not an inch of land. Now...

In summer, I gather the necessary conditions as the occasion demands; too weary to discourse on the Way, too indolent to talk of Chan. With my staff, I pick up whatever comes along, all of it perfectly complete.
There is no need to stifle the mind or eliminate delusive thoughts; everyone simply eats their fill and then goes to sleep.

That they go to sleep is not in doubt, but suppose someone were to come in a dream demanding payment for the meal—what then? It is like a melody faintly heard, just barely worth listening to, when suddenly it is swept away by the wind.
While playing a different tune, the Master said: "Jingshan, in his search for people by entering the weeds, did not realize his tongue was dragging on the ground.
To examine this closely, it is very much like 'forcing the noble to become the lowly. At Chongfu, it is otherwise: Xiong峰 (Xiongpeng) does not set aside even half a mou of land;
daily he provides alms bowls to assist in the conditions of the assembly. There is no Way and there is no Chan—how could one possibly deceive those who have come from afar?"
Ten thousand and more. There is yet another point that is truly laughable: fleas bite and mosquitoes sting while the skull remains pierced. A-he-he!
Whether there is joy or not, everyone gathers together to eat a stalk of pickled vegetables. Not to call it a stalk of pickled vegetables would be a great error.
Having defeated seventeen hundred old rascals, the iron ox breaks through the golden rope. *Hè!* (A shout). He throws down his whisk and descends.
[The Master] sat down. Throughout his life, the Master had been frugal and parsimonious, and he was extremely cautious in granting permission [to teach].
One day, he suddenly manifested slight illness and said to his disciple Chizhen, "For forty years, I have not granted permission lightly. You must take responsibility for this matter.

He then bathed, changed his clothes, and when the assembly requested a verse, the Master said in a stern voice, "If there is no verse, would you rather I did not die? Thereupon, he passed away while sitting upright.
His worldly age was sixty-four, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇera-vassa) was forty-two.
His disciples enshrined his entire body and buried it to the right of the robe-and-bowl stupa of the Elder Dajue.
Chan Master Six Jie Xingheng of Zhulin at Jia Shan in Runzhou was the son of the Liu family of Jiangyin.
When he reached the age of twenty, he received his monastic training under the veteran master Weixin at Qianming Temple in his home district.

At the age of twenty-two, he went to visit Master Xiu of Qing Shan, who presented him with the koan regarding the state before one's parents were born. Subsequently, having received full ordination, he heard a neighboring monk receiving food in his alms bowl.

As the bowl made a sound, his body and mind suddenly leaped with joy. He immediately entered the room and informed Qingshan. Qingshan said, "Try saying it. As the Master was about to respond, Qingshan suddenly covered his mouth and said, "Speak!

Speak! The Master hesitated, and Qingshan struck him. Later, after Qingshan passed away, he followed the Elder Dajue at Baoen Monastery. When the Elder raised the koan of "swallowing all the water of the West River in one gulp," the Master gave the following verse:

A single gulp swallows the West River; The whole world is contained within the mouth. If you wish to know the meaning of this, Look at the face of the old man. (Note: The original text ends with "the Master gave the following verse" and provides the first line of the verse.)
His words did not accord [with the Master’s intent]. While crossing the Qiantang River, he attained realization. His verse says: The Western River’s single mouth swallows it all dry;
Shrimp, crabs, fish, and dragons—their lives are now secure. A man of great character, his spirit fully realized, From this very day, his belly is wide and vast.
In the autumn of the *Xinchou* year of the Shunzhi era, he accepted an invitation from Jia Shan Zhulin Temple, where he resided for nine years.
In the tenth month of the winter of the *Xinhai* year, he returned to reside at Jiashan Temple in Yunyang. A monk asked, "What is the Venerable One of Immovability?

The Master said, "The donkey goes away by itself; the horse comes by itself. A monk asked, "What are the Three Jewels as a single essence? The Master said, "One bowl of congee, two meals of rice. A monk asked. [The text ends here.]
"If one’s breath does not come for a moment, where will one go? The Master said, "Neither south of the River, nor north of the River.
He ascended the hall and said: "The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the grasses, trees, and forests—all these are the number of thousands of Buddhas throughout *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
They pierce your eyes; there is nowhere to evade them. 'On the water walking on the mountain; sitting in the fire at West River. [He] suddenly struck the meditation staff upon the desk."

Descending from his seat, the Master addressed the assembly. He cited the occasion when the World-Honored One was about to enter nirvana and Mañjuśrī requested that he turn the Wheel of Dharma once more.
The World-Honored One called out to Mañjuśrī, saying: "I have dwelt in this world for forty-nine years, yet I have never spoken a single word.
You ask me to turn the Wheel of Dharma again; have I ever turned the Wheel of Dharma? The Master said: "Mañjuśrī was pushed aside by the World-Honored One."
It was indeed so. Had I been there at that time, waiting for the World-Honored One to speak thus, I would have struck the gavel and declared:
"Behold clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King.

On the sixteenth day of the tenth month of the Ding-si year of the Kangxi era, the Master passed away at Hanyin-an in Bagongdong, Runzhou. He was sixty-five years of age and forty-four years since his ordination.
The disciples enshrined his entire remains to the right of Han Yin and erected a stupa there.
Chan Master Xingben of Xin’an Dao was a native of Xin’an. He attended upon the Elder Dajue at Chongfu Temple. One day, he presented two verses;
the first, a verse on the "Plucking of the Flower," said: "The Buddha-dharma is fundamentally no-dharma; it is but the everyday talk of those who eat porridge and rice."

"Water pouring on water; deceiving people and again picking up a flower. A verse regarding a non-Buddhist’s question to the Buddha says: "Mountains to the left, waters to the right, revealed in full majesty.

Silent transmission and secret entrustment—how could they be discussed? Only those who awaken know the true nature of human bone and marrow; it is difficult to take empty space and measure it with a bushel.
Jue remarked: "The Master was originally not skilled in literary composition; yet with these four characters, 'water pouring on water,' he instead scratched [the itch]."
This struck at the monk’s itchy spot and brought forth the events of the past; it was quite appropriate.
The Master (Jue) called to him again and asked, “When you were at Vulture Peak, what was it like when the World-Honored One held up the flower? The Master replied, “That was his point of failure.
Jue then raised his whisk and said to the assembly, “Everyone, speak! After a long silence, he said, “A single thread of cold is cast beyond the thousand peaks; the vastness...”
The fish and dragons stir in the desert; the thunder rolls in the earth. Later, the Master began to propagate the Dharma at Huashan in Xin’an, where a stone pagoda stands.
His attendant, Chan Master Xiaoyun Xingmou, was a native of Chu. He attended the Elder Dajue at Baoen Temple and realized the fundamental matter of his own being.
In the autumn of the Gengzi year of the Shunzhi era, he served Dajue once again when the latter received imperial edicts at Wanshadian and ascended the seat to preach.
The Master came forward and asked: "To have one's mouth swallow the Buddhas and Patriarchs is still to enter the mud and the water, where there is host and guest.

Why, then, are you instead atop the peaks of a thousand mountains? Jue said, "I am precisely seeking for you, Dharma brother, to speak in this manner. The Master said, "In this way, the wind of the School will be forever sustained, and all things will look up to it in reliance.
Jue said, "Pass over to that side; the site of enlightenment is complete. Jue then ascended the seat once more. The Master...
Another question was raised: "In the past there was Zhaozhou; today there is the Master. Jue gave a shout. The Master said, "One who praises another has something to test.
Jue said, "You have twice frustrated me. The Master said, "On the contrary, it is you who commit the offense."
Later, he returned to Chu. He passed away before entering the world [of public teaching].
Regarding the monk Xiangxue: he was a native of Changzhou in Gusu. He entered the monastic order under the Elder Dajue.
Jue Riyue asked the Master, "What is it that has not lacked salt and sauce for thirty years? The Master replied, "I have not been sparing with my display.
Jue then desisted.
Chan Master Xitang Qinshui Xingshao was originally from Jintai; having spent a long time in lecture halls, he went to attend upon Old Master Dajue.
Ren'en served Jue again at Tianmu Mountain, where he clarified his own realization. One day, Jue asked:
"Why is it that while the head, horns, and four hooves have all passed through, the tail cannot? Ren'en replied: "To sit and cut off the ten directions is still to receive a mark on the forehead;
move one step secretly and behold the flying dragon. Jue certified him with a verse: "The river of teaching enters deeply without getting wet."
Jiao. He reached the depths of the Chan realm and composed the verse "Seeing the Sun withered. Later, he returned to Jintai and entered nirvana at Changhua Temple.
Chan Master Fushi Dizang Hongji Yan of Chushu was the son of the Zhang family of Jiangzhou; he followed Da jue Xiu.
The Emperor summoned him to the Wanshan Hall. One day, while sitting together with Xiu, the Emperor asked the Master, "Where are you from?
The Master replied, "Pingyang, Shanxi. The Emperor asked, "How long has it been since you left home [to become a monk]? The Master replied, "Half a year. The Emperor then looked toward Xiu and said:
The Emperor asked, "Is it already late? Xiu replied, "It is. The Emperor said, "What about your former vows? Xiu said, "I have already seen my original face.
The Emperor asked, "What is your original face? The Master said, "Today I see Your Majesty in person.
The Emperor said, "What about you, Monk? The Master said, "That would be a double case. The Emperor was greatly pleased and gave him money for rain-offerings.
The Hermitage Master closed his quarters for retreat and gave a small discourse: "The entire great earth is this meditation room;

fundamentally, there is no coming or going. The entire great earth is this Dharma-body; fundamentally, there is no movement or stillness. Since there is neither coming nor going, and neither movement nor stillness, why do you make such a special effort today?
He then held up the envelope and said, "Do you understand? With a sudden stroke, he cuts off ten thousand layers of clouds—this is an iron wall."
The Silver Mountain must be pulverized.
On New Year’s Day, the Small Assembly (Xiao-chan) of Chan Master Zu-shan Dihai of Wan’an, the Master took up his whisk and drew a circle, saying:
“One year has twelve months; one month has thirty days; one day has twelve hours. Year after year, month after month...”
Day after day, at every hour, the Buddha Hall, the mountain gate, the lanterns, and the pillars—Hū Zhangsan and Hē Lìsì—bump heads and knock foreheads as they bow for the New Year.
Face-to-face, they present themselves; there is neither self nor other. [The Master] puts down his whisk and says: "It is still cold in the first month of spring.
I pray you take care. The Master asked a monk: "Going out through the rain and wind, returning under the stars and with the moon. As if...
"What is the master amidst the dust? The monk advanced and said, "The north wind fills my face. The Master smiled and said, "It has been troublesome for you, *śrāmaṇera*.
In the autumn of the Bingwu year of the Kangxi era, the Master manifested a slight illness. He spoke to his disciples, saying, "The four elements are but a provisional combination;
I shall not remain in this world for long. He then spoke a verse: "The golden wind whistles, scattering yellow leaves; The bright moon is round, pervading the nine realms. A single phrase..."
He was clearly enlightened, transcending all phenomena; there was no need for groundless doubt or conjecture.

On the fifth day of the eleventh month, he assembled the community to reveal the essentials of the Dharma, and subsequently appointed the West Hall Master Chaoding to succeed him as abbot of the Fangzhang. At the hour of midnight, he sat in the lotus posture and passed away.
He was fifty-one years of age and had twenty-one years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*). After his cremation, several *śarīra* relics were obtained.
Several days later, there were still those who found it among the grass. In the summer of the Wushen year, a stupa was erected at the mountain’s base;
Gong Dingzi, Minister of War of Huainan, composed its inscription.
*Zhengyuan Lueji*, Scroll Five.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Śramaṇas (Bǎolún, Jìyuán, Gāomín, Liǎozhēn) of Wéiyáng;
edited by Dázhēn of Guīng Temple, Tiantái.
Chan Master Zhengming Yangzhuo of Da Mei in Tanzhou,
the thirty-fifth generation descendant of Nanyue and dharma heir of Chan Master Xue of Wufeng, was born into the Chang family of Puzhou as the second son of Lu Shan.
From childhood, he yearned for the supramundane Dharma. At twenty, he took leave of his parents and shaved his head at Putuo Shan.

He first visited Jinsu (Yunqi Zhuhong), but he was unable to grasp the essential meaning under the master’s staff. One day, seeing a monk reading the *Record of Wanfeng*, he encountered the koan regarding "Where does one return?
and began to investigate it with great intensity. At that time, Wufeng Xue was serving as the West Hall Attendant at Jinsu; the Master went to seek instruction from him. Wufeng used a bamboo...
Biji struck him, saying, "To perceive even a single object with the eyes is not it; to see even a hair’s breadth is already dust.
At that moment, the Master forgot both mind and environment, yet there remained only a single concern, like a hundred-jin load he could not set down.
One day, upon entering the room for instruction, Shul asked, "What have you come for? The Master replied, "I am carrying water. Shul asked, "Where is the bucket? The Master—

As he was about to respond, Xulu struck him on the head with his staff and said, "It is broken! From this point on, the Master realized the essential point of the mind. He served [Xulu] for six years.
A fellow practitioner wished to live in seclusion together with the Master, but the Master said, "I have three conditions for living in seclusion:

first, that my primary task is completed; second, that there is no military conflict to travel through; and third, that there is no virtuous teacher presiding over a hall. Only when these are met will I stay."
Later, he resided at Mount Daguai under Master [Fengxue] as the Chief Administrative Officer (Jianyuan). Addressing the assembly, the Master said: "A man of great character need not deliberate;
He turns his body and draws forth a blade of keen-edged hair. The Great Eagle spreads its wings beyond all obstruction, Passing straight through a thousand layers and ten thousand folds."
The Master entered nirvana in the spring of the Jichou year of the Shunzhi era. His stupa was erected on the front ridge of his home mountain.
Among the fourteen dharma heirs of Chan Master Han Yue Cang, there was Chan Master Sanfeng Fanyi of Suzhou, a son of the Tao family of Haiyu. In his youth, he followed Master Lang of Baoyan.
Tiyu went to Sanfeng, who instructed him to contemplate the "Cane" koan. One night, upon hearing the sound of pines, he attained realization. Sanfeng asked, "Where do you currently practice?
The Master replied, "Seated firmly upon the stone bench at midnight, a single cry of a cold wild goose breaks through the clouds.
Sanfeng nodded in approval. In the seventh year of the Tianqi era, he succeeded him as the abbot of Sanfeng. [Ascending the hall,] he broke [the silence]: [...breaks...]
The cave of ignorance—where is its home? Treading over and overturning the mountain of self and person—who is the master? Entering as a demon or entering as a Buddha, acting spontaneously and freely;
calling for a horse, calling for an ox—who can point it out? The water flows on of itself and the clouds have no destination;
the waters are vast and the heavens are boundless. He let out a shout and said: "Which of these is the originally abiding Buddha-mind-ground? The Master fell silent.
In the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era, the pagoda was constructed at the home mountain.
Chan Master Cheng Yimo of Dou-shui in Hangzhou, a native of the Huang family of Qiantang, was twenty-three years old when he went to Zhenru Temple to receive the tonsure.
He entered Yunqi to receive the *śrāmaṇera* precepts, subsequently visited Yunmen for full ordination (*upasampadā*), and thereafter studied under Master San.
Feng practiced for seven years without attaining realization. At that time, his fellow student Danyu Yuan urged him, saying, "This matter has been neglected for many years;
if you do not understand it clearly, how will you ever resolve it? The Master was so overcome with shame and perspiration down his back that he could not answer.
That evening, they sat until the fourth watch. Yuan brought up the story of the bamboo whisk to question him. As the Master was about to respond, Yuan—

The Master suddenly covered the teacher’s mouth with his hand, whereupon he attained realization. He said, “I understand. Yuan said, “Setting aside your understanding for a moment, what about when birth and death arrive?
The Master then gave a shout. Yuan asked, “What is the meaning of that shout?
The Master replied, “It has already cut off your old brother’s tongue. He then proceeded to the abbot’s quarters to present his realization. Feng nodded in approval. One.

One day, while serving at Feng’s peak, the Master heard a monk request instruction on the "Three Mysteries" (sanxuan). Feng took a sheet of red paper in his hand, turned it over, and showed it to him.
Suddenly, the Master realized the meaning of the two water buffaloes with their double horns having no enclosure.
Feng expressed his joy for him and appointed him to the position of First Seat. Later, he went out to reside at Mount Heng. A monk asked: "What is the Buddha-dharma?"
[The monk] asked for the general meaning of the *Dazhuo*. The Master struck his mouth with his staff, saying, "Swift as an imperial decree.
As the monk hesitated, the Master struck him three times. A monk asked, "What is the upward-moving pivot? The Master said, "A tiger's head grows two horns."
The Master passed away in the *Xinsi* year of the Chongzhen era; he was sixty-seven years old and had been a monk for forty-four years.
His stupa is at Dengwu. Chan Master Wenshi Cheng of Jiaoshan in Runzhou was the son of Xiong of Jingling.
He attended Sanfeng Zang, and one day while standing in attendance, a monk asked Zang: "When there are no walls on the ten directions and no gates on the four sides, what then?"
Zang let out a thunderous shout. The Master attained realization from the side. He went forth into the world at Jiaoshan on Haimen. Later, he moved to the Hall at Jiufeng.
He covers heaven and earth; he penetrates past and present. The vast void cannot be used as a metaphor for his greatness; a mote of dust cannot be used as a metaphor for his minuteness.
When demons and spirits hear him, their gallbladders split; when ghosts and monsters encounter him, their souls dissolve. But tell me, what is it?
"What is this? A three-headed wooden horse neighs as it gallops into the wind; a one-legged earthen ox bellows as it comes under the moon.
The Master successively presided over Jiufeng Zhengjue, Taiping Xingguo, and the two mountains of Jinshan and Jiaoshan in Runzhou.

In the Dingchou year of the Chongzhen era, Prime Minister He Zhiyue invited him to head Tianlong Monastery in the White Gate (Nanjing). He sent numerous letters inquiring about the Way. In the Jimao year, the Prince of Chu invited the Master.
He arrived at Wuchang and preached the Dharma at Xiaota Temple on Hongshan. Later, he resided at Baiyun on Shenshan as a means for his retirement in leisure.
One day, manifesting a slight illness, he gathered the assembly to bid them farewell, saying: "You all should arouse diligent and courageous effort;

then you shall awaken to the principle that accords with the occasion, unimpeded and indestructible. He then wrote a verse and passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. At that time, it was the year of Yihai in the Shunzhi era.
The year was the eighth month of the You year, the twentieth day. His age was sixty-one. His disciples erected a stupa at the summit of the mountain behind Baiyun Temple.
He was posthumously titled Huizhao.
Chan Master Dacu Zheng of Huazang Monastery in Wuxi, a native of the Zhu family of this very locality, ascended the hall.

Brandishing his whisk, he said: "With a single stroke of this white whisk, I tear down the demonic palaces of the five aggregates. Taking up his staff, he said: "By wielding this black rattan cane, I shatter the Buddha-lands of the ten directions.
Raising one hand, he said: "Stretching forth my hand causes the drunken elephant to flee in terror. He snapped his fingers once.
He said, "By snapping his fingers, the venomous dragon was subdued. Among these four statements, one has the guest but lacks the host;
one has the host but lacks the guest; one has neither guest nor host at all; and one has both guest and host fully present.
Can you all discern which is which? On the sixteenth day of the ninth month in the third year of the Shunzhi era, he passed away at the age of fifty-nine.
Tafeng was at Sanfeng.
Chan Master Dingmu Cheshi of Suzhou’s Ruiguang Temple was the son of the Bai family of Jinling. He went to attend upon Master Sanfeng Zang;
when a bamboo chair fell over and made a sound, he attained great enlightenment. Sanfeng immediately expressed his joy. Dingmu subsequently presided over Sanfeng and later moved to Ruiguang.
Guang ascended the hall. "Where the cliff stands ten thousand fathoms high, the trap for tigers is deep; when arrow-points meet, the crossbow is heavy as a thousand-jin weight.
Is there anyone here now who can achieve the auspicious light? As soon as a monk stepped forward, the Master struck him and addressed the assembly:
"A shout that splits the face! Standing ten thousand fathoms high, one violently collides with it and shatters the skull, straightway making even stone..."
The man clenched his two feet into fists and shrank back into the herd of oxen. Startling the wooden fish, he turned over and leaped up, plunging into the pool of the venomous dragon.
When the wind and rain had ceased throughout the heavens, the bright moon rose once more from the sea.
On the eighth day of the ninth month of the Wuzi year of the Shunzhi era, he passed away peacefully. A stupa was erected to his right at Qionglong Nianhua Temple.
Chan Master Xianning Danyu Yuan of Hangzhou was the son of Zhu Guyun. He was of robust and imposing appearance, earning him the nickname "Jade Maitreya.
At the age of ten, he left home to become a monk at Sengxiang Temple in Taicang; at nineteen, he visited Yunqi and asked:
"What is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? Qi smiled but did not answer. The Master was perplexed by this.
Later, he met Xuelang at Xishan and listened to the lectures of the two Dharma Masters Chao and Yu; yet he found no point of entry for himself and remained filled with anxiety day and night.
Finally, he visited Master Sanfeng Zang. He attained a slight degree of awakening, yet had not yet reached a state of total clarity.

Consequently, while traveling with Lingyin Li, they were detained by snow at Chang'an Town. There, he repeatedly received the Master's exhortations and encouragement, and suddenly attained a realization of the truth.

Since this is so, then at this very moment, my seven-foot black staff has no use whatsoever here. At such a time as this—

Furthermore, guest and host are clearly distinct. As for the phrase "total release and total gathering," how is it? He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Sometimes I plant it atop a thousand peaks;
I cleave through the soaring clouds so they do not rise too high. He struck the ground once with the staff and descended from his seat.

In the summer of the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, he manifested a slight illness, yet he continued to receive visitors as usual. On the twelfth day of the eighth month, he spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, saying: [Verse omitted per instructions]
For seventy-five years I have struggled in vain; nothing extraordinary has emerged beyond the ordinary.
Now, casting off my hands as I go over the precipice, let all quarters speak of illusion or reality as they please. To anyone who asks, I simply write "Thirteen" and point it out to them.
Upon reaching the thirteenth day, he passed away with auspicious signs. He was interred at the foot of the Chui Terrace by the White Gate.
Chan Master Zhimuchan of Jiaoshan in Chuzhou was the son of the Xie family of Shaoxing.

At the age of twenty, he received the full precepts under the elder master Wukong of Chongsheng Temple. While contemplating the koan of "the original face," he made no progress; thereupon, he went to Tiantong.
He requested the precepts. At that time, Shi Qi-yun served as his *kalyāṇamitra*. One day, the Master asked, "What is my original face? Yun immediately struck him with his palm.
As the Master was about to ask again, Yun covered the Master’s mouth with his hand; he then attained great enlightenment.

In the seventeenth year of the Chongzhen era, when Yun became the abbot of Xuedou, he appointed the Master to oversee the duties of the *vinayadhara* (Rector). In the ninth month of the seventeenth year of the Shunzhi era, [he began...]
Holding his robe and whisk, he went to reside at Jiaoshan, and subsequently at Xuedou. He ascended the hall and said:
"Nineteen and twenty-nine—when they meet, they do not take their hands out of their sleeves. Yangqi’s donkey and Hushan’s dog trample through the void, running head-over-heels.
This very body has nowhere to hide its traces; what does it possess? Why then is the stone 'Gandang' at the street corner frozen stiff?"

White sweat flowed from his entire body. In his later years, the Master retired to Yungai. On the seventeenth day of the second month in the *renxu* year, at midnight, he asked for a brush and wrote this verse:
"Stately and majestic, there is neither going nor coming; The true wind is revealed, utterly free of dust.
At the point of certainty after seventy-one years, I follow the flowing stream into Tiantai. Having cast down the brush, he passed away. [His] stupa...
Beside the Wondrous High Terrace of Xuedou, there was Chan Master Hongyuan Shao of Mingzhou Xuedou; his clan name was Wang, and he was of noble lineage from Guanhai in Yue.
One night, his mother dreamed that an old man led a monk into her room, and she gave birth to him. When the Master reached the age of seven, he shaved his head and donned the white robes of a novice.
He went to visit Tiantong Wuzhuo to investigate the koan "Who is reciting the Buddha's name? Although he applied himself with great effort, he did not attain realization.

Later, he visited Shiqi Yun at Lingjiu to investigate the Yunmen koan regarding the "East Sea Carp. He harbored doubts about it. One day, while attending upon Yun, a monk standing nearby raised this question.
[The monk] spoke. Yun then struck him. The monk asked again; Yun struck him again. The monk asked once more; Yun struck him yet again.
Upon seeing this, the Master suddenly attained great enlightenment and said, "What a pity! Those three blows were not worth a single drop [of merit]. Yun asked, "And what about you?
The Master shook his sleeves and said, "The heavy rain is coming! He then departed and presented this verse: "One blow—thunder peals, rain pours down."
Tilting his body, he turned over and threw himself down, striking Yunmen. Now, face-to-face, there is no evasion:

the East Sea and the West River are swallowed in a single gulp. Yunran assented. Having resided successively at Haigan, Nan, Guang, and other places, he ascended the hall on the fifteenth day of the eleventh month.
"Ten thousand *li* of a single iron bar—Linji and Deshan, what dry dung-sticks are they? Now they are hidden away."
Before the Milk-Peak (Nanyue), I have pulled out the wedge from the crown of your head for you. Observe closely: a thousand mountains shiver in a cold hue.
The Master was born on the thirtieth day of the fourth month in the Bingchen year of the Wanli era. He passed away on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month in the Wuchen year of the Kangxi era.
He was seventy-three years of age and forty-nine years since his ordination. His stupa was erected on the southern slope of Mount Dongshan.
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Muchunmen (ten persons):
Chan Master Xingwei of Xiuyun at Xihu Xiufeng in Suzhou, a native of the Gu family of Changzhou. At the age of twelve, he...
Benru received the tonsure at Xiyin Hall on Mount Huqiu. He went to attend upon Muchen Yunmen at Gunan, where Yunmen appointed him as the First Seat.
One evening during the late assembly, Yunmen said, "The mind gives rise to great joy; one knows for oneself that this is what must be done.
It is only the final character below that I, this mountain monk, cannot supply. I ask the assembly to provide it. Benru stepped forward from the crowd and said, "Thief! Yunmen [applauded].

He approved of this and bestowed upon him his robe and whisk as a transmission of the lineage. He then departed for Mount Xingxiu. Next, he resided at Xingfu Temple on Tiger Hill and ascended the hall to address the assembly:
"The summer days are long; at the fifth watch, the moon is bright. Before the courtyard, the poppies—those with red bases are red, those with purple bases are purple.
In the pond, the new lotus leaves—some large, others small. While the mountain monk was sleeping upon his bed, suddenly—"

Hearing the sound of the bell and the crowing of the rooster, they all announce the dawn together. Putting on long robes and rising, look: how much of the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West has been left in disarray?
Then he descended from his seat for a small discourse (*xiāocān*). He raised the case: "If you do not look back when the case is raised, you will immediately go astray;
if you attempt to deliberate, when will you ever awaken? "Venerable Wei," [the Master said,] "I raise it right now: the new moon is like a bow, the frosty wind is like..."
"Arrows! I call upon all people to take care of your heads and faces. In the sixth month of the Bingchen year of the Kangxi era, the Master manifested a slight illness.
On the twenty-first day, he bathed, changed his robes, and left behind this verse: "I am sixty-seven years old; my worldly ties have now come to an end."
A long song for returning home: the sun first rises over Fusang. All is still and silent. His entire body was interred at the foot of Mount Wujia.
Chan Master Chongji Jun of Jiaxing Zudeng was the son of the Shi family of Wuxing. At the age of twenty-five, he shaved his head and received the precepts.
Chan Master Muyun visited Tiandong Monastery and received the seal of approval. He ascended the hall and said: "The cold wind is piercing, the night rain falls in torrents.
Cranes cry atop the pines; clouds rest at the mountain’s waist. What occurred before the empty kalpa is no different from this very day.
Entering through the gate of immediacy, one completely transcends past and present. It does not leak with anything; it does not waver with anything. To have intention—"
When the breath moves, it adds to one’s spirit; even where there is no leisure, there is leisure. In the summer of the Jiayin year of the Kangxi era, the Master fell ill.
On the ninth day of the ninth month, he bathed, changed his robes, and said to the assembly, "What kind of season is this?
The assembly replied, "It is now midday. The Master said, "To the northeast of Mount Xu, the void has split open. To act exactly as one speaks—this is precisely it."
Regarding the timing: tell me, where has this old monk gone? Was there anyone among the assembly who could say it? The assembly remained silent.
He then let out a great shout and passed away. His stupa was erected to the left of the hermitage.
Chan Master Mingjue Baozhang Xuefeng Daobai, styled Lengweng, was a native of the Niu family of Suzhou.

He ascended the hall and said: "Wondrous eloquence has nothing to do with the tongue; when discussing the profound mystery, the mouth does not open. The crows cry and the magpies screech, while earthworms dance upon the Three Terraces.
A hundred mouths share but one tongue—bring forth your questions together. As a monk stepped forward intending to pay his respects, the Master [continued]:
He said: "Lift up the horse-stand before the gate. To the assembly: "Half rain, half no rain;
within the cloth bag of a thousand peaks, it wishes to clear but cannot clear. A pale sun emits its full orb. I am alert; you too are alert.
If you have not yet seen through to the bottom, New Korea struck the third watch last night. To the assembly: "Mid-winter has passed; the wind and snow—"
Like an arrow piercing a wall or passing through thin thatch, it strikes the head and face; such a wondrous opportunity for awakening, no one can recommend.

All one wins is a hungry bird coming from outside the window, pecking at two or three pieces of plum blossom. A question was asked: "Dongshan’s 'Ruler and Minister' and Linji’s 'Host and Guest'—are they the same or different?
The Master said: "Carving into empty space to seek the tracks of birds. The Master successively presided over Mei-shu Mida Temple.

On the eighteenth day of the tenth month in the Ding-si year of the Kangxi era, at the hour of Chen, while at the Dharma-Cloud [Hall] in the Great City of Repaying Gratitude (Daobaoen Wangcheng), he took up his brush and wrote a verse on departing this world, as well as instructions regarding the sealing of his reliquary chamber.
He then cast down his brush and passed away with a serene countenance, yielding to the natural course of life. A stupa was pre-constructed in the eastern corner of the temple;

Sima Lu, his grandson, composed its inscription. His collected works include the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings), the *Xuexiang ji* (Collection of Snow-Sounds), and the *Jiu zheng lu* (Record for Rectifying and Correcting).
*Yunmen Fangwai Zhi* (The Record of Yunmen Beyond the World) in several volumes has circulated in the world.
Chan Master Nan-yin of Foguo Monastery at Jīnlíng Mount Jiāoshān, whose courtesy name was Zhēndùn Sǒu, was the son of the Líng family of Hǎining.

At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and donned the robes of a monk. He subsequently visited Gūnnán Mén, with whom he once went boating on the river. While on the boat, they saw [something] on the bank.
The peach blossoms were in full bloom. Master Men asked him about the kōan concerning Lingyun and Xuansha, challenging him with it. The Master replied, "The wind blows the willow catkins like a ball;
the rain beats the pear blossoms as butterflies fly. Men nodded in approval. Later, he returned to his hometown to care for his parents.
Because Grand Master Ren had a hall for supporting his mother, he named his monastery Huangmei. He subsequently served in succession as the abbot of Zhenxiang and Kuang'an.
Ascending the hall at the Yuanjue Monastery on Qingxi, the Master stuck out his tongue and said, "Do you see the great jewel-light emanating from my tongue-wheel as I expound the Mahāyāna Dharma?
He then let out a shout and said, "In the presence of fools..."
"How can one speak of dreams? With these words, he descended from his seat. Ascending the hall: A clap of thunder at the onset of Lesser Heat turns the season back to Plum Rain.
Blown by the wind and beaten by the rain, the clouds of sorrow cannot be parted. When they are suddenly parted, it is the sun of the sixth month—a grandmother’s fist.
Nevertheless, though not struck, the circumstances are hard to endure. This mountain monk speaks thus; let there be rest. Let there be rest.
"Stop, stop! Why do you act so? Why does Mount Huai act like an ox? With these words, he threw down his whisk and descended from the seat.

On the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month in the Jia-yin year of the Kangxi era, the Master gathered the assembly and spoke this verse: "The tortoise has a body of white jade; The arrow-head possesses the appearance of gold.
Who awakens to the emptiness of Nirvana? A solitary moon rises over the sea-gate. He passed away peacefully at the age of fifty.
Sixth. His monastic seniority was thirty-six years. He was interred behind the Huangmei Monastery.
Chan Master Wuliang Kesheng of Suzhou, whose secular surname was Cheng of Hexi, gave this small discourse:
"Is the Way distant? It is true in every encounter. Is the Sage distant? To embody it is to become divine. Thus, the entirety of reality is the very embodiment."
The whole body is the truth itself. It does not diminish among ordinary beings; it does not increase among sages.

It does not diminish among ordinary beings, for even when sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all saved, the Buddhas have never saved a single person. Nevertheless, tell me: what do you say to this?
"The mountains are not mountains; the waters are not waters. How do you understand this single phrase? He struck his staff and said: "From this point on, one need not go;
upon returning, it is attained. Who can vie for the misty scenery of the Five Lakes?"
Chan Master Shi Yin-zhen of Fahua Temple on Mount Nanyue, a native of the Liu family of Wuning in Jiangxi, ascended the hall and said:
"To capture tigers and rhinoceroses alive; to seize fierce dragons alive; to drive away the plowman and snatch his food;

to point at iron and turn it into gold—if one were to maintain this according to the fundamental division, even the Elder Śākyamuni, with his broad and long tongue, could not say a word of it. Even the Patriarch Bodhidharma could not employ it."
Exhausting all supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), one still cannot point it out. But tell me: by what means does the Wheel of Dharma open this great mouth?
Then, holding his staff crosswise, he said: "Holding the Mo-he sword crosswise, I maintain the full command; in the realm of Great Peace, I slay the deluded and the stubborn."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Elder Zheng of Fahua is just like an oil-presser.
Whether it be rapeseed, paulownia seed, or camellia seed, he gathers them all together onto the press bed. Cold, he strikes once; hot, he strikes once.
He strikes until not even a trace of breath remains. Then, turning the barrel over, he intends to strike two more times. But tell me, why is it so?"
After a long silence, he looked at the assembly and said, "This is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
The Master passed away on the first day of the fifth month in the Gengshen year of the Kangxi era. His stupa was erected atop Mount Jiumu.
Chan Master Xuetang Si of Chongsheng Yuantong on Mount Lu, whose original style name was Xuetian, addressed the assembly:
"The wind does not come, the tree does not move; stop fooling around with this leper toad. After a long silence, he looked at the assembly and asked, "Do you understand?
A chicken from Chu is no phoenix from Mount Dan. A monk from Wanshan came to inquire: "Does any army pass through here, Master? The Master said: "One."
"A melon is like a coconut; it is large and weighs seventy catties. The monk was bewildered. The Master said, "It does not even require dipping in salt.
The monk asked, "How high is Mount Lu? The Master picked up his staff and made a gesture of measuring it.
The monk said, "Ultimately, how high is it? The Master struck him and said, "It is this high! The monk remained bewildered. The Master beat him severely.
Chan Master Yuan of Sigui, whose courtesy name was De’an Xiaohuo, was the son of the Hu family of his native district. He received the tonsure under the elder master Da’wen.

He first visited Tiantong Wuzhun and subsequently relied upon Xuedou Yun for eight years. Later, he met Gounan Men, who, finding his realization to be profound and subtle, appointed him as the Second Seat.
At the end of the summer retreat, Yuan took his leave to return home. Gounan asked, “Why do you not...?”
They stayed together for a long time. The Master said, "I am taking Gunan to live in Chu. The Gatekeeper said, "You possess great spiritual power.
The Master replied, "I have come along with you. The Gatekeeper was pleased and inscribed a portrait of his head upon a tablet to bestow upon him.

The Master traveled through various places, including Huangcaoshan, Longchi, and Shishan, where he established retreats and ascended the hall to preach. "The Great Jewel of the Dharma King is fundamentally..."

The perfected nature is the topknot jewel upon the crown of the head; it has never been obscured throughout past and present. There is no need to seek it externally, nor is there any reliance on another.
[The Master] suddenly strikes the meditation staff: "If you can take this up and carry it here, then you will know that by the side of the brazier, no tongs or hammers are required."
"The Lion’s Den is thus made even more radiant. Had it not been so, this mountain monk would today have turned his face around and tied up his sack.
He then struck the ground with his staff and descended from the seat.
Chan Master Niyuanjian Xuan of Yushan Zhizhi was the daughter of the Cao family of the district. She entered the monastic life in her youth and received full ordination at Baoguo Temple.
She maintained the precepts and monastic regulations with strict rigor. Initially, she went to visit Jin-sul (Jinshu) Wuzhuo; as she was about to prostrate, he raised his fist.
Wuzhuo immediately struck her with his staff, saying, "What is this? The Master replied, "Not recognized by the thousand sages. Wuzhuo said, "Let it go. The Master said: [letting go].
"What is there to put down? Awakening is simply rest. Later, he visited Gunan and received the Dharma. He then closed himself in retreat at Yushan.
One day, the Jinshi Huang Chunyao arrived at the gate and asked, "I have long admired the Master of this retreat. The Master replied, "I do not know you at all."
The scholar said, "Opening one's mouth is already a tangle; I want the Master to give a full presentation. The Master said, "Let it go. The scholar was greatly delighted.
Lady Qian, the wife of the Imperial Censor Qian, asked, "What is 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'? Where does the One return? The Master said:

The waters of Xiushui are beautiful year after year; the green mountains remain verdant age after age. On the eleventh day of the second month in the *Guichou* year of the Kangxi era, he suddenly ordered his hair to be shaved without illness.
Having bathed and changed his robes, he sat in the lotus position and spoke this verse:

"Seventy-three years of borrowed names, Not a single dharma can withstand the scrutiny of the mind. Now the four elements disperse according to their conditions; I have already offered my gratitude to the donors."
He uttered a distinct sound and then passed away peacefully. His *yulu* (recorded sayings) and *nianpu* (chronological biography) have been circulated in the world.
Ruru Lanren Fangwei Jushi was a native of Hexi. From his early childhood, he possessed a resolute aspiration for the Way.

One night, he dreamed of a Daoist practitioner wearing a square headband who led him to the base of a pagoda at the Three-Forked River in Yangzhou; there, he observed that the shadow of the pagoda was leaning.
Xie ordered an attendant to prop up the stupa to straighten it. As the attendant opened the door of the stupa and exerted himself, Xie awoke with sweat pouring from his entire body.
He realized that the world of body and mind was entirely empty; throughout all time, past and present, there is only this one self, and even this self cannot be described in words.
He composed a verse, saying: "Dreaming within a dream is vividly real; How can listening with the ears compare to listening with the eyes?"

"From amidst a heap of bubbles and shadows, grasp the solid reality; the living word of the great chiliocosm belongs to us. From that time on, she sent away her maidservant to observe the vegetarian fast, seeking the Way with even greater urgency.
One day, she visited Mochun at Helin. Mochun asked, "What is this mind that is neither born nor extinguished?
The lady replied, "This disciple crossed the river this morning. Mochun said, "The wind and waves upon the river were fierce; how did you manage to cross it?"
The Master said, "The tiller is in the hands of my disciple. Yunmen said, "Now that you have already stepped onto the shore, where is the tiller?
The Master said, "The Abbot of this monastery, Master Mi, does it. Yunmen said, "What business do you have with Master Mi?
The Master bowed and said, "I take my leave of the Master at once. Yunmen smiled and nodded, saying, "The plum has ripened," and then he transmitted [the Dharma] to him.
The verse says: "Parted beneath the flowers on Vulture Peak; met again at the ferry-head of Jingkou. You now depart in this manner;

for a thousand years you shall revive my school. Later, [Fahai] sought tonsure and ordination. Nanquan said, "You may construct a quiet chamber; there is no need to leave the household life. Simply transform your fellow men. Thereupon he converted his companions.
Truly rare! The Zen Master Duchi of Jile (one of five successors of the Venerable Zen Master Fushi) addressed the assembly:
"In the past, when Fenyang lay high and reclined in mountain caves, the scholar-officials..."

I have long admired his character and style. Although I invited him eight times, he did not come. Upon hearing a single word from Master Cōng, he suddenly turned over and set forth, thereby causing the Way to fill the world.
How could there ever have been a fixed method for this? Before I, this old monk, reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss, I was accustomed to disparaging all quarters;
now that I have reached the Land of Ultimate Bliss, let all quarters disparage me. Moreover, having taken up the responsibility of the ancestral founders, how could I possibly [be otherwise]?

Do you perhaps fear that the Way of the Dharma is difficult to practice? I have observed many of the younger students of recent times who, as soon as they enter a monastic community, cease to strive for spiritual progress.
They focus solely on securing abundant food and drink, spacious quarters, and the favor of their teachers.

If they are treated with generosity and receive certification prematurely, they rejoice and treat it as a serious matter; yet when subjected to the "tongs and hammer" of rigorous training, they become resentful. They do not consider practicing at all.
One who understands the correspondence [of mind and nature] is called an ancestor. Only when one’s wisdom surpasses that of the teacher is one fit to receive the transmission. Alas!

That our school has reached this point is truly a matter for bitter weeping and shedding tears. As it is often said: "It would be better to sacrifice one's own body in place of all sentient beings in the great earth."

They undergo the sufferings of hell. Ultimately, they do not treat the Buddha-Dharma as mere human sentiment; instead, they seek profit and offerings extensively, frequenting busy gateways and courtyards.
When I first attended the invitation at Sānshān Temple in Hǎimén to repay the kindness of the Old Man (the Master), a monk asked about such "monastic customs" (*jiāfēng*) of the Master.
The Old Man said: "In my old age, I dwell in a dilapidated courtyard; there are drums but no bells—the resonance is incomplete. The monk...
[The Master] said: "Suppose a guest were to arrive; with what would you entertain them? The old man replied:
"Not only is there no tea or fruit in the storehouse, but moreover, there is little rice for cooking in the kitchen. The disciple said: "How can you, O Elder, speak such words?
One of superior capacity and sharp intelligence will naturally be able to maintain austerity and endure hardship; as for one of lesser understanding—"
[The Master] saw through him at a glance. Furthermore, how could one blame him for being tormented by poverty and parched by hunger? Whenever he was struck or bumped, he gave rise to affliction.
The Old Man said, "It depends solely on you, Dharma Master; thirty years from now, you shall restore the pure reputation of Tiantong."
That I may not fall to the ground—this is my aspiration. Having personally received your instructions and benefits, I shall never dare to forget them.

Last night, while sitting quietly by the lamp in the abbot’s quarters, it was already past the third watch when I suddenly reflected upon the kindness of the Elder, who covers me like heaven and supports me like earth.
How can I repay this in this life? Only through the great virtues of all [you masters], who morning and evening engage in mutual refinement and polishing, will [the goal] surely be attained.
Only when one reaches the ultimate ground of the Buddhas and Patriarchs will one truly have accomplished the task;
thus, the title of "Way-man" (Dao-ren) will be truly beyond reproach. Take care.
Master Baozang Wenzhai of Jiangxi was a native of Wuyun in Jixian, the son of the Chen family. One day, while eating...
During a meal, he saw a black-husked insect within the rice and had an awakening. He spoke this verse: "Insect in the rice, insect in the rice!
Its original face is the same as mine. A hearty laugh—joy for all of life! Buddhas and sentient beings are both within a dream."
He presented this to Enxian, who immediately granted his seal of approval. Later, he succeeded him on the seat at Tiantong. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Upon the lump of red flesh, it stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. Only this sharp blade of spiritual insight—who dares to imitate it?

If you can realize it here, where would you place the binding and unbinding, the delusion and awakening? Now, having no choice in the matter, I shall provide a model and draw a likeness; where there is no embroidery, I shall establish embroidery."

To establish a rope where there is no rope; to cause all people, within ninety days, to suddenly leap forth from their constraints, break through the entanglements, and sever the cords, until the myriad phenomena and the vast array of things begin to dance, and the rivers and great oceans surge with waves.
At this very moment, it is precisely the time to eat the staff of the Treasure Store. Why? Because "In a world of universal peace, one strikes down the dull and stubborn.
Master Chan Master Hongyuan Hao of Haoning Dongsi ascended the hall and said: "I have a phrase, yet I dare not utter it lightly."
"Now is precisely the time. Zhuo leaned on his staff and said, "Take note, take note! He ascended the hall and said, "In my school there are no words or phrases;
truly, there is not a single dharma to give to others. Yunmen’s red banner flashes; Linji’s hot shouts roll like thunder. After a long silence, he said:
Though a sharp sword may be swift, it does not slay those who are innocent.
Master Weichan of Hongjie Duntu in Yingzhou ascended the hall and said: "I will not speak of life; I will not speak of death."
The crab walks sideways; the frog leaps straight up. A monk of his true station must not act with superficiality. (He struck his staff and descended from the seat.

One day, a temple monk was involved in a lawsuit, and the Master was implicated as well. He immediately ascended the seat with a serene expression, spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly, and passed away.
When the military commissioner of Huai and Xu heard of this, he led his fellow officials in prostrating themselves before him. The local gentry and commoners gathered funds [to honor him].
A pagoda was erected behind the temple.
During the Taiping era, Chan Master Chanchan of Qixin Monastery was staying there. A monk asked, "The physical body is subject to decay; what is the indestructible Dharma-body?
The Master said, "Today, the wind at the peak is too harsh. The monk shouted. The Master said, "An adept. As soon as the monk bowed, [the Master struck him].

The Master struck him once across the back with his staff and said, "Quickly, fix your eyes on the play! The monk laughed heartily. The Master said, "Do you suspect that I am entangling you in complications?
The monk bowed again. The Master struck him once more and said, "By all means, do not forget this."
The Dharma heirs of Chan Master Linye Qi (eight persons):
Chan Master Foyuan Zixian Jue of Jingxi was the son of the Xu family from Hezhou in Shu. He lost his mother at the age of one.

His father took him to the venerable master Lǐ Mǎshān Tàixū to have his head shaved. Not long after, his father passed away. Once he had reached maturity, he traveled extensively among the lecture halls.
Later, he journeyed to Wúyuè and stayed with Tiāntóng Wù for many years, yet he found no point of entry. Consequently, he visited Qí at Xiánzhù Liao.
Qí asked him, "If you cannot gain strength from practicing *chán*, where does the fault lie? Qí said, "Do not engage in discursive thought. The Master said:
"How, ultimately, is this so? Qiji replied, "The handle of the adze is long; the handle of the axe is short. The Master became even more bewildered and distressed.

He applied himself with great effort to investigate it, and one evening, after having cleared his mind of distractions, he suddenly struck against a pillar and penetrated the heart of the Zen school. At that time, Qiji was responding to an invitation from Guanghua, and the Master attended him as a follower.
One day, Qiji raised the case of Xinghua expelling the *vina* (steward), asking, "How do you understand this? The Master said, "To act for others, one must..."
To see through it. To kill a person, one must see blood. How extraordinary! On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month of the Xinchou year of the Shunzhi era, the Master wrote this verse:
"Upward to heaven, downward to earth; head and feet. Lift it up and go; take the head as the tail. A-he-he!
Elegance does not lie in wearing many clothes. One song returns home to sing 'Li-lo. He cast [the brush] aside.
He passed away while holding his brush. His stupa was erected at Píngfēng Mountain.
Chan Master Huìrì Shēng of Tāizhōu Hongfú Monastery, whose single-name style was Miàogāo, was the son of the Fēng family of Shǎowǔ.
