One day during tea, upon hearing Jōrō cite the verse on the "Three Blows of the Staff" by the ancient patriarch Shōchū of Rinzai, he felt as though he had leaped out from beneath a thousand-layered net.
He immediately presented this verse: "A golden palace and a crystal bed— This is what especially confuses people."
The Hall. Turning over the face-gate, who am I? Watch as the ghosts divide the loot in broad daylight. Having realized this and laughed, he ascended the hall. He raised the case:
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the samādhi of every dust-mote? Yunmen said, "Rice in the bowl; water in the bucket. The Master said:
"For several days it has been half-sunny and half-rainy; the wind grows fierce and the sky grows cold; frost fills the air."
The air is full; the sound of the river water has dried up. Before the cliff, the fallen leaves lie; Mañjuśrī shrinks his neck. Upon the branches of the wax plum, Samantabhadra breaks into a smile.
What is this? It is improper to prattle on without cause. Ascending the hall, he gave a shout and said: "In the pure breeze there is no path to penetrate;
in the fierce flames the ice naturally hides itself. To escape from this [state] is also like leaving the city of Zhengzhou for the gate of Cao."
How much more so when they "three in the morning and four in the evening"—it is no less than swinging a club to strike at the moon! [The Master] suddenly held up his whisk and said: "Look, look!
Aniruddha could view the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems as if looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand;
Xuefeng could grasp the entire earth and hold it like a grain of millet. Since you are all here, you must exert some spirit; you must not..."
Everywhere he goes, his eyes have been swapped for black beans; looking east and looking west, it is truly like a blind donkey chasing after a great herd.
[The Master] struck the desk and said: "If I were to exclusively propagate the Dharma-vehicle, the grass before the Dharma Hall would be ten feet deep.
Having no choice, I have suppressed my majestic radiance to meet you—can you grasp this yet? He struck once more.
Chan Master Wuke Zhi of Qingyuan in Jizhou was the son of Fang [surname] of Tongcheng. His grandfather was Da-zhen, a Court Counselor of the Ministry of Justice;

his father was Kongzhao, who served as a Grand Coordinator (Xunfu). In the Gengchen year of the Chongzhen era, the Master passed the jinshi examinations and held the post of Editor (Jian-tan) in the Hanlin Academy.
Subsequently, fleeing for refuge, he traveled far away and received the tonsure at Xianhui Mountain in Zhao-ying. In the Guisi year of the Shunzhi era, he visited...
The Venerable Sheng of Tianjie received full ordination. Sheng presented him with the koan of Gaofeng’s “falling pillow,” which awakened his functional capacity.
Thereupon, he closed himself in retreat at Gaozuo for a long time, until he had deeply penetrated the inner sanctum. Ascending the hall, [Sheng] said: "This is the second meaning. What is the first?
And how does one contemplate that 'one'? 'This very mind is Buddha. The yellow leaves cry out against the crimson cliffs—it has been smashed to pieces."
Neither mind nor Buddha. The incense pillar laughs at the lantern; it is smashed to pieces. Not mind, not Buddha, not a thing.
Throwing a ball in swift water; it is smashed to pieces. What more can be said? If you can directly take responsibility for the very moment [the question] "What can be said?
arises, your ears will go deaf and your tongue will fall out. If you should miss this, it is not so.
To avoid further entanglement with the "Great Synthesis" of those who previously wielded the staff, let us strike a full circuit through the four cardinal and four intermediate directions.
Chan Master Shigong Ben of Daci Temple at Hupao, Hangzhou, was the son of the Gu family of Qiantang.

In his youth, he followed his mother to visit Yunqi, from whom he received the tonsure and the full precepts. He subsequently visited Master Cheng at Mount Jing. Upon seeing him, Master Cheng immediately asked:
"One who enters the gate must have a word. The Master said, "The Abbot is advanced in years; why has he not yet heard it? Baosheng smiled and ordered the secretary to be summoned.
One day, as the Master was about to ascend the Zangtian Tower to pose a question, Baosheng seized his nose and twisted it. The Master cried out in pain.
Having attained sudden and thorough enlightenment, he ascended the hall. To beat the drum and strike the bell is already to pour foul water upon others;

to prostrate and burn incense is but to further obstruct one another. Although the sages of old cast their bodies across the edge of a sword or reached down their hands within a flame, all such acts were laborious and without merit.
How much more so when arriving here—how can one act? It is a matter of skillfully engaging [the Way].
"Words—what can they possibly accomplish? You all, upon seeing this mountain monk come up here, immediately overturned the meditation seat and shouted to disperse the assembly;
you were nearly there. Now that you cannot collectively produce even a bit of worldly discourse, I cannot help but add another ladle of foul water.
You must quickly sniff the stench of this foul water before it is too late."

Among the various venerable elders, there was the Great Master Zhuhong (Lianchi) of Yunqi in Hangzhou, a native of the Shen clan of Renhe County. At the age of seventeen, he enrolled in the local prefectural school.
He would always write the four characters "The Matter of Birth and Death" (*shengsi shi da*) upon his desk. One day, he accidentally dropped and shattered a tea bowl.
Ou had a sudden realization; he made seven strokes with his writing brush to manifest his resolve. He went to Xishan Xingtian to shave his head, then traveled north to visit Bianrong.
Later, he sought instruction from Xiaoyan at Liuxiang. Xiaoyan said, "You have come three thousand li away to seek instruction from me;
what instruction do I have for you? The Master was suddenly enlightened. He took his leave and returned home. On the road through Dongchang, he passed by.
Hearing the sound of the drum from the watchtower, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "Events from twenty years ago remain suspicious;
what such a marvel was this to encounter three thousand *li* away? To burn incense and cast down my halberd were matters of no consequence;

demons and Buddhas needlessly contend over right and wrong. Later, while residing at Yunqi, Minister Wang Zongmu asked him: "Last night the mice were chirping incessantly, as if reciting an entire volume of scripture."
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Master asked: "When the cat suddenly bolts out, what then? The attendant was speechless. The Master provided his own response:
"The Dharma Master has run off, leaving behind only the lectern. He then offered this verse: "The mouse squeaks; the *Avataṃsaka* is clearly revealed.
How extraordinary, Minister Wang! You have been deluded by a beast. The cat suddenly bolts out before the painted hall; At the head of the couch, he preaches the Dharma without end."
News. No news. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha, the Great Vaipulya, Chapter One: "The Sublime Array of Worldly Rulers.

At that time, due to a famine, pestilence was rampant, and the roads were filled with the starving. The government opened its granaries to provide relief and ordered physicians to offer medical treatment.
I was appointed by the Master to oversee these affairs. The Minister of Personnel, Lord Yu Chunchi, asked Hui Ri to mark five hundred [copies].
Regarding the circumstances of the sick monk, the Master said: "Huiri was originally but a destitute son who abandoned himself to follow others;

he yielded to the commoners of West Monastery and went from life toward death. It is a pity that five hundred monks only knew how to nod their heads in agreement and depart, yet not one remained to lie high and refuse to rise.
This allowed Huiri to manifest eccentricities and delude the masses, bringing calamity upon his descendants. The Prefectural Lord deeply [regrets this]."
Regarding all the ailments of the people, we mountain monks are pressed by the urgency of the times. In the midst of this haste, I have unfortunately lost my bamboo staff.
I cannot help but brandish my empty fist and strike the ground once upon the abscess of you, layman. I venture to guarantee that your chronic malady will be dispersed and healed.
The poisonous blood flows freely; the myriad channels circulate; the hundred limbs are relaxed and at ease. Even so, how can one person cause the multitude to arise? Have you not heard the Way said:
"When a single leaf turns back toward the sun, spring fills the thousand forests"? Let this matter rest for now.
As for holding a bamboo staff all day long, pointing east and waving west—it is not as good as remaining constantly upon the wooden block. Morning...
Hold fast to the evening watch. As you guard and re-guard, suddenly the withered tree will bloom again. This is like a dead person coming back to life. What need is there to speak of bamboo and wood?
Take it for granted that all the grasses, trees, and forests throughout the entire earth shall all attain Buddhahood. Why is this?
The empty essence beyond the green objects is precisely the Tathāgata’s solid and real mind. Question: Regarding the practice of Zen meditation (chán).

[Question: "Regarding the practice of *nianfo* (buddha-recitation), can it be harmonized [with other practices]? The Master said: "If that were so, they would be two separate things; how could they be used in such a way as to be harmonized? [Question:
"When the World-Honored One remained silent for a long time, the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) said, 'He has opened the clouds of my delusion.

When Subhūti sat in meditation without speaking, Śakra said, 'He has well explained Prajñāpāramitā. What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "At the moment of his long silence, he wished to dispel the gloom of delusion."
Ten thousand *li* away, sitting in meditation by the side [of the road], one waits for the preaching of Prajñā for a long time.

Even so, those who "catch the essential meaning at the tip of the whip" or see "flowers flying in the void"—what exactly have they seen? To those gathering ferns, he said: "The secret instruction of the mind."
"Tell me how to speak! I have missed the auspicious season before the mountains.
I raise my fist and speak to you! **New Year’s Address:** Today we celebrate the New Year; the seasons have been renewed. What was it like yesterday?
On the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth month. **The Master’s Self-Portrait:** Nine out of ten strokes do not resemble the likeness; they have vexed the artist to death.

The Master said, "A craftsman may perhaps come close to this. To leave it as a temporary offering would be to treat it as two separate things; if one were truly a man of the Way, it would remain as one.

If it were not two things, I would give thirty blows. At the time of his passing, he informed the assembly half a month in advance, saying, "I am about to depart for another place," yet no one could fathom what he meant.
When the appointed day arrived, he manifested a slight illness, sat upright facing west, and passed away.
The Great Master Zibo Daguan was the son of Shen of Juqu. At the age of seventeen, he shaved his head and traveled to study under various masters.
Upon hearing the recitation of Zhang Zhuo’s verse—“To sever delusive thoughts is to increase one’s illness; to turn toward True Suchness is likewise a deviation”—he became greatly perplexed.
One day during a vegetarian meal, he suddenly attained great enlightenment and said: “If I had been under the seats of Linji or Deshan...”
A single slap brought him to his senses. What need was there for further deliberation? He traveled north to the capital to study under Bianrong.

In the autumn of the *wuli* *jiumao* year (1623), the "Seditious Book" (*yaoshu*) incident broke out, and the Master suffered persecution. Previously, Emperor Shenzong had personally transcribed the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

By chance, sweat from his hand soaked the paper, and suspecting that the volume should be replaced, he sent a close attendant to consult the Master. The Master presented this verse: "Imperial Sweat" (御汗) [The rest of the verse follows].
"A single drop [of this teaching] serves as a bridge for ten thousand generations; from it, the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma radiates its light.

The Emperor was greatly pleased and thus paid close attention to him. Upon seeing the memorial submitted, he felt great compassion for him, yet realizing that within the Dharma one cannot escape [the consequences of transgression], he issued an edict ordering a formal investigation.
During the interrogation, the Master remained composed in countenance and maintained his principles with great rectitude, despite being frail and aged.
His body endured numerous lashings and beatings; he refused to submit even unto death. On the fifth day of the twelfth month, he was cast into prison.

When the judicial authorities passed sentence and were about to execute him, the Master spoke a verse: "A single laugh has always had its own cause; Who would have known that the Great Mass of Earth cannot tolerate a speck of dust?
From this moment on, I shall gather up my mother-born feet; The flower upon the iron stake will bloom without waiting for spring. He further said: "As for worldly dharmas..."
"What is the use of staying here for long? he said. Having finished his bath, he instructed his attendant, "I am departing. Please convey my thanks to all the Dharma protectors of Jiangnan.

He then spoke a verse: "When affairs arise, one finally beholds the hero's bone; Was it not a karmic affinity from past lives that met Master Da and Mr. Wu? I shall return westward while you go north;
Our conversations over many lifetimes are now even more chillingly clear. Having finished speaking, he sat upright and...
[Postscript:
Chan Master Wunian Shendao of Huangbo in Ruizhou was the son of the Xiong family of Macheng in Huangzhou.
Once, while traveling to Mount Dang, an elderly monk said to him: "A single grain of rice from the ten directions is as heavy as Mount Sumeru. If you do not [return it]..."
"Liaodao" (Realizing the Way) returned wearing fur and horns. The Master was struck with awe. He also heard a monk cite a question asked of Daixiu:

"What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Daixiu replied, "Yellow gourd, eggplant. The Master was greatly perplexed. He then traveled to Mount Wutai and Mount Funiu, visiting and questioning various spiritual teachers everywhere.
One night, hearing the sounds of laughter and weeping mingle together, he attained realization. Furthermore, one day, he dropped his hand from a cabinet.

He struck the ground with his hand, and as sweat flowed down his entire body, he clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "The entire great earth is this very state of non-thought; what room is there for doubt?
He then went to Longhu, where, together with the layman Zhuowu, they arrived at Sima Mountain. At that time, a lecturer arrived.

The layman asked the lecturer, "If the fundamental nature is pure and serene, how did the mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? After the lecturer had finished expounding according to the text, [Zhuowu said:]...
The layman turned to the master and said, "Try to say something. As the master prepared to open his mouth, the layman gave him a push on the knee and said, "What about this?
The master suddenly attained great enlightenment and composed a verse: "For more than forty years I did not cease my efforts;
I searched and searched until the traces vanished. Now, having searched to the point of no dependence, I finally regret the efforts I wrongly applied before."
A monk asked, "Is the Way ultimately existent, or is it ultimately non-existent? The Master said, "To say it exists or to say it does not exist—both constitute slanders.

The monk asked, "How then may one attain it? The Master said, "When there is no seeking, you have attained it. The monk asked, "What is the essence of the Way? The Master said, "It fills the mouth, yet words cannot reach it.
The monk asked, "What happens when the four elements disperse? The Master raised his fist and said, "This [fist] does not [disperse]."
Belonging to the Four Great Elements. Question: "The ancients said, 'Expel the throat, lips, and mouth, and bring forth a single phrase.
How would you speak this one phrase? The Master said: "I do not expel my throat, lips, and mouth; you, for your part, try and speak a phrase."
The monk had no reply. The Master said, "Your mouth has been stuffed shut by sounds. A monk asked, "Is it true that seeing one's nature is attaining Buddhahood?
The Master said, "It is. The monk asked, "Since nature is formless, how can it be seen? The Master said, "Nature is indeed possessed of form."
[The monk] said, "I simply do not see it. He asked, "Please, Master, point it out for me to see. The Master said, "I am telling you that you do not see it.
[The monk] asked, "How does one transcend birth and death? The Master called to the monk; the monk responded, "Yes? The Master said, "Come forth from here!
[The monk] said, "I do not understand the words spoken by the Master. The Master said, "If you were to understand them, what would you be fit for?"
Chan Master Yifeng Fangtan of Baima Temple in Kuizhou was the son of the Luo family from Dazhou.
He studied under Master Yun’an of Jinfoshan, who instructed him to contemplate: "What is the indestructible mechanism of the divine and the demonic? After three years, he attained realization.

Leaving the gorges, he visited various spiritual friends (*jñānaka*) at length. He built a thatched hut by the Double Stream (*Shuangxi*). One day while cooking his midday meal, he heard a sound from within the steamer;
suddenly, he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse containing the lines: "The white clouds and blue peaks all nod their heads in agreement.

He once traveled through Zhejiang and resided in a hermitage at Qingping in Hangzhou. The master Zhenji Yin had relied upon him since his youth. One day, the Master raised the case of Qingfeng’s *bing* (the third watch).
When Ding the Youth came seeking the story of "seeking fire," [Fayan] questioned him, saying: "Qingfeng spoke thus, and Fayan also spoke thus;

why is it that some attain enlightenment while others do not? Ding replied: "At first, one attempts to settle the mind through conscious cognition; for this reason, one does not attain enlightenment."

Later, he directly accepted [the truth] and was thus able to attain great enlightenment. The Master suddenly raised his fist, struck the desk once, and said in a stern voice, "If that is so, have you now attained great enlightenment?
Yinyuan hesitated; the Master then scolded him harshly and drove him out. Yinyuan was left with sweat pouring down his back.
From this point on, he resolved to practice with all his might. In the *Renchen* year of the Wanli era, the Master returned to Baima. A monk...

A question was asked: "What is the meaning of [the Master’s] coming from the West? The Master replied, "Fire burning at both ends, with smoke at only one. The Master constantly held a small hand-drum in his hand;
on one side was written the character "chù" (矗), and on the other side was written the character "bēn" (犇). Whenever he responded to an opportunity, he would frequently raise it and shake it.
He entered nirvana and was interred in a stupa at Longshen Mountain.
Chan Master Xing’an Xin of Ehu in Guangxin was the son of the Zhu family from Shangrao in the commandery.

Once, while visiting a relative, he encountered a practitioner discussing the meaning of the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*). Upon hearing these words, the Master thoroughly realized the great principle that all things and the self are equal.
He went to Taiping in Luoyang to shave his head. Returning south to Jiaoshan, he spent the winter there. Hearing the sound of a boat being pushed through the river, he attained a realization.
He composed a verse, saying: "The night is still and the river is vast; The sound of the boat being pushed, push, push. I know not where it is going; Half of my burden has grown light.
He visited Huashan, who presented him with the koan regarding "a lifetime's livelihood that is neither six nor seven. He remained in doubt.
Mengtí meditated for seven days; his body and mind were suddenly liberated. He soon returned to his hometown and resided at Mount Ling.
He once painted a great circle (maṇḍala) on the wall, saying: "When writing inside, do not allow it to become blackened; when writing outside, do not let it be marred by white.

To anyone who can provide a commentary—whether from within the circle or from without—he would grant them permission to study the Way without doubt. Otherwise, they would all be nothing but *mātr̥kā* (vain delusions). Later...
He moved to E’hu. For ten years, no seat-holder (abbot) was established there. When Wuxi came to attend upon him, they reached a mutual accord through the "Mu" (No) kōan of Zhaozhou.

Wuxi requested to occupy that office, and [Zhaozhou] presented him with a verse, saying: "For ten years at E’hu, the seat of the patriarchate lay vacant; For what reason, all at once, has it been established by a youth?
Two eyebrows and eight strands— One must know that Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot precede this. Furthermore, he once established...
There are no door locks. To verify those who have come, he spoke a verse within the hall: "The lock has been handed down since ancient times; I rely on you to open it with the key of wisdom.
If you lack the method to open the lock, Even if we meet, there is no need to come.

On the final day of the second month in the Dingmao year of the Wanli era, he ascended the hall to preach the Dharma, prepared a vegetarian feast, and took his leave. He further presented this verse: "For over eighty years within a dream-like illusion, The iron ox..."
He plowed through the great void; at the moment of his departure, he entrusted a single phrase: "At midnight, the golden crow bears the sun’s crimson glow.
He passed away sitting upright.
Zen Master Guangyin Wenqu of Zhenji in Hangzhou once visited Longchi Chuan; it happened that Chuan was basking in the sun on the steps.
[The Master] went down. He asked, "Where is the Preceptor? Xuedou said, "He is not here at this very moment.

After the Master had performed his prostrations, Xuedou commanded him to compose a verse on "Deshan Carrying the Alms Bowl. The Master’s verse read: "Is there or is there not the final word? Father and son, Deshan and [his heir], are too much at odds.
Born of the same lineage, yet they die of different lineages; Having lived for three years, my regrets grow ever more numerous. Xuedou was pleased with it.
He said to him again, "Why do you not take up this matter and join us in its proclamation? The Master was unwilling.
Baizhang sent him out the door, patted his back, and said, "Old nephew, I still have doubts about you. The Master asked, "Where do you doubt me?
Baizhang said, "What is the meaning of the secret transmission? The Master replied, "Today I shall not turn my back on Yixing. Baizhang laughed heartily.
The Master donned his bamboo hat and departed.
Later, when the monk Wuxue Huanchen, the Great Master of Jingzifeng in Xiangxiang, was asked by a monk, "What is the place where a student gains strength?
the Master replied, "It is like a person at home who has nothing they cannot accomplish."
The Great Master Hanshan Deqing of Caoxi in Shaoyou was the son of the Cai family of Quanpiao. In his youth, he studied Confucian learning.
At the age of twelve, he took the master Xilin of Baoen as his teacher. At nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination, becoming friends with Miaofeng.

While casually reading the *Zhao Lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), he came upon the passage concerning the Brahmin who left home and returned with white hair. A neighbor saw him and said: "In the past..."
"Is the person still there? The Brahmin replied, "I am the same person as before, yet I am not the person of before.

Suddenly, he had a realization and said, "Today I finally know that my nostrils point downward. Miaofeng asked, "What have you attained? The Master said, "Last night two earthen oxen fought and entered the water;
to this day, there has been no news at all. Miaofeng laughed and said, "I am glad; you now have a mountain to dwell on."
Taking his capital, he traveled to Yanjing to visit Master Xiaoyan. Xiaoyan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "From the South.
Xiaoyan said, "Do you remember the path by which you came? The Master replied, "Once passed, it is left behind. Xiaoyan said, "You, however, have a clear understanding of where you have come from.
The Master then prostrated himself. Later, he was falsely accused by a Daoist priest on charges of privately founding a temple and was sentenced to military exile.
At Leizhou, he traveled to Shaoyang to pay homage to the Patriarch. He offered this verse: "A single drop from Caoxi is the source of spiritual power;
It flows into the vast blue ocean, its waves splashing against the heavens. How many fish and dragons strive for transformation, Yet the single stream at the source remains ever cool and clear.

Eleven years later, he was released from military service. He remained at Caoxi for another nine years before returning to his monastic robes. He then returned to Mount Kuanglu, where he built a hermitage.
He spent several years at Wuyufeng, planning for his retirement as an elder. He was subsequently requested to return to Caoxi. Not long after, he suddenly addressed the assembly, saying:

"My karmic conditions no longer accord with the times; where shall my transformation be entrusted? My term of office has ended; I am about to depart. He then requested a bath, changed his robes, and prepared himself.
He passed away while sitting upright. His age was seventy-eight, and his years since ordination were fifty-nine. His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Tianzi Ridge.
The Master once visited Deshan to pay homage at the ancestral stupa, where he recited this verse: "In the hall, idly stretching out the alms-bowl; The lion playfully tames the cubs.

In that place where one cannot turn back upon meeting face-to-face, At the moment when one bows the head in silence— Failing to understand this final phrase, It causes [confusion] to persist even until today."
Doubt. [He] asked about the matters of the three-year period: "By what means was it possible to know so early? The verse on dwelling in the mountains says:

Throughout my life, my traces have wandered east and west; In my old age, how could I choose where to perch among the trees? Though my backbone may be as hard as iron, Alas, my leg bones are as soft as mud.
Leisurely, I watch the clouds rise from the deep ravines; Sitting opposite a solitary peak, I listen to the birds' cries. There is no need for further...
Seizing upon the phrase beyond words, the sounds and forms before one’s eyes are the full presentation.
When Zen Master Zhuan Yu Guan Heng of Yunju in Jiangxi was traveling on pilgrimage, he passed through Yunnan and visited Chen Meigong.
He presented his visiting card three times, but as the Master was occupied with affairs, he was unable to receive him. The Master then left a verse and departed. The verse:

He said: "The ink-well pools reflect the beauty of the Three Lakes; the brush-stands rise high among the Nine Peaks. Within the hall, the son who reads his books has the pure breeze blowing through his cotton robe.
Upon seeing this verse, the official hurriedly called for a boat to pursue him as far as Suzhou, but the Master had already closed his door and would not see him.
Chan Master Yuanbai Ke of Letan in Jiangxi offered incense, saying: "This one portion of incense belongs to the Dharmakāya Lord, Vairocana;
it has always been this very thing. Today I bring it forth for my ancestral forefather, the Great Master Mazu, who entered nirvana twelve hundred years ago.
His great capacity and great function have long been without news. Now that I occupy this seat, I [offer it] to him."
O children and grandchildren! A single thread has been opened. Again, he held up the incense and said: "I shall not speak of this one offering of incense for now;
if you wish me to speak, wait until next year. Entering the quarters: "A single cow-pen, a single tiger’s den—this is the realm where the Way is propagated."
In the space of a single hair-tip and a single finger-snap, one encounters the person. But tell me, what place is this? An unperforated iron hammer;
seventy-nine times it strikes the wind and the rain, never allowing them to cease. The life-force of the Patriarchs has met a poisoned hand;
for a grievance held through ten thousand ages, a single blow is the requital. The Head Seat gives a small discourse: He shouts at the eastern corridor; he shouts at the western corridor.
It will not be realized until the year of the donkey. In Guansi there is a golden-haired lion who rolls the embroidered ball alone;
how could he fail to manifest it? Layman Wensu, look! Attendant Li, call out and there is a response; above and below, hand to hand.
The staff is not in my hand, but rather in yours. However, you must not roll up the mats in the hall.
A small informal talk (shōsan) given by the Head Cook: To sift the sand from the rice, and to sift the rice from the sand—both are matters occurring at the edge of the rice basket.
Nanyuan was skilled at eating; Niu-tou was skilled at dancing. This seems close to the point where transformation gives rise to maturation.
If one possesses such capabilities, you may ask whatever you wish before the bell tolls; you may ask whatever you wish before the drum sounds.
The Abbot Lihua held a small-scale informal discourse (xiaocan). "Not far from here lies Hanyang; before the Yellow Crane Tower, across the Yingwu Isle, lies a ready-made public case.
A man of spirit has gold beneath his knees—he must not bow to a blind old monk.
Let there be a turning word, and thirty blows shall be yours to receive."
Master Daokun of Haoshan in Hengyang asked: "Standing tall and alone, revealed in its entirety and independent of anything else—who is this?
The Master said: "Clad in his monk’s robe, he passes through the marketplace. The Master asked: "In that case, he goes forth freely in all directions. The Master said:
"Riding a donkey, he tramples the waves of Lake Dongting. The Master asked: "Apart from these two ways, is there still..."
"Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "Please be seated and drink some tea.
A monk asked Master Jiyue Ti of Baohua Mountain in Jinling, "What is the place where all Buddhas emerge?"
The Master said, "Straw sandals and a staff. The monk said, "I understand this. The Master said, "Try saying it.
The monk said, "Straw sandals and a staff. The Master said, "Three lifetimes, sixty kalpas."
The layman Haidian Huang Duanbo of the Cibu (Department of Sacrifices) visited Xueqiao Xin on Mount Kuang. He asked, "I have long heard of Xueqiao;
yet now that I have arrived, I do not see a single trace. Xin replied, "The sun is great. The layman asked, "What is it like after the snow has melted?

Abundant. Moving freely back and forth without hindrance along the path to the *gū* gate, he dragged his staff and entered the Buddha Hall.
He did not prostrate before the One Endowed with Wisdom and Conduct, but instead bowed to the bamboo-stem whip. No one understands this meaning; it makes me recall Nanquan’s informal discourse:

"Where there is a Buddha, do not dwell; where there is no Buddha, flee at once. A single expanse of ancient green mountains, as white clouds encroach upon them. Where there is no Buddha, flee at once.
[The Master] said: "Too much! A clear pool does not permit a blue dragon to lie down; withered trees and cold cliffs become a subject for idle talk.

When both 'is' and 'is not' are struck away, the bright mirror stands right upon its pedestal. He looked left and right and said: "Outside the door, the tracks of dragons and elephants increase further;
inside the house, a pair of worn-out straw sandals are added. He addressed the assembly: "When a single breath does not return, where will you establish your life? The rat has no place to hide."
Investigation: The cat delivers a message; it bites through the iron coffin. The corpse cannot finish eating it.
*Small Assembly*: Yesterday the sky was clear; today the rain falls. The stone tortoise before the gate is covered over by straw sandals.
Although it manages to hide its entire body, it cannot avoid exposing its head and feet. *Ascending the Hall*: Five peaks on the head, three scars on the nose. A shoulder half-bared.
Slanting on his shoulders is a purple *kāṣāya*; when people come to ask about the Way, he remains silent. A single smile, and the clear breeze sweeps away the setting clouds.
Master Yuting Chan of Guangshou Monastery on Mount Wu in Huzhou addressed the assembly on the occasion of the Buddha’s Bathing Festival. He cited the case of Yaoshan:
once, while Zun Bunuo was bathing the Buddha, Yaoshan said, “This one you are bathing—you can bathe him. But can you bathe that other one? Nunuo...
[The Master] said, "Bring forth that one. Yanshou desisted. The Master said, "Old Zun has brought it forth; the handle of the ladle is held in his own grasp.
Yanshou desisted. [The Master continued,] "To try to see 'that one' with your tongue pressed against the upper palate—I guarantee you have not yet reached it.
How can this compare to the Elder Renshan today, who has resolved to bathe the Buddha, while Upādhyāya Yin stands by with hands in his sleeves, paying no heed to this or that?"

"An individual. I give him a ladleful according to custom. This reaches all the way to "three pounds of hemp," the "dry turd," the ox-head and yakṣa wardens inside the hall who have eyes but no nostrils, and the bamboo-stem whip beneath the Zhānglín Mountain—all of them simultaneously emit light that shakes the earth.
Not only does he sit and cut off the tongues of all people under heaven, but he also spares us from being left bewildered.
The root of the entanglements at the assembly on Vulture Peak was born today in the Garden of Lumbinī.

For two thousand years, vines have trailed and branches have spread, leaving no path for anyone to travel in this Sahā world. Striking with his staff, he said: "Today, for the sake of you all, I shall cut them all off at once."
It is understood. But where, for now, can one see that old Śākyamuni? The spring in Wulin is already late; the shade of green trees is deep within the terraces and pavilions.
Chan Master Fuyuan Jishengdu of Yangzhou was the son of the Zhang family of Qingzhou. At the age of thirteen, he entered the monastic life under Hengyan.
The Great Master left the household life and received full ordination with the Buddha as his *upādhyāya*. Later, he studied under Jieya Xiu, thoroughly penetrating the source of the Dharma.
He subsequently resided at Lisheng, Jinsu, Zutang, Shengyin, and other locations.

Occupying this room, he issues this command: "All monks under heaven shall beg for their lives; even Buddhas and Patriarchs must pass through the reforge. Here, bricks, tiles, and rubble reveal themselves.
The Heart-Seal. Now tell me, where does the point of benefit and harm lie? "When the frost-blade is raised, the hair on one's bones chills;
when the sharp sword is swung, heaven and earth are stilled. In this small discourse: When it is cold, all under heaven is cold;
speak words of sincerity. When it is hot, all under heaven is hot; such is the season. There is one who is not turned by cold or heat. Brothers, do you know him yet?
[The Master] rested his hand upon his staff and said: "Since following me down Mount Tiantai until this very day, seven feet remains seven feet, and one zhang remains one zhang.
He ascended the hall and said: "In places of stillness and cool, there is no flavor; in places of clamor and heat, it is precisely where one should deliberate.
Tripping over feet and stumbling with hands—none of it is anything other than a dried piece of dung. Bumping heads and knocking foreheads—all of it is [the same]."
Three catties of hemp—if one can weigh this out, heaven and earth will have nothing left over. If one can smell it, the entire world is filled with fragrance.
But tell me: where does one place this old fellow who has no nostrils? Last night, the bedding on the bed was warm.
Waking up at dawn, I give this small discourse (*xiaochan*). Yesterday I prepared several phrases of the Buddha-dharma, intending to come and offer a small discourse for the assembly;
however, my four limbs were scorched by the wind and fire of illness until they were completely cleared away. This morning I have again prepared several phrases.
Furthermore, you have been thoroughly beaten by a single sneeze. Today, you must not remain silent before the assembly.
Whether there is a Dharma or no Dharma, look solely at Master La-ba’s time when he was traveling on pilgrimage. Because a monk asked him: "The myriad dharmas return to the One."
"Where does the One return? The Master said, "Leaving one grove, entering another community. Later, while residing at a mountain monastery, he was asked again, "The myriad dharmas return to the One.
The Master said, "After the meal, brew a strong tea; having finished drinking it, sit by the pond on a stone and count the swimming fish.
When he later resided at Jiusheng, he was asked again, "The myriad dharmas return to the One. The Master said, "Tearing down the eastern wall to patch up the western one. Later, he resided at Fushan.
"Conditioned. He was asked again, "The myriad dharmas return to the One. The Master said, "One meal and one is full; one defecation and it is finished.
On the eighteenth day of the eighth month of the Dingwei year of the Yongzheng era, he passed away. His secular age was fifty-seven, and his monastic seniority was thirty-nine.
He was interred in a stupa to the right of Fuyuan.
The Dharma Successors of Chan Master Xiangguang Ji (two persons).
Chan Master Poyuzhi of Jinghui in Yangzhou addressed the assembly: "A bird first sings, wiping its feathers from the branch;
each and every one clearly reveals the highest capacity. He struck his staff and said: "If you can personally realize this within, you shall carry it upon your shoulder."
A fine spring has arrived.
Master Yunzhong Weizhen of Jinghui Monastery in Yangzhou delivers a small-scale discourse (*xiaochan*). An ancient worthy said: "When the sun rises, the light of the mind shines;
when the sky is overcast, the nature-ground is dark. Those who do not know heaven and earth stubbornly claim that there are the Qian and Kun hexagrams. All of you, gathered here in such numbers...
Come! This mountain monk was particularly drowsy. He then held up his whisk and said: "Those who achieve perfection are few; those who ruin themselves are many.

This was the small assembly (xiaochan) given by Chan Master Lingjie Yuan of Longxing Temple in Huai'an, a successor in the Dharma lineage of Chan Master Linlan. "To take the mind as Buddha is to fall into the den of the wild fox."
It is said that the Buddha is not the mind; even when encountering the Avīci Hell, he is utterly detached from both the middle and the two ends.
At the depth of night, he does not seek lodging among the reeds; turning back, his living eyes illuminate the world. Six times six is originally thirty-six.
Chan Master Zhongquan Kong of Xilin in Jiangzhou, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Bofan Ke, ascended the hall and said:

"I cite the World-Honored One who, before Mount Zhengjue, attained enlightenment upon beholding the morning star, and sighed, saying: 'How marvelous! All sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtuous marks, and characteristics of the Tathāgata.'"

"It is only because of deluded thoughts and attachments that one does not realize it. The Master held up his whisk and said, "The marks of wisdom and virtue—deluded thoughts and attachments—are all pierced through by this Empty Abbot in a single string.
At such a time, even if the Old Man Śākyamuni were to arrive, he could do nothing but stand by and watch. Is there anyone among you who can [respond] for the Ancients?"
Xuequ said, "What? After a long silence, he said, "Ho! Ho! Ho! When one person gives rise to the true and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions all vanishes away."
Morning Assembly at Zen Master Xinghua Gualan Pu of Yunlong in Xuzhou, Successor of Zen Master Tian’an Sheng. Holding up his staff, he said:
"Do not seek stillness by avoiding clamor; do not be self-righteous while disparaging others; do not give rise to saintly interpretations; do not harbor personal views. Simply eliminate..."
Discernment is utterly clear and bright. What is this matter of clarity? (He plants his staff upright and gives a shout, saying:
"The mountain facing [the monastery] is high; the mountain behind it is low."

Chan Master Xuehong Xin of Juesheng Monastery in the Capital, a successor of Chan Master Huai Guangcan, was granted the honorary title Wenjue. A native of Gusu, his family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

While attending the local school, he read the Golden Light Sutra and attained a profound realization; he subsequently shaved his head and donned the monastic robes. He studied under Chan Master Huai Guangcan and received his certification. *Small Assembly Sermon:*
The single stroke of the upward leap is not the diamond circle; the one phrase that penetrates the summit is not the *liji* thorn.

Every day, twice a day, when you place your spoon and chopsticks beneath the alms bowl to eat gruel or rice—if, mouthful by mouthful, you have never bitten into a grain of rice, then you have penetrated the diamond circle but cannot swallow the *liji* thorn. If, however, mouthful by mouthful you do bite into [the grains]...
Rice. One may swallow the thorn-bush of the *kaṇṭaka*, yet one cannot penetrate the diamond circle. Even if you can swallow it and penetrate it, consider this:
what kind of person’s realm is it that suspends Mount Sumeru on a lotus fiber and receives the four worlds with a single hand?
Do you know? After a long silence, he said: "It is still just a faceless fellow. Evening discourse: "The wielding of the staff and the shouting of the shout."
This old monk has never had such leisurely energy. His brows are arched and his nose is straight. You all fortunately lack even the slightest flaw; you simply come and go.
Be careful not to trample the single flake of snow before the steps, lest it reveal the bricks and clods of earth beneath.
To strain your eyes and gape with your lips tires you out; suddenly, a speck of dust is added to your vision. *Evening Sermon.*
A group of practitioners of withered meditation surround a sick monk; each has brows arched and a nose straight. How can you allow the Buddha-dharma to be thus neglected?
Apart from the two times of rice gruel and meals, there is no need to apply any other mental effort.
These days, the head gardener wants to plant vegetables and the head farmer wants to sow grain. Even so, everyone must look after one another. But tell me, how do you look after?
What is this? Morning after morning, the plow and rake move against the wind; turning over the mud, it is originally just earth.

Small Assembly (Xiaocan): "Originally there is not a single thing; Where could dust and grime settle? The Patriarch loved the path of "nothingness," While the Master of Awakening favored the path of "existence."
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth exist; people, things, men, and women exist; body, mind, and the world exist.

Yet, if one seeks even a single thread or a speck of dust, nothing at all can be found. Now tell me: is the Patriarch’s point of view correct, or is the point of view of one who perceives the arising of awakening correct?
If you can distinguish between these two clearly, I shall grant that you possess the eye of a true seeker. The Fifth Year of the Qianlong Era. The Master.
He retired to Amidaji Temple and passed away in the fifteenth year [of the Kan’ei era]. Summoning his disciples, he said, "Burn these words of Dharma.
Thereupon, he departed peacefully. He was eighty-seven years old; a stupa was erected at the temple.

Chan Master Zisù Yuǎn of Pánlóng on Zhōngnán, a successor of Chan Master Wénruò, was the son of the Zhao family from Wúwéi Prefecture. His mother dreamed of a monk riding an ox-cart who sought lodging with her, and she subsequently conceived him.
Even as an infant, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture. After entering the monastic order, he went to visit Chan Master Wénruò and asked: "The Unborn..."
"This mind is not the Buddha, nor is it a thing. What is it? Wén struck him with a staff that split his head open.

Later, upon hearing the verse "Holding a hoe empty-handed," the Master attained great enlightenment. One day, when Wén entered the hall and had just taken his seat, the Master stepped out from the assembly, seized the staff, and flung it before him.
Wén said, "This fellow Meng Bāláng comes to pull at the tiger's whiskers. The Master then—
He laughed heartily and ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Mañjuśrī is the teacher of the seven Buddhas;
why was he unable to emerge from the woman’s samādhi? The Master said, "Zha. The monk followed up, "Wangming is a Bodhisattva of the first stage; why was he able to emerge? The Master said, "Lu.
He then said, "When the occasion arises, the faculty is unclouded; the thousand eyes open at once. When the mirror of wisdom is clear and penetrating, the ten directions are revealed."
Puyuan said: "To say that Mañjuśrī was bewildered and the woman entered samādhi—even the old fellow Gautama would have to lose his body and forfeit his life.
But tell me, where does the point of benefit and harm lie? He struck the meditation staff and said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ!"

Chan Master Nanchan Housong Cheng of Wuxi, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Guming Fu, went to visit Chan Master Wei of Longchi. Wei asked, "What is the meaning of 'the myriad dharmas returning to the One'?
Without hesitation, Wei struck him on the head with his staff. The Master said, "Where does the One return? Wei struck him again. The Master then let out a great laugh.
Xiao Wei asked, "What principle have you seen? The Master gave a shout. Wei struck him again. The Master shook his sleeves and departed.
Later, he went to consult Gujing, who questioned him about what he had attained. The Master presented this verse: "All dharmas return to the One; to what does the One return?
Grasping empty space, I sharpen it with living effort. It startles the white clouds into flying ten thousand miles; A clear breeze blows as I sing 'Li-lo' in tune."
Jing approved this. A monk asked, "What is one's original face? The Master said, "The sun shines and the moss withers;
the rain falls and the leaves flourish. The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "When naturally wealthy and noble, act according to wealth and nobility."

Master Jie, acting as the Dharma successor to Zen Master Zhou, presided over the Hall for Zen Master Tanhua Biyun of Hanyang. He ascended the hall, and a monk asked: "Without deploying any sharp edge or blade, how can one achieve victory?
The Master said: "The eight-sided staff within the hand of Vajrapāṇi. The monk said: "I would overturn the meditation seat! The Master said: "You do not..."
"This is hands and feet. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Emei Bai, Elder! He then continued, "The phoenix dwells where the wu tree grows;
the dragon roars when the mist rises. To give rise to the mind while responding to that which has no abode—this is the Venerable Lu Neng.
Meeting the pestle-head where flowers bloom, he drags the nostrils of his mother-born self. I, this mountain monk, am a humble descendant; I do not shrink from the vastness of heaven."
A criminal! To speak directly of that old fellow’s pot size and ladle length, he could do nothing but have the crane settle and dance, while Qingchuan knit his brows.
A "startling crowd" line—one brings forth before a startlement crowd; a "marvelous" line—one proclaims before marvelous people.
Gathering and releasing according to the occasion, bestowing and withholding with sovereign ease. Even if there were those standing by...

The path of sweetness. Suddenly encountering one who surges through the clouds and breaks the waves, with what will you deal? (Zhuo) strikes his staff and lets out a shout, then descends from the seat.
[This was] Master Cold Hall Lin, successor to the Dharma lineage.
Chan Master Dazhe Li of Chengshan in Xiao County, Yuezhou, ascends the hall and says:
"The first phrase has never transcended this very moment; The final radiance—who understands it today? The myriad worlds of the great chiliocosm are waved in the palm of one's hand;
Mountains and rivers of the great earth realize perfect enlightenment. The appearance of flowers before the eyes is long or short in spring; A lifetime within illusion is thus spent."
Not something created; perfectly round and vibrantly alive. Like a pearl rolling on a platter, or a platter rolling a pearl—a single cold radiance forever illuminating.
[This is the record of] Master Wanyin Sheng, successor to the Dharma lineage.
When Chan Master Fuzhou Huguo Duofu was ascending the hall, a monk came forward and let out a shout.
The Master said, "The ancients said, 'One shout does not function as a single shout. Where does this shout of yours fall? The monk shouted again.
The Master said, "In the previous shout, there was both host and guest; in this subsequent shout, is there still host and guest, or not? The monk—
As he was about to offer words, the Master struck him down with a series of blows, saying, "You empty-talking liar! He then said:
"Set aside Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout; if you possess the correct eye of the crown, take another path and advance forward with fierce intensity."
Killing and giving life are free; rolling up and unrolling are unhindered. Holding up his staff, he said:
"This very slight enigma—how many monks, upon reaching this point, find themselves unable to open their mouths! Today it has fallen into the hands of Tian-sheng; let him act as he pleases."
"Strike if the Buddha comes; strike if the Patriarch comes. At such a time as this, is there anyone who can speak out on behalf of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
He let out a thunderous shout and said: "To offer this profound mind to every dust mote and land—this is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness.
Addressing the assembly, he said: "This staff overturns Dongshan’s five ranks and turns upside down Linji’s three mysteries, until it reaches the point where—"

Ancient Dingguang rode out from the Buddha Hall through the triple gate; he struck down Huiming Cliff, shattering his bones and pulverizing his body, startling the Mount Jidao into rising up—yet there was not a shred of substance to it.
You people, have you yet perceived whether your eyebrows even twitched? This is the Minor Session. All things are unimpeded:
great clouds rise majestically beyond the thousand forests. All dharmas are without discrepancy: a wild goose flies across the Han River.
The river’s pale shadow slants; the pine waves harmonize with the evening bell’s toll night after night. Plum buds gather fragrance amidst the iron flutes’ blossoms. Do you not see?
Fú of Tàiyuán—his straw sandals have worn through as he has wandered the ends of the earth. Where in Yángzhōu does his painted shadow fall?
Chan Master Yunwu Yin of Helin in Runzhou was a dharma successor of Chan Master Hantai Tao. The Master asked a newly arrived monk, "Where have you been staying recently?
The monk replied, "At Tianmu. The Master asked, "Have you ever seen the Abbot there? The monk replied, "I have lived there for several years; how could I not have seen him?"
The Master took up a bamboo stick and said, "Heaven’s Eye (Tianmu) Zen Master—how does he compare to this? A monk was at a loss for a reply.

The Master said, "Even if you stayed here for several more years, you would not see it even in your dreams. In the evening assembly, he said: "Chrysanthemums bloom by the eastern fence; their fragrance drifts through the inner courtyard.
Crows cry in the ancient trees; their echoes answer back from the empty hall. It is vividly clear before the birth of one's parents; it is perfectly manifest where seeing and hearing do not reach."
Therefore it is said: "The affairs of kalpas past reside only in the present. A single phrase, free from self-interest, reveals the solitary spark of spiritual mechanism.
Do you understand this thoroughly? "Familiar faces fill the world; how many truly know my heart? Small Session (Xiaocan):

Lately, those who occupy the curved bamboo seat in various quarters strive to make their sermons sharp and novel; they insist on making their utterances mysterious and wondrous. Little do they realize...
Bimō always held aloft his fork; Heshan only knew how to beat the drum. Master Dazhu had never a thorny phrase or a hooking verse;
Master Zhizhao never once gathered flowers or clustered brocade. Fenzhou simply said, "Do not engage in false imaginings";
Jūchi only raised a single finger. Furthermore, Old Niǎokōo did nothing more than say, "Commit no evil, do all that is good."
Practice. Such is this unadorned Chan; how could people of today ever be willing to speak of it? I have often said:

when the ancients spoke of Chan, it was like a lotus flower—the blossom is there and the fruit is also there. When people of today speak of Chan, it is like peonies or peaches—there are flowers, but no fruit.

What can be done? The grain and millet do not flourish in the sunlight; instead, people compete to plant peach and plum trees in spring. This causes those who toil at the plow to become, for the most part, sellers of flowers.
[The Dharma Heir of Master Longxi Chan]
Tea Talk by Chan Master Qianzhiduang Yi of Longwangshan Qingliang: Fresh tea and tender bamboo shoots; fragrant grasses and drooping willows.
Strolling leisurely through the mountain valleys with an iron-stone heart, fine birds call to one another, their voices resonant and clear.
How is it that white clouds fly in and fill the bed? Below the mountain there are fields where vegetables and wheat are green and yellow; beyond the mountains there are houses amidst misty trees.
Vast and boundless. Suddenly, the bright moon arises upon the crag, casting its light. Who acts as the attendant? To the left and right, pines and cypresses stand.
Transversely brandishing his staff, he shatters the King of Space. At this very moment, the sun rises in the east like a great mass of fire.
Ancient and modern writings flow like mountain springs; their pure sounds do not run wild. The golden-maned lion roars atop the high ridge, startling all into flight.
There is no path. Goblins, foxes, and wolves. One shout, two shouts, and the Buddhas and Patriarchs hide away. No one can be a companion. The home of the Spirit Tree.
Enjoyment for a long time. A garment of a hundred patches. The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. A clever lad.
My teacher’s transmission, never forgotten from moment to moment. Hehe. Now tell me: is this a poem? Is it a verse? Is it worldly truth? Is it the Buddha-dharma?
"Yes. He then raised his cup and said, "In any case, go ahead and drink the tea.
[This concludes the section on] the two Dharma heirs of Chan Master Mihu Li:
Chan Master Nanyang Xuelu, who presided over a small assembly (xiaochan). "A single thought is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are a single thought. A single thought—"

"Unborn; the past and future limits are severed. Then, calling out to the assembly in a loud voice, he said: "O Great Assembly! Before your eyes there is no teacher; here in this place there is no old monk.
Tell me, how do you see one another? After a long silence, he said: "Let the blue seas change as they may, I shall never grant passage to you. He ascended the hall and said:
"Last night, the Old Man of the Southern Pole relinquished his position and settled into leisure within the Big Dipper."
Mastery! The Son of Mount Sumeru claps his hands and sings aloud; the four great continents join in chorus.
Now tell me, who is the one who understands? After a long silence, he said: "Mahāprajñāpāramitā."
Chan Master Tanshao Gao, State Preceptor of Tokyo, held a small assembly. Holding his bamboo staff crosswise, he said: "Do you understand?
This is that which all Buddhas and patriarchs have been unable to speak of; yet I, this mountain monk, have now spoken it. As for you all, what do you say?"
After a long silence, he said: "Failing to recognize [the Buddha] face-to-face, one is as if separated by a thousand mountains, merely playing with light and shadow—how difficult, how difficult!
Ascending the hall, he said: "The *maṇi* jewel, people do not know; the Tathāgata-garbha has personally obtained it.
He called to the assembly, saying: "What is the *maṇi* jewel? What do you call the Tathāgata-garbha? After a long silence, he pointed his finger and said: "This venerable monk here."
Fat! Which of those elders is thin? Small Lecture. [The Master] cites Dongshan Wushan: "What is Chan?
The Jambu tree is on the southern shore of the sea. Near, it is not separate from the square inch of the mind; far, it is one hundred and eight thousand miles.
Ultimately, what is it? "Chan, Chan. The Minister also has his own way of saying it: "What is Chan? A three-legged frog leaps up onto..."
The heavens swallow clouds and breathe mist; they spread rain and stir smoke. When there is intent, seeking it, heaven and earth are separated;
when used without mind, it is at the tip of the lips. After all, how is it? Zen, Zen.
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Yun’uo Xi (three individuals):
Chan Master Xianxiu Gan of Xixian Xingfu Temple, a native of the Hu family of Long’an in West Sichuan. Ascending the hall, he said: “Three times he was struck with the staff;
Old Huangbo’s heart was one of thoroughgoing compassion. The lad returned the punch from his ribs; when matters are urgent, even a small fellow acts.”

Transformation! It manifests the great function and awakens the great potential. Whether in the light or in the dark, it accords with all; seizing and releasing alternate, and illumination and function are both fully revealed.

To hide one’s body within the Big Dipper and to gallop a horse upon the point of a needle—when you reach this state, Śākyamuni Buddha’s mouth is like a millstone, and Master Bodhidharma’s eyes are like wooden stumps.
For the Ten Sages and Three Worthies, there is no door for praise; for sentient beings...
Demons and heretics persist in their doubts and slanders. Only those exceptional practitioners who transcend conventional boundaries—clever monks—are permitted to understand directly;
they have no need for preliminary signs. They strike the jade drum openly and unfurl the iron banner in secret. Wherever they go, all things bow like grass before the wind;

wherever they turn, there is none who does not submit without thought. This is truly what is meant by "Zhong Kui singing the Liangzhou melody in his intoxication, while his younger sister secretly signals at the gate."
Head. After meeting with the Sea-Roaming Yakṣas, everyone claps their hands atop the high tower. Entering the retreat, I ascend the hall:
This old brazier of Jingu Temple is deep and vast, beyond measure. The single path is fundamentally equal; the holy and the ordinary have never been distinct.
When sparks fly forth, the void splits asunder. When cold, the heavens and earth are cold throughout;
when hot, the heavens and earth are hot throughout. The Buddhas of the three periods turn the Great Dharma Wheel amidst the flames, all without contradiction.
You people today sit, lie, and walk within this—feel free to treat it as "three catties of hemp" or "dry dung."

The stake: cast it all to one side; it has no concern whatsoever. It is just like when drowsiness and sleep are not permitted—if you do indeed nod off, your eyebrows will be singed by fire, and you cannot blame Jinxu for that.
Chan Master Xuezhao Xing of Fengxue and Baiyun in Ruizhou ascended the seat and said:

"It is truly laughable that in his youth Qu Boyu thought he had reached the age of fifty before finally knowing the right path. From beginning to end, he reflected on it one by one, realizing that for forty-nine years, everything was not it.
'I wish to diminish my faults, yet I have not been able to do so. When Confucius heard these words, he felt a deep resonance with them. As for me, this year..."
Forty-nine. Whatever the hand grasps, there is nothing that is not so. Year after year, one carries the blue sky upon one’s head;
year after year, one treads the solid earth with straw sandals. Only this year, drawn by the force of karma, have I followed the wandering monks to enter retreat.
Without cause, I have taken up this broken earthen bowl and burdened you, my fellow brothers. There is not the slightest bit of Chan or Buddha-dharma here—just ghosts.

The face-god has no fundamental basis; how can one compare this to overturning the mechanism of the iron ox? Go straight into the thousands and tens of thousands of peaks, so as not to let them twist and pinch the nostrils of one’s mother.
Hanging up a sheep to sell dog meat—what benefit does that accomplish? O Great Assembly! The nostrils of one’s mother!
Let it be twisted and turned as you wish. Before your mother gave birth, where were your nostrils?
*sulu sulu*, *sili sili*.
At the Buddha Hall of Chan Master Heng Jin-su-chong-han of Henan: Adorned with the ten thousand virtues, a mass of purple-gold light;
encountered suddenly—dare anyone look directly? Then, spreading his sitting cloth, he said: "Because of me, you receive my prostration.
Having no basis for either, he then performed three full prostrations. Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "What is the Buddha? The Master said:
"Distant relatives are not as good as neighbors. The student asked, "What is the Dharma? The Master said, "Much emptiness is not as good as a little reality.
The student asked, "What is the Sangha? The Master said, "Seeking others is not as good as seeking oneself. The Master then took his whisk and drew a circle (○), saying:
"Neither tile nor rubble, neither precious jewel; perfectly round and bright, it shatters through the time of Wei-yin."

Snowy Valleys in Spring. Illumination opens the void; the jar-heaven dawns. Each of you must exert yourselves; do not be negligent. If you miss this moment facing the sun, there will be no place to seek it.

He then called out in a loud voice, "The assembly! The assembly listened intently. The Master suddenly struck the meditation seat once and said, "If you do not realize it now, when will you ever realize it?
On the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival, he ascended the hall. "Profound, empty, wondrous, and exquisite—only through realization can it be known."
Know it! This landscape that strikes the ground is sudden and difficult to discern. Externally, it is free from embellishment; how could there be room for "this" or "that"?
Internally, all investigation and analysis cease; what need is there to probe its singular or manifold aspects? Do you know where the Golden Grain Man resides? [He raises his whisk and says:
"When you see the moon, stop looking at the finger; once you have returned home, cease asking about the path."
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Wugai Che (two individuals):

Chan Master Tian’ai Jing of Mount Wanian, Tiantai, son of the Gao family of Huzhou. Ascending the hall, he said: "Directly cutting through to the source, neither sages nor ordinary people can fathom it.
As for that one step beyond, even Buddhas and Patriarchs do not recognize it. It is only valued by the masterful artisan who settles it right before his eyes."
To seize [the truth], one must transcend all deliberation and hesitation; it is as vast as the distance between heaven and earth. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:

"When the Buddha at Vulture Peak held up a flower, among the assembly of hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, only Kāśyapa truly understood. When Huangbo wielded his staff, among the thousand dragons and elephants, only Linji alone took it up."

For such a matter, one must have such a person. For ten or more years, I have spread my nets and set my snares, striking from the east and from the west, wishing to find even one or half a person to continue the ancestral lineage. Alas, the land is vast and people are few;
those who encounter me are rare. Suppose there were a man who, hearing this said, came forth to overturn the Dharma-seat, shout to disperse the assembly, and—

This mountain monk gives a random blow with his staff; this not only serves to repay the unrequitable debt of gratitude and assists in the transformation of non-action, but also spares future generations from being successively left stranded in dullness.
One must be a person of transcendent capacity to achieve this. Why?

For without the strength to lift a tripod and pull up a mountain, one cannot easily ride a thousand-li black steed. Ascending the hall on the day of the autumn harvest, he said: "The rattan staff is overturned."
Grasping it, one strikes the jade dew at the break of dawn; holding the sickle crosswise, one cuts the golden wilds in broad daylight.

Amidst the tips of the hundred grasses, there is full vigor; this is the manifest power of great wisdom. Within a single mote of dust, the wheel of Dharma is turned; this is the vivid realm of Samantabhadra.
Throwing east and casting west, do not falsely claim these are not your own treasures; running north and scurrying south, they are present everywhere.
This is no ordinary treasure. Advancing and retreating, how many patriarchs have you missed beneath your heels?
Glancing left and looking right, you have lost the one true eye atop your crown. A master of universal penetration should act in accordance with the moment;
as for those deluded seekers of Chan, their prying ears are but a waste of effort.
Master Nianyu Heng, a native of the Wan family of Shangyuan in Jiangnan, ascended the hall at Tianzhu Yongqing Monastery.

"The wind cannot enter; the rain cannot moisten it. Throughout the four quarters, there is not a single deficiency. Beyond the curtain of the night-bright moon, let the crane stand as it will upon the withered pine.
Within this field for selecting Buddhas, how can a fox be allowed to hide in a lion’s den? Those within the gate who wish to exit—"
One cannot go out; one is a man outside the gate. Yet one cannot enter even if one wishes to enter. He holds fast at the vital ford until daybreak, remaining unrevealed.

When he flings open the doors and windows, one sees that it is perfectly bright even in the middle of the night. Those who have emerged above the heavens still remain outside the gate upon reaching this point;
those who sit securely within the room were previously difficult for even the Buddha-eye to perceive. If you say they roam freely outside the gate, [it is not so]. Mā...
For what reason did Mahākāśyapa seal his room? If you say it was because the hall was secure and private, why did Mañjuśrī refuse to enter the door?
If you can discern the truth within this, you may then stride freely through the thicket of thorns and dwell in the reality atop the crown of Vairocana.
To condense ten kalpas into a single thought-moment and to gather the great trichiliocosm into a single speck of dust—ancient and modern are unified as one; internal and external are identical.
If you do not understand this, do not be surprised that this mountain monk establishes these gateways; you must know that there is another "heaven in a jar. Descend from your seats.
Chan Master Bianyan Hai of Zhulin at Mount Jia in Runzhou, a successor of Chan Master Qufu Yi, resided at Dading. A monk asked, "What is the realm of Dading?
The Master said, "The wind is warm and the birds' songs shatter; the sun is high and the flower shadows deepen. The monk said, "What an excellent couplet!"
The Master said, "How do you understand this verse? The monk replied, "I understand it only as a verse; how do you, Reverend, understand it?
The Master said, "A sweet melon is sweet from the tip to the stem; a bitter gourd is bitter from root to branch. The monk stepped forward and asked, "What did you say, Reverend?
The Master said, "Refinement does not depend on wearing many clothes. The monk then bowed, and the Master struck him.
On the Spring Equinox, Chan Master Yong Shenggan Jilun, a successor of Chan Master Dao Anjing, ascended the hall and said: "The crows caw and the magpies chatter;
the eye’s discernment is not as good as the hand’s touch, and walking to the place is not as good as speaking of it. When the fifty-nine days have ended, spring is met once more. Ancient.
The house faces the morning sun and the cold air is sparse; this is the Small Sermon for the Eve of the Year. The Master Vairocana is the Lord of the Dharma-body;
he has neither birth nor death and forgets both cold and heat. From the beginning, he has been the master of the twelve hours, rather than being mastered by those twelve hours.

The sacred meaning is brilliant and the true wind is vast. He lets out a shout and says: "Amidst the sound of the firecrackers, a hundred anxieties are dispelled"—this is the excellence of triggering the mechanism.
A crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jun weight. Entering the hall: Mountain flowers are like brocade; upon each flower lies a Buddha-land. Birdsong is like a lute;
within each phrase lies a pearl-count. A thousand sages share the same orbit; ten thousand functions arrive all at once. Ascending to a flourishing age equal to that of Tang and Yu.
Returning to the pure winds of antiquity, the fruit of blessings is upright and dignified; the Wheel of Dharma is eternally firm. (He lets out a shout and says:
"Verify it right before your eyes in the midst of the sun: it is clear, distinct, and without ambiguity. (He lets out another shout. Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s Birthday:
Śākyamuni Buddha drew one stroke; Fuxi drew one stroke; Qianfeng raised one stroke; Yunmen employed one stroke. It is a single character.
A single stroke across; eight characters, not two strokes. This is not that which the other does not know; that is not this which the other does not recognize.

Since the time of the assembly on Mount Ling, things remain as solemn as ever. Everyone possesses the eye—whom can one truly rely upon? *Hè!* (A shout). The Early Morning Session for the Opening of the Retreat.
Yongjia attained awakening after staying for only one night; Gaoting beckoned with his hand and strode across. Examining this from the start, he was still but a dull-witted fellow.
"If there is among you a monk of transcendent caliber who can accord with my pivot, I shall provide him with proof.
He suddenly held up his *ruyi* (willow-leaf whisk) and asked, "Tell me, which pivot is this? The assembly stood silent. The Master threw down the *ruyi* and said, "Let it cool before you touch it."
Come and look at the evening session. The secret words of the Tathāgata, the true instructions of the Patriarchs: water does not wash itself; a blade does not cut itself.
Awakening must be self-awakened; speaking is done by oneself or another. (The Master) strikes the meditation staff and says:

"This time I press down heavily; two mouths have but one tongue. The Master enters the hall and says: "Just now, the West Hall monk went to the Abbot’s quarters to submit his report; he has awakened to it within the hall."
The two men who had awakened stepped forward. The old monk said, "I bear witness for you," asking this several times in succession. The assembly stood silent.
The Master said, "Xitang speaks deceptively; the old monk speaks the truth. All you Bodhisattvas in this hall, you are truly objects of pity."
Chan Master Yingwu Xiu of Longshan in Chenzhou, successor to Chan Master Minshu Xiang, ascended the hall and said: "The ultimate principle is wordless; those with clear eyes discern it.

The true mechanism is uniquely revealed; those who understand the universal way know it. If you try to comprehend it through Zen, you will be utterly off the mark; yet if you do not comprehend it through Zen," [he paused].
To miss it face-to-face.
Master Jue of Yuyang at Mount Baizhe, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Taibai, ascended the hall and said: "At the mountain passes and crossroads, the swift shortcut and the essential ford."
From time to time he seizes hold; in every place he lets go. Those who pass through reach that other shore;
those who cannot do so remain right here. On the eighth day of the intercalary fourth month, he ascended the hall:
Twice a year on the eighth day of the fourth month, One knows not on which birth-day Siddhārtha was born. Pale yellow willows harbor roosting crows; Tender green ponds conceal sleeping ducks.

Master Xiangyang Juzhan of Ezhou, a Dharma heir of Chan Master Baishang Rong, presides over the small *can* (sermon) at the conclusion of the retreat. Before the retreat was bound, his nostrils reached the heavens;
after the retreat was concluded, his nostrils remain as they were. He has loosened the hemp sack and tightened his straw sandals. The wild weeds...
Chasing horses and oxen through the inner quarters; with wine and meat before one's eyes, one intoxicates even the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If your ground is firm and secure, you may walk alone across the crimson heavens as you please. Even if you are as dull as a lacquer bucket, take care that the road ahead does not become slippery.
