The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Huishan Hai of the Thirty-Seventh Generation under Nanyue (Seven Persons):
Chan Master Yufeng Zhi of Damei, Shaoling, ascends the hall and says: "An acre of land; three snakes and nine rats."
Biting through the hempen rope, he turns over and recognizes the master; throughout the southern provinces and northern counties, he roams at will.

He runs headlong through tiger dens and lion forests, overturning every distinction and differentiation. The spirit of this man pierces the Ox and Dipper constellations. (He lets out a shout. Evening Session:
Having attained the root, one need not worry about the branches; with his whole body, he sits squarely upon the highest barrier. A millstone spins in the void.
Eight corners; weaving east and circling west, surging south and vanishing north. Right before one’s eyes, he casts down the head of a dead snake;
the Ten Sages and Three Worthies stare wide-eyed in bewilderment. Chewing the void until satiated—who can utter "Mo Mo" when the moment arrives?
Chan Master Mili Yumei of Daguangshan in Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "The rain urges the woodcutters back home; with every step they press on faster.
The wind carries the fisherman’s boat to the shore; he lowers his oars and stops his rudder. At such a moment as this, what is it?
The village elder knows nothing of the labors of Yao and Shun—*dong dong* goes the drum as they sacrifice to the River God. Evening *can*: Stepping [upon the path].
Tearing up straw sandals, he runs barefoot; shrinking his neck, his elbows are exposed. Yesterday on the riverbank, he broke off a branch of plum;
meeting someone, he called it a willow by the embankment. He is very much like a crane among a flock of chickens; he is very much like a dog that has lost its master.
I do not know whether he is a sage or an ordinary man. Shut your dog’s mouth! Addressing the assembly, he struck the meditation seat and called out to them: "No one!"
"I have seized your bag of salt and tea; you must inspect the contents of your storehouse. Calamity does not enter the door of a prudent family.
Should someone call you a 'bitter gourd,' these are merely idle household accoutrements that you must cast away. Thieves do not strike the homes of the poor.
He then clapped his hands once.
Chan Master Yigan Ying of Daopei in Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "Spring has already arrived, yet the night is still cold. Slowly, the warming sun climbs the balustrade.
Its clear, shallow sound follows the flowing water as it moistens; the light, gentle breeze stirs the wild clouds as they turn. The weather is bright and warm, the green shadows thick.
Flowers bloom on the southern branches, yet look toward the north. Great assembly, when the myriad phenomena dance, joy arises."
**To the Assembly:** The willow eyes sway in the breeze like dark blue pigment; The peach cheeks, moistened by dew, are as crimson as fire.
The profound discourse on the true nature is the chatter of the beam-dwelling swallows; The *kāṣāya* robe bites through the midnight bell at the fifth watch.

**To the Assembly:** Riding backward upon an iron horse, he ascends Mount Sumeru; With confident steps, he casts off all destinations. Reaching the summit, he fixes his gaze and looks beyond the heavens; Therein lie hundreds of thousands of [Buddhas].
The Buddha descended from hell.
Chan Master Daomeng Kuang of Tiantong Monastery in Tanzhou ascended the hall and said: "The rushing wind howls; this is the sublime teaching of the ancient Buddhas.
The green water murmurs; this is the livelihood of the Way-man. If you can understand it thus, Śākyamuni and Maitreya shall stand aside."
If this is not yet so, then with the mouth born of one's parents, one will ultimately never speak for others.

*Small Assembly (Xiao Can)*: He held up his whisk and said, "Gathering water, the moon is in the hand. He gave a stroke with the whisk and said, "Playing with flowers, the fragrance fills the robes. He threw down the whisk and said, "Cease, cease!
There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. *Evening Assembly (Wan Can)*: Having grown old, I dwell in a village temple; my teeth no longer function.

The wind: whenever it encounters a person, it immediately scolds them; thus, intimacy and estrangement are both severed. Only when the emotional measurements of both sage and ordinary being have been entirely exhausted will one recognize that every word of this mountain monk is true.
Chan Master Quan, Yuelu Ham, of Shanglin Monastery in Tanzhou, ascended the hall and said: "The one path that points directly upward leaves not an inch of ground upon the great earth;

it is something not transmitted by the thousand sages, yet its family style pervades the entire world. It reaches the point where every single thing is free from preference and aversion, and everywhere is utterly beyond obstruction.
Though the imperial son does not realize spring has departed, deep in the night he still hears the crying of birds in the treetops."
Chan Master Zhan of Yuetai Hall at Longshan in Shaoling ascends the hall to open the furnace. The tongs and hammers are first displayed;
the forge and bellows are grandly opened. Whether saint or commoner, whether Buddha or patriarch—everyone is bound together as one bundle and cast into the midst of the fierce flames.
Once forged by this single fire, on another day you shall have your nostrils reaching toward heaven and your eyes emptying the four seas; do not fail this.
Xichan ascends the hall: The white moon first emerges through the paper window; It smiles, breaking open the jade-white cheeks of the cold plum.
The ancient ravine is deep and secluded, rarely visited by men; The scents-seeking gentleman need not harbor doubts or suspicions.
Chan Master Qiannru of Meixiong Mountain in Shaoling ascended the hall and said: "If no one speaks of the Buddha-dharma, even those with wisdom cannot comprehend it.
Right now, I, this mountain monk, take the entire Great Canon and the seventeen hundred cases of entanglement and offer them to you all as a single phrase.
After a long silence, he said: "A hawk flies over Silla."
Small Assembly by Zen Master Xuepu of Fenglin, Dharma Heir of Zen Master Mudewen. The Way not transmitted from antiquity cannot be concealed from a monk with true eyes.
[He] lets out a shout and says: "Tell me, from where did this one shout come? Again, he [lets out a shout].

He shouted, "Those with eyes, discern this! On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, he ascended the hall. The morning clouds were vast and dim, severing the views of the sages and the emotions of the common folk.
The night moon was deep and profound, submerging the palaces of demons and the halls of Buddhas.

Reaching this point, although there is not the slightest leakage, one cannot avoid the chill that dampens the ancestral reputation of those who came before. He raised his whisk and said: "The morning star appears! Pay close attention!"
Avoid making a great fuss over small matters.
Master Yan Leipeng of Jiuhping at Yunju, a successor of Chan Master Huishan Xian, ascended the seat. Waving his whisk, he said: "The full raising of the staff."
Pervading past and present, a single staff—turning over every path, it is crimson and rotting within the thorn-brake forest.
Having hollowed out the very marrow of one's bones, one digs deep into the earth behind a living person. Enlightenment is right before one’s eyes; its divine radiance is ten thousand fathoms high.
Yet it is banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains. How can you discern its traces therein? [He throws down his staff and descends from the seat. He then ascends the seat.

When exiting or entering a gate, Śākyamuni and Maitreya touch foreheads and exchange shoulders; they then call out names like Yang and Zheng. Within the purple silk curtains, a treasure so precious it could rival the beauty of a kingdom is difficult to repay;
it is a pity that such things are treated as common "swallow-stone" (worthless pebbles) and scattered away. If one’s spiritual ground is stable and secure, [this treasure will remain].
Overturning the spirits of all sages, this "unencumbered man" (chuan-han) did not abide in the position of primordiality before the kalpa, nor did he fall into the present time.
He moves with spontaneous ease, uniquely elegant and refined. Therefore it is said: "Before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaras, there was self-awakening without a teacher."
This is the second phrase; give me back the first phrase! [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

Chan Master Juehuilu of Diti, successor to the lineage of Chan Master Guotao of Yunlin in Hangzhou, ascended the hall and said: "The separate transmission outside the teachings—what kind of thing is that?"
Filling the ears, yet not sound; filling the eyes, yet not form. If you can recognize this perfect, round totality, why need you ask Maitreya?
It is pure and fundamental from the beginning; do not give rise to doubt. As soon as there is a mind that seeks the extraordinary, the holy and the profane are already separated.
Today is the fifteenth, the opening of the furnace; simply look at the flames erupting in the void. Even if they roll like jade and turn like pearls, one must still seek it within.

Refining: Cast bronze and scrap iron are gathered together; if it is truly gold, it will not change. The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings have originally not been separated by so much as a single thread.

Year after year, how fresh and radiant the plum blossoms bloom. Year after year, the mundane world is vast and boundless, as one awakens and falls into intoxication again and again.
We who have left the household life strive to eliminate worldly burdens; we choose the Buddha, not an official post—take care not to fall into the trap of seeking status.
(He strikes the meditation staff and says: "Only this staff remains, regardless of the shifting changes of cold and heat. How could it...
Willingly following the crowd and the pack, one examines to the end whether the flower branches are long or short; who cares for the remnants of years or old ages?
If one can simply be compliant, at ease, and harmonious, this is itself the samādhi of universal integration. After a long silence, he said: "Has the white ox on the open ground been cooked yet?"
Chan Master Shuiyue Yuan of Huilong, a successor in the lineage of Chan Master Deyun, ascended the hall and said: "A single phrase facing the sun is uniquely detached from sense bases and objects.
A single pivot beyond the ordinary soars like a flash of lightning. By the time you blink your eyes, it has already fallen into the second or third stage. What can be done about this?"
White clouds stretch ten thousand miles; it has been thus for a thousand ages and ten thousand ages. The Buddhas of the past and the Buddhas of the future are no different.

Vast and expansive, there is nothing outside it; the myriad worlds of the great trichiliocosm are contained within it. Silent and desolate, yet not within; the floating pavilions atop the banners rise from within the fragrant waters of the ocean.

The "bazi" (the true nose) is revealed alone, displaying all inconceivable powers of spiritual penetration.
The moon embraces the vermilion cassia tree from afar; the stars bow toward the high North Star.

The Abbot Tiancheng of Chongren, a successor of Chan Master Zhishuiyuan, ascended the hall for the long-term assembly. "One, two, three, four, five—counting from the beginning by bending one's fingers.
When the count reaches the year of the donkey, it turns out there is neither past nor present. He does not involve himself in the cycle of spring and autumn; how could he have ever [existed]?"
"Cold and heat. This is the retribution for those who investigate the mystery. Recommend the 'Master within the Master. Now tell me, which one is the Master within the Master?
After a long silence, he descended from his seat.
Chan Master Changming Jing of Tahe in Yuanzhou, a successor of Chan Master Yingwu Xiou, ascended the hall. As soon as a monk stepped forward, the Master said, "Cease, cease!
There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. The monk struck his sitting mat, and the Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted, and the Master then—

[The Master] struck him. Another monk came forward and said, "Is it this person who should prostrate, or is it not? The Master raised his staff and said, "Should this mountain monk strike you, or should he not?
The monk stepped back three paces, then advanced three paces. The Master said, "Not so, not so. He then continued:
"Today, these monastics, when meeting the situation, apply the single flavor of both staff and shout together; yet they needlessly create complications."
Section. There must be someone who can turn their skin inside out. Is there anyone in this assembly who can do so? If not, then look at Old Man Mu; he is turning it himself.
(He throws down his staff and descends from the seat.)

everywhere they moisten the banks of the Jin River. A bright moon rises with auspicious radiance reaching a thousand fathoms; every household bathes in the pure breezes of the four fields."
The song played is the melody of non-arising; the cowherd girl harbors the sound of primordial antiquity. There is an eye upon the tip of the staff; the level board has no stars.
All you practitioners of Zen, take up the alms bowl. How many times has it ascended to the imperial court? Guard your eyebrows. Look through the eastern wall.
"The sound of the stream is entirely the broad and long tongue"—tell me, what is it that is being discussed? The Master said: "Rarely encountered."

Chan Master Xuan of Mount Jinshan in Runzhou ascended the hall and said: "A solitary peak standing like a sheer cliff;

a thousand mountains bow their heads. A gate that spills out toward the heavens; ten thousand streams flow toward the source. He reveals the true eye of Mahesvara and upholds the grand regulations of the Ultimate."
To seize upon a single pivot, all pivots respond at once; to reveal a single dharma, all dharmas are perfectly complete. It is as bright as the radiant sun and as vast as the great void.
When the great function manifests, it abides by no fixed rules. Wielding the sharp sword of the Vajra, one eradicates the nesting places of both sages and ordinary beings;
employing the tongs and hammer beyond the conventional, one cuts off the life-root of the patch-robed monks. Thus, the ancestral style of the ancient Buddhas is once again displayed.
The realm of the Great Being is fully manifest. It is as if at the heart of the Yangtze River, the wind is calm and the waves are still;

atop Mount Wutai, the mist disperses and the clouds withdraw. The sun and moon increase in brilliance, and heaven and earth shine with clarity. At such a time, we pray for the prolongation of the Sage’s life.
"A single phrase that assists the imperial way—how do you speak it? The Golden Wheel governs the three thousand worlds;
the precious reign extends for ten million years."—Master Tianze Lin, Dharma Heir.
Master Dongchan Haichao Yin of Huangmei Cao Factory addressed the assembly: "To speak of Chan is to be deluded by Chan; to speak of the Way is to be obstructed by the Way.
It is better not to bring anything up at all; let us all simply chant 'La-la-li. Now tell me, what tune is this? After a long silence, he said:
"Those who harmonize with it will find it bothersome, and those who listen will grow weary. If you wish to avoid both bother and weariness, each person must [realize it for themselves]."
Seeking an expedient means, he then let out a great "ha-ha" laugh, descended from his seat, and addressed the assembly:

"Those who study the Way must possess the eye that discerns the Dharma and investigate the natural radiance of their own original ground. The monastic community (*saṃgha*) was originally established to refine sages and worthies.
Those who occupy positions therein must uphold the Dharma-gate, receiving the life-force of wisdom from before the Seven Buddhas above and opening it for all future ages below."
"The eyes of all sentient beings! What a great burden this is! One must surely fortify one's bones and strain one's joints;

perhaps by doing so, one may succeed in receiving even half a person [of realization], and then one will have no cause for shame. When Governor Li arrived at the temple, during tea, he asked, "The Sixth Patriarch attained the Dharma while pounding rice here.
Is there still a piece of the 'waist-stone' remaining? The Master replied, "It is here. The Governor said, "Master, this..."

Someone asked, "Has there ever been a monk who dropped this stone? The Master said, "Why drop it? Shoushan said, "Since you are a descendant of those who have left the household life, how can you not be willing to take up this burden?
The Master said, "I am afraid of becoming a patriarch. Shoushan laughed heartily.
The Dharma Heirs of Chan Master Meng’an Ge (two individuals):
Chan Master Kaliṅga-yin of Dajue Temple in the Capital, a native of the Li family of Shenyang. His mother was of the Xu clan;
he was born when she dreamed that a great sun disc fell into her lap. At the age of twenty-four, he went to the monk Pilu Zhenyi at Gaoyang to receive the tonsure and enter the monastic order.
After receiving full ordination, he went to visit Master Meng’an. Meng’an asked, “I shall not ask about Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms;
why did Yuansha say that [Lingyun] had not yet reached the ultimate? The Master said, “Old man, old man! You are caught in a defeat right here. Meng’an said:

This was a question regarding the true nature (*dharmatā*). The Master spread out his sitting mat and said, "For now, let it cover [the truth]. Xuefeng nodded in agreement, whereupon the Master bestowed upon him the robe and whisk and commanded him to lead the assembly.
He went forth to reside at Qianfo, Li'an, and Guizong. Ascending the hall, he said:
"If you step onto the hundred-foot pole, you will naturally attain mastery in all directions. Heaven is clear and earth is tranquil; day is bright and night is dark. To shift—
One cannot alter it by even a hair’s breadth. The pine is straight and the thorn is crooked; the duck is short and the crane is long. One cannot increase or decrease it by even a hair’s breadth.
To those who are versatile and eminent, it is understood without being spoken. Were one to turn their head or shift their gaze even slightly, they would inevitably be burdened by it.
He who took seven steps around the world cannot sit still to this day; he who faced the wall for nine years cannot walk to this day. Now...
The Sun-Horse-Headed One (Sūryāśva-mukha) truncates its horns and hurls this Sahā world to another realm;

the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Abhirati) is shifted here as easily as a strong man extends his arm, like a lion’s stride. If someone were to come forth and ask, "What is it that establishes the fundamental tenets?
What is it that revives the ancestral wind? you must strike them down and only then examine them further. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Buddhas have..."
A single stroke at the crown of the head; before the age of Weiyin, one has already offered one's tribute. Gazing toward West River from atop the Bridge at Baling, the Patriarch has his "final word.
After Loushi, one steps upon it: amidst a mound of dust, a wicker basket is shattered. Picking up a single mote of dust, one blocks the mouth of empty space. It is not that one cannot do so;
one must simply cast off the bellows and manifest a separate divine radiance. Alas! How can this be?
The scholar who uses the lever frequently encounters [the world], while those who carry water in jars rarely meet [such a one]. In this small *sīmān* (private instruction), he exhales once and says:

"The strength of the three furnaces is exhausted; though all things pass through, none return. Truly, he is an iron man. All the people of the great earth have their blades blunted and their tongues tied."
He gathers up his fishing line and returns to his old hermitage, leaving it to those who become dragons to ascend to heaven and those who become snakes to slink into the grass.
Yet, alas for the bamboo switch; within his heart he remains restless and indignant. His eyes, even when not blowing, resemble copper bells;
in the end, he refuses to act as a mere drone. Whether they are similar or not, once he finds one, he immediately calls out, "One of my own kind!"

A Small Sermon for My Fellow Monks: In these five hundred quarters of our monastic dwellings, you may wander at your leisure; in these one hundred and fifty hearths, you may sit in meditation as you please.
Whether you come from the south or the north, all are equally provided for. Those who arrive shall eat their fill and sleep soundly, without the need to shoulder the burden of soliciting alms.
Nor shall those who depart be asked for the cost of ninety days’ worth of food. This is done to avoid being ridiculed by others.
What a petty, vulgar sort! Indeed, there is one who eats the rice of Baolin and voids the excrement of Baolin, yet does not meditate on the Chan of Baolin.
Today, he offers the seven treasures and gold-rope pathways as an offering. Looking left and right, he says: "But you are deceiving me!
In this small assembly, he takes the waters of the four great oceans and places them within his alms bowl, performing his work within a ghost cave.
The Samādhi of Enjoyment: He took up his alms bowl and returned it to the waters of the four great oceans. Even if you had the strength to blow [the wind] away, it could not assist you.
This is the teacherless wisdom, the spontaneous wisdom. It is like a cow’s tail—pointing clearly to each and every part.
Why scatter pearls behind a purple silk curtain? Again, he laughed and said: "It would be better to have one's head cut off before a person of wisdom than to be before a person without wisdom."
A Small Sermon for Newly Ordained Monks: Planting flowers upon a stone; seeking oil from sand. When mental effort reaches its limit, one’s efforts will naturally not be in vain.
When Zhaozhou was a novice, when Deshan saw Longtan, and when Xuansha stubbed his toe—these were moments when mental effort reached its limit.
If you ask about the spiritual practice of these three great elders, all you can do is blow on the ashes.
To repair what is ruined and to mend what is broken—this is the Small Assembly (Xiao Can). When one’s skillful means are insufficient for the moment, all places are level and even.

Among a thousand or ten thousand people, one does not face a single person; the white horse enters the reeds, yet does not turn its back on a single person—the morning sun shines upon the flowering grove.
With hook and snare cast out, ordinary and sage dwell together; how can one avoid being mutually deceived? If you wish to pursue [the truth]...
When the scattered mind is present, scattered thoughts naturally cease. You must know that this old monk does not instruct the assembly from within the realm of clarity.
The blow administered three days prior was taken up by Ke-fu; the blow administered three days later was borne by Pu-hua.
At the very moment of those three days, I did not establish a school or doctrine, nor did I require anyone to pass judgment on it. If you can see through the blowing [of the conch]...
In other established places, the staff of a lowly servant does not strike in vain.
If you merely come and go like this, I shall let everyone off with a crime that cannot be contested. Regarding Master Bufan, everyone says, "People today are far inferior to those of old.
To speak according to reality, it is actually the ancients who were inferior to people today. Look!

Before the ancients had attained realization of the Ground, their sustenance consisted merely of sustaining the vital breath; they ate but once at midday, wearing necklaces of bone and swallowing acorns.
They used round logs as pillows, wore robes of quail feathers patched a hundred times, and removed the warmth from their bedding, never lying down for the rest of their lives.

Once they had attained it, they dwelt by watersides and beneath forest trees, contentedly submerged or seated on wooden boards. As soon as the world came to know their dwelling places, they would again move to thatch huts.

To enter deep mountains—how foolish were the ancients! People today, before they have even attained anything, fear only that their food will not fill their mouths or their clothing will not be abundant.
They practice "face-saving" Chan; if things do not go as they wish, they wave their sleeves and depart.
This is truly like those who seek after others: once they have gained even a little, they only regret that people do not know of it, and they flaunt it everywhere.
With eyes that overlook the four seas, you vainly revile the ancients. How wise you are today! Yet at the very end, when it matters most, you find nothing of value;
you grieve in secret, but it is too late for regret. Great Master, it is better to be an ancient of the present than to be a contemporary of the ancients.
[This was] shown to the attendant Bingjie. Buddha after Buddha transmitted and received the Dharma, passing the Dharma from patriarch to patriarch.
It is traditionally said that "to seal mind with mind," yet nowadays one speaks only of the gate and courtyard.

Having not yet entered the monastery, one gazes upon Jingzhou like a tiger, devising all manner of schemes and employing power and force until one succeeds in entering. This is like a venomous snake clinging to its den, clawing and tearing at it day after day, only ceasing when death arrives.
Matters even reach the point of gathering lawsuits and filing petitions, leaving no means untried. Observe but this: the Hundred [Cases].

From Baizhang, Mazu, Huangbo, Linji, and Xinghua, down to Longchi Huanchan, Shitou, Yaoshan, Yunyan, Dongshan, and Yunju, and even down to Xiaoshan Shuzhu—did you not all regard the protection of the ancestral temple as your very eyes?

Why then do you treat it with such contempt, as if it were worn-out sandals? From thousands of miles away, you show not the slightest concern. As for this mountain monk’s retirement from the Thousand Buddhas Hall...
He handed over the temple to its former resident and departed with his staff. Retiring from Bailing Monastery, he was solitary and austere, possessing only a single bowl.
This was because the monastery was the permanent dwelling of dragons and devas; how could you possibly apply your mind or exert your strength there?

If an attendant wishes to be a true descendant of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, it is sufficient simply to maintain the Dharma within the mind. In his later years, the Master dwelt among mountains and slept by waters, having no fixed abode.

He remained in meditative stillness. Petitions for his appointment arrived from all four directions, which he declined in their entirety. On the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the fourth year of the Yongzheng era, he passed away.
He was posthumously honored with the title Chan Master Yuantong Miaozhi. The imperial treasury granted funds to construct a stupa for him at Dajue Temple on Mount Xishan.
His *Recorded Sayings in Ten Assemblies* and the *Zongjian Faling* (Forest of the Dharma Mirror) were circulated throughout the world.
Chan Master Wanshou Diaomeiding of Kyoto was the son of the Feng family of Chu and Huang.
At the age of eight, he received the tonsure under Master Shi at Huiyuan Temple and received full ordination at Wanshan. Later, he went to attend upon Master Meng’an.

When the Master asked about the koan of the Yellow Crane Tower, the student was about to respond when Meng’an struck him on the head with his staff, saying, "Break down the Yellow Crane Tower! At that moment, the student attained liberation.
He then presented a verse, saying: "The Yellow Crane Tower is broken by the wind; the three thousand Buddhas are all buried alive. Startled, the Venerable Peak stands upright;
on the Qiantang River, wind and thunder roar. The Abbot (An) nodded in approval. Later, after paying homage at Wutai Shan and returning to the capital, he ascended White Pagoda Mountain.
Suddenly, seeing the sunlight within the clouds, he attained great mastery (*mahāsvatantra*). He left [seclusion] to reside at Qing Shan and manage its affairs.
Small-scale Sermon at the Wan-shou Temple in An-bai-lin. Nanquan could not lift it up; Yunyan could not press it down.
From morning until evening, they were all in harmony and accord. But as for this "cannot lift up" and "cannot press down"—tell me, what is it?
The mirror is the bane of the ugly woman; wisdom is the affliction of the fool. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, he held morning assembly:

"For six years he froze his mouth until it was completely numb; when his skills were exhausted and his strength spent, what could he have planned? He plucked out a single star from the tip of a hair."

Half-adorned face, half-concealing shame; right now, a single sheet of snow is spread across the vast sky. Above and below, all-penetrating clarity is one and the same; yet you still wish to open your eyes and seek some other view. I dare guarantee that you will find it on a donkey-year. Early Assembly: Entering the water without disturbing the waves, entering the forest without stirring the grass—why is it that when you step on the south, the north shakes? The duties of maintaining the monastery are manifold. Thus it is said: "All day long one goes east and west, yet not a single step has been moved beneath one's heels.
Throughout the morning one speaks of the ancients and the present, yet upon the tip of the tongue there is not even a trace of joy. It is just like the warbling of spring birds.
The spring breeze is harmonious and pleasant. Does this mean you have attained the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? "The Buddhas of the three ages do not know it exists;

the black oxen and white cows, however, do know it exists. Evening Assembly: When the World-Honored One beheld the morning star at midnight, Kāśyapa smiled at the flower before the assembly of humans and devas.
When the Sixth Patriarch heard the sound of the sutras from next door—these three fellows saw with their own eyes.

"The eyes see—this is real. The ears hear—this is false. The mouth is the gate of calamity. You people, having distanced yourselves from these three places, how will you then realize and certify with Wanshou?
Three dots like flowing water; the curve is like a sickle for cutting reeds. Evening Sermon:
"In the long summer, while refining the rhythms of the Vinaya, one still fears the meditation seat might shake. To bestow blows and shouts before the wind leads to the Dharma..."
The grass before the hall is a fathom deep. You all, sweep it clean and come up! "A flushed face is not as good as straightforward speech.

Before the mountain gate, behind the meditation hall, beneath the green canopies of ancient pines, amidst the secluded seclusion of stone grottoes—shake off the stench from your entire being and bring forth the True Person of No Rank.
Like observing fish scales in a pond, ripples arise upon the surface of the waves; follow along.
The flow is wondrous. Without joy and without anger, for years I have been indolent and have nothing more to say. Laughing, he points toward the pavilions where the fragrant breeze blows.

When the Master reached his seventieth year, he requested to retire from his post due to illness and went to the Candana (Flower Sandalwood) Hermitage to recuperate in peace. One day, he addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have long been steering this bottomless boat across the sea, with a spirit’s head and a demon’s face. Now, I shall turn back my mother-born nose."
He left it entirely to others in all directions to transmit his teachings as they pleased. He passed away while sitting upright; his entire body was enshrined in a stupa at Qing Shan.

Chan Master Xi (Furi) of Lian'an, Hangzhou, a successor of Chan Master Yuejian Che, was a native of the Chen family in Jiangxi. He entered the monastic order under the senior practitioner Yuming. He shaved his head...

Having received full ordination, he later went to attend upon Master Yuejian, who appointed him as the recorder (*jilu*). After a long time, he finally received the seal of approval (*yinke*) during a small assembly (*xiaocan*).

The *chīwen* (the dragon-head ornament on the roof) exercised great supernatural power (*mahā-abhijñā*), biting through the ridgepole of the Buddha Hall; the *xījī* (a tiny insect) performed a great Buddhist service (*buddhakārya*).
He overturned the storehouse and the vinegar jars, joined his palms, and said: "For this reason, I now take refuge in and pay homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
As for saying that he cultivated and realized [enlightenment] over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas—that is something I would not dare to claim.
I, Mingxi, have created deluded karma and should receive an evil retribution; I shall enter the Avīci Hell."
The prison has been left behind. But tell me, do you still find enjoyment within it? [He waves the whisk. "The wind is serene and vast; my heart is at ease.
Shortly, we shall sit together with you all in the Pavilion atop the Pines, brew the spring water of Dharma-rain, and gaze upon the spring colors of Luoyang.
Each of you shall draw lots for a rhyme and compose a poem. If there is no brush to capture the essence and compete for excellence, I fear the flowers themselves will laugh in return.
People, here is a small instruction. For a long time the hall of Yaoyao has not been ascended; for a long time the drum of Yanguan has remained unstruck.
Alas, Yunmen’s fan has suddenly gone wild; it leaps up to the thirty-third heaven, beating a black wind and pouring down torrential rain.
Right within those raindrops, he rolls the Great Dharma Wheel and expounds the essentials of the Great Dharma—not merely with a gentle drizzle...
Drip-drip. Clang-clang. Drop-drop. The patterns on his body shine brightly; the meaning of the phrases is radiant.
Furthermore, surging and rushing, swirling and eddying, it gushes forth like a vast flood, pouring over mountains and rivers, continuing without ceasing from dawn until dusk.
Then, he raised his whisk and said: "The whisk in Mingxi’s hand cannot restrain its impatience; it wishes to intervene and snatch the market share. But let us proceed with these ten [cases]."
Before the Hall, he entered the Samādhi of the Immovable Ground; sweeping away the clouds and leaves, the countenance of the numinous heavens was revealed.

Relying solely on the young maiden, he drove the sun’s chariot to sway the face of the mountain, depending only upon Xiyi. At dawn, for the communal labor, they hauled out the great boulder before the mountain with a laugh.
Small Sermon: One person dwells atop the peak of Mount Sumeru, yet remains at the bottom of the sea performing calculations.
"Sha! One person dwells at the edge of the diamond waters, yet they are floating a raft upon the Milky Way.

Another person dwells within half of empty space, yet they are planting flowers before the eyes of the Śūnyatā-deva. If these three people were to arrive at Lian-an, I would give them thirty blows of the staff each.
Why? Because 'having completely clipped the bamboos before the frost, one does not transform into a dragon when facing the stream.'"—Small Session Sermon.

A single sheet of autumn cloud, thin as a cicada’s wing, The high wind blows it flat against a thousand-fathom cliff. Wishing to polish hard jade to record this faint chant, I send it to Li Babo at the ends of the earth.

Babo, Babo, do you know or not? At this time of dewy cool, I wander fallen at the world’s edge. Go back, go back—you must hurry while there is still time; Do not wait for the sound of the mortar to urge you on.

The severe frost has struck down the autumn grasses. —Master [Xuefeng] (Note: This is a poetic composition by Xuefeng Yicun, likely intended for his disciple Li Babo. The final line "The severe frost has struck down the autumn grasses" is traditionally attributed to Xuefeng himself as a concluding admonition.)
On the seventeenth day of the eighth month in the Ren-shen year of the Qianlong era, he passed away. His secular age was seventy, and his monastic seniority was fifty-one.
His stupa was erected on the southern slope of Lotus Peak.
Chan Master Lingjiu Cheng of Chongfu Monastery in Hangzhou was a successor of Chan Master Nangu Ying.
He was the son of the Xie family from Ninghai, Taizhou. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination.
Later, he went to attend upon Master Nangu, who asked him: "How can you turn over the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?"
[The Master] said, "To what do you refer when you speak of 'oneself'? Gu said, "I give you thirty blows!
Gu then asked, "How does one turn oneself back into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? The Master said, "With what do you refer when you speak of 'oneself'?
Gu said, "I give you thirty blows! The Master performed a dance and departed. He ascended the hall and said: "The World-Honored One..."
In the stage of causal practice, he cast off his physical body to seek a half-verse. I, this mountain monk, possess a complete verse;
if someone were to cast off half their body, I would immediately give it to them. Suppose someone were to say, "I have no eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, or mind—what is there to cast off?
